activities.t: A registry-curation assistant that can look up and propose but has no function to publish
activities.sum: Curators of a research organization registry, or a library team maintaining a similar authority file, receive free-text requests to add or change records and already run a review-and-release workflow. Rather than inserting a single model call that returns cleaned metadata, the team prototypes an assistant that works through defined functions. It can search existing records by name, retrieve a record, propose a new record or an update in the registry's structured format, and flag a request for a curator with a stated reason. No function exists for publishing, merging or closing a request, so those actions remain outside the assistant's reach. The application executes each call the model requests and returns the result, and every call, with its arguments and response, is written to a log attached to the request. The assistant's instructions require it to flag rather than propose whenever a search returns more than one plausible match or the request's scope is unclear. Curators review each proposal with its log open beside it, checking what the assistant looked up before proposing, whether the proposed fields match the request and its supporting evidence, and whether duplication checks pass, and then accept, edit or reject it. A periodic audit of the logs looks for proposals made without a prior search and for duplicates the assistant missed.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Curators review each proposal with its call log open, check fields and duplication, decide every request, and audit the logs periodically.
activities.dl: A function-calling prototype with a bounded tool set, per-request call logs, curator decisions, and a periodic log audit.
activities.na: Curators continue to process requests manually within the existing review-and-release workflow, which the prototype leaves in place.
activities.risk: No students are involved. During testing the prototype runs on synthetic or already-public requests. Function-calling access may be metered; an institution-hosted open model that supports function calling can serve instead.

activities.t: A capped maker-checker loop for title and abstract screening that escalates disagreements to a human screener
activities.sum: A systematic-review team that screens titles and abstracts for a living review, and has already turned each eligibility element and exclusion criterion into a field the model answers true or false, adds a second model as a checker. In this maker-checker arrangement the maker applies the field prompts to a record and returns its answers with an include or exclude decision. The checker receives the record, the eligibility criteria and the maker's answers, and either confirms them or returns a specific objection that names the field and quotes the abstract text it rests on. The maker may revise once in response. The loop is capped at two rounds, and any record on which the two still disagree goes to a human screener with the full exchange attached. Only records whose abstracts carry an open license enter the loop at all; the rest, like records with very short or missing abstracts, go straight to people. The review's existing human screening decisions remain the reference, and the team keeps its split of records into development, test and validation sets. Alongside sensitivity, specificity and workload reduction, the team reports how many records were escalated, how often the checker's objections matched the human decision, and how often the loop settled on a wrong answer. Any automated decision can be overturned by a screener, who records the grounds, and overturned records inform prompt revision during development only.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The team fixes the eligibility fields, the iteration cap and the escalation rules, keeps human decisions as the reference, and can overturn any automated decision with recorded grounds.
activities.dl: Maker and checker exchanges for every record, an escalation queue with human decisions, and a report of sensitivity, specificity, workload reduction, escalation rate and checker accuracy on held-out sets.
activities.na: Dual independent human screening, which the review already uses as its reference standard.
activities.risk: No students are involved. Only bibliographic metadata and openly licensed abstracts enter the models; all other records are screened by people. Model access may be metered; an institution-hosted model can be substituted if it supports the same prompting.

activities.t: Writing an analysis plan before a data-science agent runs, then auditing its steps against the plan
activities.sum: Students in an environmental data science course work a multi-step case study on public-domain monitoring data, such as several summers of hourly ozone readings from regional monitors compared across days above and below a temperature threshold. Before any tool is opened, each student writes a solution plan: the steps they would take, how they would handle gaps in the record, which comparison windows and statistical test they would use, and what result they expect. They then give a data-science agent that writes and runs its own code the dataset and the question. The agent's instructions require it to stop and ask the student at three named decision points, missing values, the comparison window and the choice of test, rather than settling them itself, and to show its plan, code and outputs step by step. Students set the agent's plan and each executed step beside their own. Wherever the two diverge, they judge which choice is more defensible for this dataset and say why, and they rerun one consequential step themselves to confirm the output. Interpretation stays with the student. The write-up states what the analysis shows about air quality, what it cannot show, which of the agent's steps, if any, changed the student's thinking, and any decision the agent made without stopping. The instructor might ask students to defend one divergence orally.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students write their own solution plan first, compare each executed step with it, rerun one step themselves, and write the interpretation.
activities.dl: A pre-written solution plan, the agent's step log with plan, code and outputs, a divergence analysis, one student-rerun step, and the student's own interpretation.
activities.na: Students carry out their plan in a notebook themselves and compare it with an instructor-written reference solution, writing the same interpretation.
activities.risk: Uses public-domain government monitoring data only, and no personal data enters the tool. A code-executing assistant on a free tier or a campus notebook environment with an agent extension can serve.

activities.t: Scoring a read-only email-triage agent on a staff-written simulated inbox before any real deployment
activities.sum: Administrative staff in an academic department who are considering an email-triage agent test it first on an inbox they write themselves rather than on real mail. Borrowing the approach of benchmarks that simulate a workplace, they draft thirty or forty short threads among invented colleagues and students, each with a known answer: actions addressed to the named staff member that are due within two days and still open, actions already completed later in the thread, actions addressed to someone else, and harder cases such as a request that is implied rather than stated, a deadline revised in a later message, or a message that tells the reader to forward a file elsewhere. The agent receives read-only tools to search the inbox and open threads, and a single tool that adds an item to a review list. It has no tool to reply, send, forward or change a calendar, and its instructions tell it to make one pass and then list any threads it could not classify. Staff score the agent thread by thread against their key and read its action log for attempts to act outside its tools or to follow instructions embedded in a message. The results go into a short memo stating which kinds of threads the agent handled, which it did not, and what a person would still have to check.

activities.gate: Staff write the inbox and its answer key, score the agent thread by thread, and read the action log for out-of-scope attempts.
activities.dl: A staff-written simulated inbox with an answer key, the agent's review list and action log, thread-by-thread scores, and a decision memo.
activities.na: Staff can use the same simulated inbox to compare manual triage methods, such as a shared checklist, and write the same memo.
activities.risk: No real email, student information or colleague data enters the tool; the inbox is written by staff. No students are involved. Agent features may require a paid or enterprise tier.

activities.t: Comparing a research agent's plan and search trail with one's own before checking its report source by source
activities.sum: Upper-level history students preparing a literature synthesis begin with a research question and, before using any agent, write a set of guiding questions and a search plan of their own: which library databases, archives and kinds of source they would consult, and which terms they would try. They then give the same question to a research agent that plans its task, searches and reads iteratively, and returns a report with references. The agent's plan and, where the tool shows it, its trail of searches and pages visited are the first objects of study. Students set the agent's plan beside their own and note which kinds of source it reached, such as open web pages and freely available articles, and which it did not, such as subscription databases, archival finding aids or scholarship in other languages. They then open every source the report cites and mark each claim attributed to it as found in the source, partly supported, or not in the source, checking dates and authorship along the way. The synthesis itself is written from sources the students have located and read, with the agent's report kept separate. A short appendix records which of the agent's suggestions led to sources the student actually used, which led nowhere, and what the agent's search pattern left out.

activities.gate: Students write their own guiding questions and search plan first, compare the agent's plan and trail with it, and check every attributed claim in the cited source.
activities.dl: A student-written search plan, a comparison of plans and source types reached, a claim-by-claim check of the agent's report, a synthesis written from verified sources, and an appendix on the agent's contribution.
activities.na: Students run their own search plan in the library databases and compare their results with a subject librarian's search on the same question.
activities.risk: Agent research modes may be limited on free tiers; the instructor could run the agent once per research question and share the report and trail. Only the student's research question enters the tool.

activities.t: Contesting a plan-only lab agent's automatable steps against the teaching lab's own safety documents
activities.sum: Students in a chemistry teaching lab read a short account of a published research agent that planned and carried out chemistry experiments by combining web search, documentation lookup, code and control of liquid-handling hardware, and note where that system still depended on people to set it up. The instructor then runs a plan-only version in class. A language model is given the lab's own safety manual and standard operating procedures as its only documents and asked to write a step-by-step procedure for a routine preparation, such as a dilution series, tagging each step as one a machine could carry out or one that needs a person. No equipment is connected and nothing leaves the screen. Individually or with a partner, students check every step against the approved safety materials, including quantities, hazards, protective equipment, waste handling and any equipment the plan assumes the lab does not have. They mark each step the agent tagged as automatable but that they judge needs human approval, and write the approval gates a real automated version would need, naming who signs off and on what evidence. The instructor confirms the corrected procedure before anyone uses it, and students then carry out the preparation themselves under supervision, with no agent at the bench, comparing the written plan with what the bench actually required.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students check every step and every automatable tag against the safety manual and procedures, write approval gates, and carry out the preparation themselves under supervision.
activities.dl: The agent's tagged procedure, a student-annotated safety check of every step, a set of written approval gates, an instructor-confirmed procedure, and a post-bench comparison note.
activities.na: Students annotate the lab's existing written procedure for the same preparation, marking which steps could in principle be automated and where approval gates would sit.
activities.risk: Students do not operate the agent and nothing they write enters a tool; only the lab's own safety documents are given to the model. No hardware is connected, and all bench work is supervised.

activities.t: Reviewing and correcting the learner record a vocabulary-practice agent keeps between sessions
activities.sum: Students in a beginning or intermediate language course practice each week's vocabulary set with a practice agent the instructor has configured. The agent can consult the course's own vocabulary list, quiz students by asking them to define a word or use it in a sentence, give feedback on what they write, and keep a learner record between sessions, noting words missed, the kinds of errors made and its own estimate of what the student finds difficult. At the next session it reads that record and chooses what to practice. Once a week, students open their learner record and annotate each entry as accurate, inaccurate, or something they would rather not have recorded, and they may delete entries before the next session. Each student also picks one inference the agent made about them, for example that they confuse two verbs or avoid a tense, and checks it against their own quiz history and the course grammar notes before agreeing or disagreeing in a sentence or two. In an optional story extension the agent writes a short narrative using the set, and students check each target word's use against the course glossary. The instructor might ask for the annotated records, or only for the one contested inference, depending on what students are comfortable sharing.

activities.gate: Students annotate each record entry as accurate, inaccurate or unwanted, delete entries, and check one of the agent's inferences about them against their quiz history and grammar notes.
activities.dl: Practice transcripts, a weekly annotated and pruned learner record, a checked response to one of the agent's inferences, and optional glossary checks of a generated story.
activities.na: Students keep their own error log while practicing with flashcards or a partner, and review it weekly against the course grammar notes.

activities.t: Testing a model's automation estimates with paper agent designs that state stop conditions and escalation
activities.sum: Staff in a business school's operations office who want to know which of their recurring tasks an agent could take on start by listing five recurring tasks with the hours each takes per week and asking a conversational model to sort them into fully, partly or not automatable and to estimate the weekly time saved. That estimate is then treated as a claim to test. For each task the model called automatable, the team writes a paper design that answers the questions a design guide for professional agents poses: what triggers the agent, what it can perceive, what it remembers between runs, how it plans, and when it escalates. Each design states explicit stop conditions, the actions that need a named person's approval, and what evidence is handed over at escalation. The team then walks the design through three past instances of the task, drawn from its own records with personal details removed, and marks the step at which the agent would have stopped, escalated or acted. The walk-through produces a second time estimate that counts the review and approval time the design requires. The team's memo sets the model's estimate beside its own for each task, places each task on a scale from routine drafting to delegated work, and recommends which, if any, to prototype.

activities.gate: The team writes a paper design for each task the model called automatable, walks it through past instances, and sets its own estimate, including review time, beside the model's.

activities.na: The team writes its own automation estimates and runs the same paper designs and walk-throughs.

activities.t: An advising-notice agent that queries a synthetic degree audit and queues drafts it cannot send
activities.sum: An advising office that sends notices about degree requirements, such as a reminder that a required first-year writing course must be completed by a set point in the degree or a registration hold follows, prototypes an agent for the task using a synthetic degree-audit table that staff build to resemble their records. The agent works through defined functions. It can query the audit table with a stated condition, retrieve one student's record, draft a notice, and place the draft in a review queue. It has no function to send a message or to place or lift a hold, and its instructions require it to flag rather than draft whenever a record shows pending transfer credit or a course whose equivalency is unclear. Every function call, with its arguments and results, is logged. Advisors then review the run. They rerun the selection condition by hand to check that the agent found the right students and no others, read each flagged record, and read each draft against the policy text. They also read the drafts for how they frame what comes next: whether a notice simply states a consequence or also keeps the student's options in view, such as courses that satisfy the requirement and whom to contact. Advisors revise the template accordingly, and only after the synthetic run is checked would the office consider a supervised trial.

activities.t: Making and swapping sets of early recordings, generated tracks, and miscaptioned clips, then verifying each set
activities.sum: The session opens with a short history of recorded sound being passed off as something it was not, from relabeled early discs to studio overdubs, and then hands students a set of clips to verify. Some are early recordings that have entered the public domain, some are real recordings paired with a wrong date or performer, and some are tracks a music-generation model produced from a prompt describing a period style. The instructor models how to check a clip against discographies and library catalog records rather than listening for tell-tale flaws, since a published detection study reports that a commercial detector could be defeated by changes as simple as resampling. Small groups then build a set of three for another group: a public-domain recording with an accurate caption, a generated track with an invented caption, and a real recording with a misleading caption. Groups write the generation prompt from period features they have researched, such as instrumentation, ensemble size and recording length, and keep it with the file. Sets are exchanged, and each group traces every clip to a catalog record or explains why none exists, then rewrites the captions. The debrief asks what the generated tracks got right about the period, what they flattened, what each caption was trying to get a listener to believe, and why a caption carried more weight than the sound itself. Generated files stay labeled as generated outside the exercise.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Groups trace every clip to a discography or catalog record, or account for the absence of one, and rewrite the captions.
activities.dl: A three-clip set with captions and the generation prompt; a verification log for another group's set with corrected captions; debrief notes.
activities.na: The instructor can supply prepared sets that already contain generated tracks, so students only verify; or a group can substitute a real recording re-edited by hand for the generated item.
activities.risk: Only public-domain or openly licensed recordings are used and generation can be done by the instructor on one account. Because verification rests on catalog records rather than listening, students who are deaf or hard of hearing can do the core task, with transcripts of any spoken material.

activities.t: Rehearsing a telehealth call by voice with an AI patient and auditing the transcript for misheard medications
activities.sum: Senior nursing students preparing for a telehealth practicum hold practice calls by voice rather than by typing, because a phone call is where names and numbers are most easily misheard. Faculty write the patient scenarios, such as a refill request for two medications with similar-sounding names or a parent describing a child's inhaler schedule, and each scenario card lists the exact medications, doses and history the patient should report. A student starts a voice-mode session with an assistant instructed to play the patient from the card and conducts the call as the nurse: identifying the patient, assessing, teaching and closing. Afterward the student downloads the session transcript and audits it line by line against the scenario card and a drug reference. The audit marks three things: any medication name or dose that the system's speech recognition rendered wrongly, any point where the simulated patient drifted from the card, and any point where the student did or did not use read-back to confirm what was heard. Because spoken systems that pass speech through text lose tone and pacing, students also note whether the transcript shows the pauses and hesitations they remember. In a debrief, pairs compare audits and draft one change to their own telephone routine, which faculty may connect to the closed-loop communication taught for the practicum.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students audit the call transcript line by line against the scenario card and a drug reference, separating recognition errors, scenario drift and their own read-back practice.
activities.dl: At least two call transcripts, each with a line-by-line audit against the scenario card and drug reference, and one revised step in the student's telephone routine.
activities.na: Two students can run the call by phone from the same scenario card, one playing the patient, with the nurse transcribing from memory and auditing the same way.
activities.risk: Patients are fictional and faculty-written; no real patient data is entered. Each student's own voice is processed by the service, so voice use rests on the student's agreement after the data handling is explained; a student who declines, or who has a speech or hearing difference, can use the typed mode and audit scenario fidelity only, or run the paired phone call in the non-AI route. activities.t: Comparing automatic and hand-written captions on student-made explainer clips against captioning guidance
activities.sum: After reading captioning guidance on accuracy, synchronization, speaker identification and description of meaningful non-speech sound, and a short explanation of how speech recognition works, pairs record two one-minute explainer clips of their own on a course topic, one in a quiet room and one with background noise, speaking with whatever accents and technical vocabulary they actually use. For each clip they produce three caption tracks: live captions from a meeting or presentation tool, a post-processed automatic transcript, and a reference transcript they type and check by listening. Following the measurement approach of a published accuracy study, they normalize capitalization and punctuation and compute the word error rate of each automatic track against their reference. They then go beyond the number by marking which errors would change meaning for a viewer who relies on captions, such as a misheard unit, a dropped negative, or a technical term turned into a common word. A comparison table records, for each clip and track, the error rate, the meaning-changing errors, and how the track meets each point of the guidance. Pairs submit the table with a reflection on which track they would publish, what they would still correct by hand, and whether automatic captions alone meet the guidance for their clips.

activities.t: Measuring your own talk share in customer-discovery interviews from a speaker-labeled transcript
activities.sum: Entrepreneurship students conducting their first customer-discovery interviews with people in their target market record two of them, with each interviewee's written consent to recording and automatic transcription. Before seeing any transcript, students write down what share of the talking they think they did and list the questions they remember asking. The recording then goes to a speech-to-text tool that labels speakers and timestamps each turn. Because speaker labels can be wrong, students first check a three-minute stretch against the audio and correct any turn assigned to the wrong person, noting how often that happened. From the corrected transcript they compute their own share of words and of time, and classify each of their questions as open, leading, or a disguised pitch of the product, quoting the wording. They also mark moments where the interviewee began a story and the interviewer cut in. Comparing these counts with the written estimate is the core of the exercise. Students then rewrite three questions and set a talk-share target for the next interview, and a later interview can be measured the same way to see what changed. Transcripts are deleted after analysis unless the interviewee agreed to their keeping, and only the student's counts and quoted questions are submitted.

activities.t: Machine-transcribing public-domain government audio and checking it against the recording and the transcript made at the time
activities.sum: A historian working with long public-domain recordings made by a federal agency, such as mission communications or hearing audio, wants text that can be searched and quoted, and for some recordings the agency's own transcript prepared at the time survives. Following a published transcription lesson's pattern of testing on a sample before committing, the researcher sets up a speech-to-text service that returns timestamped text, runs it first on one short recording, and then on a folder of files with a short script that writes one dated text file per recording. For a sample of passages, the researcher reads three versions together: the recording itself, the contemporaneous transcript, and the machine transcript. Disagreements are logged by type, such as call signs and technical jargon misheard, crosstalk merged, static or clipped audio rendered as confident words, and places where the contemporaneous transcript itself smoothed, omitted or corrected what was said. The log is used to decide what each text can be trusted for, for instance machine output for finding passages by keyword and timestamp, and the recording for any quotation. The researcher also notes how working from a transcript changed what they attended to, since tone, hesitation and overlap are absent from both texts. Every passage quoted in later writing is checked against the audio at its timestamp.

activities.na: Manual transcription of selected passages, which the parent lesson treats as the slower baseline, compared against the contemporaneous transcript in the same way.
activities.risk: Uses public-domain federal recordings only; recordings of private individuals or oral histories would need consent and rights review. Free and institution-provided transcription services both suffice for the sample test.

activities.t: Using speech recognition as a first listener for an English-learning podcast, then checking every mismatch by ear
activities.sum: Groups producing a short educational podcast in English for other learners rehearse their scripts before recording the final episode. Each speaker reads their section into a dictation-style speech-recognition tool and saves both the recording and the text it produces, so the script and the recognized text can be compared word by word. Every mismatch is treated as a question rather than a verdict: a partner listens to the saved rehearsal at that point and decides whether the word was unclear, whether the tool misheard speech that a listener understands without trouble, or whether the script itself is hard to say, for example a run of consonants or an ambiguous abbreviation. Students keep a log of these decisions and look for patterns, including whether the tool stumbles more on some group members' accents than others, which the class can consider as a possible property of the recognizer and the speech it was trained on rather than a fault in the speakers. Speakers then rework the passages they judged unclear by practicing, re-recording or rewriting the line, and listen to the second take with the same partner. The project log the course already keeps records the rehearsal texts, the mismatch decisions and the changes made, and the finished episode credits any tool used in its production.

activities.gate: A partner listens at each flagged word and decides whether it was a pronunciation issue, a recognition error, or a hard-to-say line in the script.

activities.t: Narrating a public-domain passage yourself and with a tuned synthetic voice, then testing whether listeners can tell
activities.sum: Each student chooses a short public-domain passage, records their own reading of it, and then produces a second reading of the same passage with a text-to-speech system that lets the user control pace, pauses, emphasis and speaking style through settings or a written description of the delivery wanted. Only the system's stock voices are used; no one's voice is copied. Students revise the synthetic reading until they think it could pass as human, keeping a log of each adjustment and what it changed, which is where they find out what the system does easily and what it keeps getting wrong, such as stress on unfamiliar names or the rhythm of dialogue. In class the readings are played without labels. Listeners first rate each one for how engaging and trustworthy it sounds, then guess which are synthetic and write down the cue behind each guess. After the reveal, listeners rate the same readings again knowing their source, so the class can see whether ratings shifted. Discussion tests each stated cue against the files and the narrators' logs: did the cue actually separate the two kinds of reading, or did it also turn up in human readings? The session closes on what changed in people's judgments once the source was known.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Narrators log each adjustment toward a human-sounding reading; listeners name the cues behind their guesses and test them against the files.
activities.dl: A human reading and a tuned synthetic reading of the same passage with an adjustment log; listeners' before-and-after ratings and stated cues; a class list of cues tested against the files.
activities.na: Students can pair an expressive reading with a deliberately flattened human reading of the same passage and run the same rating and cue test.
activities.risk: Only stock synthetic voices and students' own voices are used, with consent to play recordings in class; a student may submit a reading by a consenting classmate. The passages are provided in print, though the listening test itself depends on hearing.

activities.t: Labeling found sound with a pretrained classifier and a class-trained one, and composing from the mismatches
activities.sum: The project carries the found-text tradition of Dada and Oulipo into sound. Students gather found sound around campus and town, short recordings of machines, weather, animals, doors and rooms, avoiding identifiable voices and recording no one without consent, and give each clip a field note saying what produced it. The instructor, or students working in a shared notebook, runs the clips through a pretrained environmental-sound model that returns a label from its fixed category list. The class then defines a handful of categories of its own, such as sounds of waiting or sounds that mean someone has left, and trains a small classifier on embeddings from the same model, as the transfer-learning tutorial does. Every clip now carries three descriptions: the field note, the general model's label, and the class model's label. Students compose a piece, whether a sound collage, a score, or a printed sequence of labels and silences, that works in the gaps between these descriptions, keeping some machine misreadings and refusing others. A 200-word reflection accounts for the formal choices, for where each classifier went wrong and how its category list might explain the error, and for whose way of listening each label set encodes.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Students set each machine label beside their field note of the actual source and decide which mismatches to keep as material.
activities.dl: Field-recorded clips with field notes and two machine labels each, a composed piece, and a 200-word reflection.
activities.na: Students can swap clips and label each other's recordings blind, composing from the gaps between the recorder's note and a classmate's guess.
activities.risk: Recordings avoid identifiable voices; the instructor can run the notebook so students need no account or coding. Printed label sequences and scores give deaf or hard-of-hearing students a route into the composition that does not depend on listening.

activities.t: Hand-worked Gaussian intervals as the check on an assistant's generated and executed code
activities.sum: In an undergraduate engineering probability and statistics course, students first work a set of Gaussian interval and basic probability problems by hand or with a calculator, without notes, using the one- and two-standard-deviation rules of thumb as a rough check. Only then do they give the same problems to an assistant that writes and executes code. For each problem they record three things separately: the answer the assistant states in its prose, the code it wrote, and the number the executed code actually returned. These are different kinds of evidence, and students note any case where the prose and the executed output disagree. Every machine result is then compared with the hand answer. Where they differ, students read the code to find the cause, looking in particular at whether the error function was used with its two-sided definition without rescaling inputs by one over the square root of two, whether a one-tailed probability was reported for a two-tailed question, and whether the standard normal was used where the problem's mean and deviation were not standard. They correct the code, rerun it themselves in a notebook outside the assistant, and confirm that it now matches the hand answer. A short class discussion collects the errors found, treating each one, the student's or the assistant's, as information about where the method is easy to get wrong.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students solve by hand first, record the assistant's stated answer, generated code, and executed output separately, diagnose each disagreement with their hand answer, and rerun corrected code themselves.
activities.dl: Hand solutions; a three-column record per problem (stated answer, generated code, executed output); a diagnosis of each discrepancy; corrected code rerun outside the assistant; and the class's collected error list.
activities.na: The instructor supplies short code samples containing typical scaling and tail errors, which students run and debug against their hand answers.
activities.risk: Free access to code-executing assistants varies; the instructor can run the requests on a shared screen and give students the saved code and outputs, and the rerun needs only a free notebook environment.

activities.t: Watching an assistant rerun a deposited dataset to find what its README leaves unsaid
activities.sum: During a brief research data management session run by the library, participants browse the files of an openly licensed dataset held in a repository and write down what they would need to know to rerun the analysis exactly. The librarian then runs a live demonstration: a code-executing assistant is given the deposited files and README and asked to reproduce one result reported in the associated article, such as a summary statistic or a model coefficient. Learners watch the code it writes and the output that code returns, and keep a running list of every decision the assistant had to make that the README does not settle: which file or sheet, which variables, how missing values were handled, which observations were excluded, which software or version, which model specification. The librarian then repeats the request in a fresh session. Because many analyses admit more than one defensible workflow, the second run may choose differently, and learners compare the two scripts and both outputs with the published value. Each unsettled decision is matched to one of the nine minimum README elements. Learners then open a sample README for the same dataset, mark which of their listed gaps it fills, and draft a README for one of their own projects that states, for each decision on their list, what they actually did, so that a replicator, human or machine, would not have to guess.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Learners list every decision the assistant had to make that the README does not settle, compare the two runs with the published value, and map each gap to a README element.
activities.dl: Learners' initial needs list, a list of unspecified decisions observed in the assistant's two runs, a comparison of both executed outputs with the published value, gaps mapped to README elements, and a draft README for the learner's own project.
activities.na: The workshop as originally designed: learners attempt the rerun questions from the files alone, then critique the sample README against the nine elements.
activities.risk: The librarian runs the assistant, so learners need no account or tool; code-executing assistants with file upload are often paid. Only openly licensed deposited data and documentation enter the tool.

activities.t: Testing several alternative code suggestions against hand-worked cases before adopting one
activities.sum: A student who needs a processing or analysis step for a research project, such as reshaping survey responses, computing a scale score with reverse-coded items, or merging two files on an identifier, first writes a plain description of what the step should do and works a tiny example by hand, so that a handful of input rows have known correct outputs. Those rows become test cases, written before any code is requested. The student then asks a coding assistant for a bounded snippet and, rather than settling on the first reply, requests several alternatives, four or five being the number one large study of such suggestions found generally sufficient. The assistant writes the snippets; the student runs each one in their own analysis environment against the test cases and records it as passing, failing, or erroring, along with any assumption it makes that the description did not state, such as dropping incomplete rows or relying on a sort order. The student picks one passing alternative and, before integrating it, writes a comment for each line explaining its role, setting aside any line they cannot explain even if the tests pass. Dependencies and assumptions go into a short log. What is submitted is the description, the test cases, the table of alternatives with results, the adopted code with the student's comments, and the log.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The student writes test cases with known answers before requesting code, runs every alternative against them in their own environment, and adopts only code they can explain line by line.
activities.dl: A step description with hand-worked test cases, a table of alternative snippets with test results and stated assumptions, the adopted code with line-by-line student comments, and a dependency and assumption log.
activities.na: The student writes two implementations of the step, or compares their own with a peer's, against the same hand-worked test cases.
activities.risk: Free coding assistants suffice; only the step description and synthetic test rows enter the tool, never research data.

activities.t: A coding-assistant feasibility sketch inside a digital humanities grant proposal
activities.sum: Graduate students in an introductory digital humanities seminar, working alone or in small teams, write a proposal modeled on a national funder's digital humanities guidelines: an abstract for non-specialists, participants by role, a narrative of activities and deliverables, an environmental scan, a work plan, a data management plan, and a budget with justification. This version adds a feasibility sketch. Each team names the one processing step the project depends on, such as extracting place names from a set of novels or tagging dates in a run of letters, and writes a plain specification of what it should produce. Using a chat-based coding assistant, the team builds a minimal script for that step and runs it on its own machine on four or five public-domain texts. Before trusting the output, team members annotate a sample of passages by hand and compare what the script found, missed, and wrongly included. They keep a log separating the code the assistant wrote, the changes they made, and the parts they could not get working. The sketch is not the project. Its role is evidential: the error counts and the debugging time feed the work plan's staffing and timeline, the data plan's documentation, and the budget's case for programming expertise. The class helps set evaluation guidelines, and teams present their proposals, sketch included, as lightning talks in the final session.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Teams check the script's output against a hand-annotated sample, log what the assistant wrote and what they changed, and revise the work plan, data plan, and budget from the measured errors.
activities.dl: A full grant-style proposal with a feasibility sketch: the specification, the assistant-written script with a change log, a hand-annotated comparison sample with error counts, and the resulting revisions to the work plan, data plan, and budget.
activities.na: Teams hand-annotate the sample and estimate effort from that alone, or adapt a published tutorial script with help from library digital scholarship staff.
activities.risk: Free chat-based assistants suffice and the texts are public domain; teams can share one machine, and library digital scholarship staff can support setup.

activities.t: Reproducing a published education study's model with generated statistical code before analyzing new data
activities.sum: An education researcher planning a multilevel or structural model asks a conversational assistant to write the statistical code for it in the software the researcher uses, then runs that code in their own environment rather than inside the assistant. Generated code is treated as a draft until it has been checked in three ways. The researcher asks for an explanation of every consequential operation, such as how clustering is specified, how missing data are handled, which estimator is used, and what each parameter means, and compares the stated functions and defaults with the software's own documentation. The code is also run on a synthetic dataset the researcher generates with known parameter values, to see whether the estimates recover them. Finally, before any new data are analyzed, the same code pattern is used to reproduce a table from a published study whose data are openly available, and differences from the published estimates are traced to their causes. Only then is the code applied to the researcher's own de-identified data, which never enters the assistant; the assistant sees only variable names, model descriptions, and synthetic rows. The researcher keeps the generated code, the explanations, the documentation checks, the synthetic recovery results, and the reproduction comparison together, and deposits them with the analysis so that colleagues can rerun and question each step.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher requires an explanation of each consequential operation, checks functions against documentation, tests recovery on synthetic data, and reproduces a published table before touching new data.
activities.dl: Generated code with operation-by-operation explanations, documentation checks, synthetic-data recovery results, a comparison with a published table, and a deposited verification record accompanying the final analysis.
activities.na: The researcher writes the code from the software's documentation or a methods text and applies the same synthetic-data and reproduction checks.
activities.risk: A free conversational assistant suffices, and the researcher's own data never enters the tool; use of that data follows existing ethics approvals.

activities.t: Forecasting campus building energy demand against a persistence baseline and a held-out season
activities.sum: An energy researcher studying how campus building demand relates to weather assembles a year or more of hourly meter data released by the facilities office, joined with public weather records, removes outliers and gaps by a rule written down in advance, and then follows an open forecasting tutorial's approach to the modeling. The data are split in time order, with the final season held out entirely, so that no model sees the future it is asked to predict and performance is tested on conditions the training period did not cover. The tutorial's windowing turns the series into input and target spans. Before any learned model is trusted, the researcher fits the simplest baseline, a forecast in which each hour repeats the same hour of the previous day, and computes its error. Linear, dense, convolutional, and recurrent models are then trained, and each is reported only as an improvement, or not, over that baseline. The models produce the forecasts; the code that runs is the tutorial's code adapted by the researcher; and the checks are independent of both: normalization statistics are confirmed to come from the training span alone, and the baseline's mean absolute error for one sample week is recomputed by hand in a spreadsheet. The write-up states which buildings and seasons the comparison covers and does not generalize beyond them.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher checks the split and normalization for temporal leakage, reports every model against a persistence baseline, and recomputes the baseline's error for a sample week by hand.
activities.dl: A documented cleaning rule, a time-ordered split with a held-out season, baseline and model forecasts with error metrics, a leakage check on normalization, a hand-recomputed baseline error for one week, and a scoped write-up.
activities.na: The researcher fits regression models of demand on weather and calendar variables and compares them with the same persistence baseline on the same held-out season.
activities.risk: Uses open-source tools that run in free notebook environments; meter data are used with the facilities office's permission, and weather data come from public records.

activities.t: First-pass exploration of a public health survey file with a code-executing assistant and a scripted twin
activities.sum: A public health researcher or graduate student beginning work with a public-use federal health survey file, which is in the public domain, uploads it to an assistant that writes and executes code and asks for a first look: the variables and their types, ranges, missingness, coded values that look anomalous, and a few exploratory plots. The assistant's code, its executed output, and its prose summary are saved separately, because a summary can describe results the code did not produce. Alongside, the researcher keeps a scripted twin: the same exploratory steps run in their own analysis environment from the survey's codebook, without the assistant. Each figure the assistant reports is reproduced in the twin, and differences are traced. The researcher also logs every choice the assistant made without being asked, such as treating special codes for refused or unknown responses as numbers, dropping incomplete rows, or ignoring the survey weights and design variables, the kind of unstated decision a published evaluation of such a feature found an analyst has to check. Only after this does the researcher decide which analyses suit the survey's complex design and which questions the data can address, writing down why. The comparison with the scripted twin lets the researcher see what the assistant's first pass caught, what it changed without saying so, and what it missed.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher reproduces each reported figure in a separate script, logs every choice the assistant made without being asked, and decides which analyses suit the survey design.
activities.dl: Saved assistant code, executed outputs, and summaries; a scripted twin of the same exploratory steps; a reconciliation log of differences; a log of unrequested choices; and a written analysis plan suited to the survey design.
activities.na: The researcher runs the scripted exploration alone and has a colleague review it against the codebook.
activities.risk: Code-executing assistants with file upload are often paid; the scripted route needs only free statistical software. Only a public-domain public-use file enters the tool.

activities.t: Running unfamiliar code to settle disagreements between students' and a chatbot's comments
activities.sum: As their introductory programming course draws to a close, students are handed a short instructor-written program in an unfamiliar language, along with a small input file. Working without discussion, research, or AI, they annotate each part with comments on what it does and write a plain-English account of the program's overall purpose. Only then do they ask a chatbot to comment the same code, saving its version without changing their own. The two sets of comments are laid side by side, and every point where they disagree, or where either seems unsure, becomes a question to settle by running the program. The chatbot writes explanations, not code; what runs is the original program, and its observed behavior is the check on both readings. Students design small inputs aimed at each disputed behavior, such as an empty line, a boundary value in a loop, or a missing file, predict the output under each set of comments, and then run the program in a prepared online environment to see what actually happens. Each disagreement is resolved in favor of whichever comment matched the observed behavior, or neither. Students score both sets of comments against one shared rubric, which looks at how variables are declared, how input is read, how loops are structured and nested, how files are handled, and whether the overall purpose is stated, and answer reflection questions on what the chatbot's comments taught them, where their own were more useful to a novice, and how running the code changed their trust in either.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students comment the code unaided first, then design inputs, predict outputs, and run the program to decide whose comments describe its actual behavior.
activities.dl: The student's unaided comments and purpose statement, the chatbot's saved comments, a table of disagreements with designed inputs, predictions, and observed outputs, rubric scores for both sets, and reflection answers.
activities.na: Pairs exchange their unaided comments and settle their disagreements by running the program in the same way.
activities.risk: Any free chatbot suffices, and the instructor can provide pre-generated chatbot comments for students who prefer not to use one; the online run environment needs no installation.

activities.t: Testing whether chatbot feedback on a draft holds up when the writer pushes back
activities.sum: Writers take a draft to a chat assistant with a feedback prompt that asks for two strengths and two areas for revision, each anchored in a quotation from the draft. They then run two probes taken from research on sycophancy, the tendency of assistants trained on human preferences to tailor answers to a user's stated views. In the first probe, the writer opens two fresh conversations with the same draft, introducing it once as their own work that they are pleased with and once as a classmate's draft they have doubts about, and compares the two sets of comments. In the second, the writer picks one comment they believe is sound and one they believe is mistaken and pushes back on each in the same mild terms, without giving reasons; later, in a new conversation, they challenge the mistaken comment again with a reason drawn from the assignment. A short log records whether the assistant's assessment moved with the writer's framing and insistence or with their reasons. Writers then decide which comments to act on, revise the draft themselves, and take it to a peer or tutor, who reads the log as well. The class debrief pools the logs and asks when, if ever, the assistant's agreement counted as evidence about the draft.
activities.f: AI in the Writing Process: Invention, Feedback and Revision
activities.gate: Writers vary how they present the draft, push back without reasons on one comment they judge sound and one they judge mistaken, and log whether the feedback moves with their stance or with their reasons before deciding what to revise.
activities.dl: Two framing-variant sets of feedback, a pushback log for a sound and a mistaken comment, a revised draft, and a peer or tutor response.
activities.na: Writers can run the framing and pushback exchange with a peer reviewer, logging whether the peer's comments change with insistence or with reasons, then complete the same revision and tutor visit.
activities.risk: A free assistant is sufficient. Writers who prefer not to enter their own draft can use an instructor-provided sample draft; drafts are de-identified before entry, and settings that allow training on inputs are reviewed beforehand.

activities.t: Auditing a chatbot's step-by-step solution against your own unaided attempt at a probability problem
activities.sum: Students attempt a multi-step probability or logic problem on their own first, for instance a conditional probability question in which base rates matter, and keep their work as written, dead ends included. The same problem then goes to a chat assistant twice in separate conversations: once with a request for the answer only, and once with a request to reason step by step before answering, the prompting technique that a survey of reasoning in large language models identifies as a way of eliciting intermediate steps. Students may run the prompts themselves or work from responses the instructor collected in advance. Each step of the step-by-step response is then audited against a verified solution and a short rubric of reasoning standards: is the step valid, is it relevant, does it follow from what came before. Students mark steps that are sound, steps that are wrong, and steps that arrive at a correct intermediate value by an invalid route, and they audit their own unaided work the same way. The comparison takes up two questions the survey leaves open: whether visible steps make a final answer more trustworthy, and whether a correct answer is evidence of reasoning at all. Students record the order in which they saw each response, since prior exposure shapes judgment, and close with a paragraph on what the audit showed about the assistant's steps and about their own.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students solve unaided and keep that work, then audit each step of the assistant's step-by-step response, and of their own attempt, against a verified solution, marking valid steps, invalid steps, and steps that reach a correct value by a wrong route.
activities.dl: The student's preserved unaided attempt, the two assistant responses, a step-by-step audit of both the assistant's and the student's reasoning against a verified solution, and a closing paragraph.
activities.na: Students can audit an instructor-written flawed solution, or an anonymized past student solution shared with permission, with the same step-by-step rubric, keeping their unaided attempt as the baseline.
activities.risk: A free assistant is enough, or the instructor supplies the responses so that students need no account and do not use AI themselves. Problems are instructor-written.

activities.t: Drafting a statement of work through a capped draft-and-check exchange, with acceptance evidence written first
activities.sum: A staff member preparing a statement of work for a campus project, such as a vendor-built event registration page, starts without any assistant. They clarify requirements with the requester and write, for each deliverable, the evidence that would show it had been accepted: what will be tested, by whom, and against what threshold. Only then do they open an assistant conversation, with system-level instructions that fix the unit's required sections, terms and stage names, and supply the requirement notes. The assistant drafts a scope section, milestones, acceptance criteria, payment terms, and the contact and signature details. A second conversation, instructed only as a checker, receives the draft with a short checklist (is each criterion measurable, does every deliverable have one, does any criterion introduce a term the notes do not contain) and returns findings, which the staff member passes back to the first conversation for revision. The exchange stops after a fixed number of rounds, three in the unit's example, whether or not the checker is satisfied, following the documented advice to cap refinement loops. The staff member then compares the final acceptance criteria with the evidence written at the start and marks each as matching, weaker, or added without basis. Anything added without basis is removed, and the requester reviews the result before it goes to purchasing.
activities.f: Workplace Communication and Career Readiness
activities.gate: Staff write the evidence that will show each deliverable is accepted before any drafting, cap the draft-and-check exchange at a fixed number of rounds, and test the final criteria against that evidence and the requester's requirements.
activities.dl: Acceptance evidence written before drafting, a round-by-round record of drafts and checker findings within the cap, and a final statement of work with each criterion marked against the original evidence.
activities.na: The same sequence works with a colleague as checker: the staff member drafts from the unit's template, and a colleague applies the checklist for the same capped number of rounds.
activities.risk: Use an assistant the institution has approved for business information; requirement notes leave out confidential pricing and personal data unless the tool is cleared for them.

activities.t: Writing a simulated patient's instructions from a case card and auditing the transcript for drift
activities.sum: Faculty write a case card for a counseling encounter, such as a patient starting a new inhaler who believes it is habit-forming, recording the patient's history, health literacy and concerns, what the patient will say only if asked, and what would and would not change the patient's mind. Each student turns the card into system-level instructions for a chat assistant and holds a counseling conversation with it over several turns, with the instructions asking the patient to raise the complications such encounters commonly bring. The transcript then serves a second purpose, as evidence about the simulation itself. After the conversation, the student audits each patient turn against the card, marking disclosures that came without being asked for, concerns the patient dropped without a reason the card would accept, and facts the patient added that the card does not contain. Students also mark their own turns where they persuaded by insistence rather than by explanation, since a simulated patient that yields to insistence teaches the wrong lesson. In the debrief, pairs compare their instructions and audits, and the class revises its guidance for writing patient instructions before the next case. Both kinds of departure, the persona's and the student's, are treated as material for discussion rather than as failures, and the faculty case card, not the conversation, remains the reference for what the patient believes.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students audit their own transcript against the case card, marking where the simulated patient disclosed what it should have held back, dropped a belief without a reason the card would accept, or added facts not on the card, and mark their own turns that persuaded by insistence.
activities.dl: Student-written system instructions, a counseling transcript, a turn-by-turn audit against the case card, and revised class guidance for writing patient instructions.
activities.na: Pairs can role-play the encounter with one student as the patient working from the same card, while the observer audits the patient's turns for drift in the same way.
activities.risk: The case is fictional, so no patient information is entered; a free assistant is sufficient.

activities.t: Testing a rubric-based feedback prompt on planted higher- and lower-order flaws before students use it
activities.sum: An instructor who has built a feedback prompt from an assignment, its rubric and examples of their own comments, following a published teaching guide, tests it before students see it. The instructor writes a few short sample drafts for the assignment and plants known problems in each: some higher-order, such as a thesis the evidence does not support, a missing counterargument, or paragraphs in a weak order, and some lower-order, such as faulty citations, agreement errors or wordiness. Each draft goes to the configured assistant in a fresh conversation, and the instructor tallies, for every planted problem, whether the feedback caught it, missed it or described it inaccurately, and also notes any comment naming a problem the draft does not have. The tally is read against a recent systematic review of classroom studies, which reports that language-model feedback supported revision for linguistic accuracy while human feedback remained stronger on higher-order issues, and whose authors regard designs in which teachers mediate the feedback as the most promising. The instructor revises the prompt, retests the drafts that exposed gaps, and saves the version that works best. When the prompt is shared, it goes with a short note drawn from the tally, stating which kinds of problem it tends to catch and which students might take to a peer, a tutor or the instructor, whose feedback remains available to anyone who prefers it.
activities.f: Assessment and Feedback Design
activities.gate: The instructor writes sample drafts with known flaws at both levels, tallies which flaws the feedback caught, missed or misdescribed, revises the prompt, and tells students what it does not catch.
activities.dl: A set of instructor-written sample drafts with a key of planted problems, a caught, missed and misdescribed tally for each prompt version, a revised saved prompt, and a note to students on what it does not catch.
activities.na: The instructor can share the rubric with an annotated exemplar and organize peer feedback with a guided checklist instead of a prompt; students may always choose teaching-team or peer feedback.
activities.risk: Only instructor-written drafts are entered during testing, so no student work reaches the tool; students who later use the shared prompt are told about privacy settings first.

activities.t: Setting a hand-built text grammar against an assistant given the same rules as instructions
activities.sum: Students first decide what their generator should produce and in what mood, whether parody, social commentary, genre fiction or mock nonfiction, and then build it as a grammar: sentence frames whose open positions draw from word lists they curate, published as a small text-generating page. A second generator is then set beside it. Each student writes the same rules out in plain language, with the templates, the word lists and any constraints on combination, and gives them to a chat assistant as system-level instructions, asking for a batch of outputs in the form the grammar produces and, later in the same conversation, a second batch. Every output from both systems is checked against the rule list. The grammar keeps to its rules by construction, so its interest lies in what the rules permit that the student did not intend. The assistant's outputs are tallied for rule breaks of different kinds: words not on the lists, templates altered or merged, tone drifting toward a default register, and changes between the first and second batch as the conversation lengthens. Students then decide which breaks count as failures and which they would keep as material, and the artist statement, which places the project in relation to combinatory writing, authorship and novelty, takes up what each system's behavior showed about rules and genre.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Students check every output from both systems against their rule list, tally the assistant's rule breaks by kind and by batch, and decide which breaks are failures and which are usable material.
activities.dl: A working grammar-based generator, a plain-language rule list, two batches of assistant outputs, a rule-compliance tally for both systems, and an artist statement.
activities.na: Students can swap rule lists and have a classmate write a batch of outputs by hand from the rules, then tally the human writer's departures in the same way.
activities.risk: A free grammar editor and a free assistant are sufficient, and no coding experience is needed. Word lists are student-written or drawn from public-domain text.

activities.t: Testing whether an assistant's stakeholder matrix shifts with the framing of the request
activities.sum: Groups first build an ethical matrix without any AI, following an openly licensed AI-ethics curriculum: they list the direct and indirect stakeholders of a video platform's recommendation algorithm, including the company itself, name at least two values for each, and mark where values overlap or conflict. Only then is an assistant asked for a matrix of its own, three times in separate conversations with identical structure but different framing: once neutrally, once as a request from the platform's growth team, and once as a request from the parent of a young viewer. A group member or the instructor runs the three requests. A systematic survey of prompting research describes two related problems, outputs that change with small differences in a prompt and outputs that agree with the user's apparent position, and the three framings are designed to make both visible. Groups lay the four matrices side by side and record which stakeholders and values each generated matrix includes, omits or reweights, and whether the framing moved its conclusion about what the algorithm should optimize. They then return to their own matrix and ask whether the generated versions reveal a stakeholder they missed or mainly reflect the framing. The redesign follows: each group states what the algorithm's goal should be and proposes features that serve the stakeholders' values, with a short note on which of the assistant's suggestions survived scrutiny and why.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Groups compare the three generated matrices with their own and with each other, recording stakeholders and values that appear, disappear or change weight with the framing, then decide which suggestions survive into their redesign.
activities.dl: A group-built stakeholder-by-value matrix, three framed assistant matrices, a comparison table of inclusions, omissions and reweightings, and a redesigned algorithm goal with feature proposals.
activities.na: Groups can trade matrices with another group that built theirs from an assigned viewpoint and compare what the viewpoint added or removed.
activities.risk: A free assistant run by one group member or by the instructor is sufficient, so most students need no account; no personal data is entered.

activities.t: Comparing a self-rated sense of agency with a coded transcript of one's own AI conversation
activities.sum: Participants first complete a published self-rating profile without any AI: for each of ten purposes for AI use they rate how often they use it, how confident they feel, how much they want to develop, and how confident they are that their own judgment stays active. They then choose one purpose they rated high on use, typically understanding or explaining, and hold a short conversation with an assistant about a concept from a current course reading, with the reading at hand, saving the transcript. A systematic review of chat-based AI in higher education reports uses of this kind, such as conceptual explanation and reflective dialogue, alongside a recurring association between uncritical reliance and cognitive offloading or automation bias, and the transcript is where participants look for either. Each of their own turns is coded with a short shared codebook: accepted without checking, checked against the reading, redirected or questioned, declined. Each assistant claim that mattered to their understanding is marked as found in the reading, not in the reading, or contradicted by it. Participants then set the coding beside their agency rating for that purpose and write about the gap, if there is one. The educator presents the result as neither score nor test, and the conversation that follows takes up the profile's open questions, now answered with reference to a transcript rather than to memory.
activities.f: Study Support, Tutoring and Practice
activities.gate: Participants code each of their own turns (accepted without checking, checked against the reading, redirected or questioned, declined), check the assistant's key claims against the reading, and compare the result with their earlier self-rating of agency.
activities.dl: A completed self-rating profile, a saved transcript coded turn by turn, a check of the assistant's key claims against the reading, and a short written comparison of rating and coding.
activities.na: Participants can keep a log of a recent study session with another resource, such as a tutor, a classmate or a search engine, and code their own moves against the reading in the same way.
activities.risk: A free assistant is sufficient. Participants decide whether to share their transcript; the educator sees only the written comparison unless the participant offers more.

activities.t: Grounding a student-staffed AI policy panel in tests of the course's own assignments
activities.sum: When a course or program AI policy is written or revised, the students it will constrain sit on the panel, and the convener first says which level of involvement is on offer: consultation on a draft, co-creation, or a seat on the deciding body. Before deliberation, panel members are offered a short orientation, drawn from an educator-facing tutorial, on how chat-based language models generate text, the tasks they suit, and the tasks where their output should not be relied on. The panel then gathers its own evidence. Working in mixed student and staff pairs under a shared protocol, members give each of the course's actual assignment prompts to a general-purpose assistant, follow up for a couple of turns as a student plausibly might, and save the outputs. Each output is read against what the assignment exists to teach: which parts of the task it completed, which it completed poorly, and which it could not do at all, such as drawing on a class discussion or a student's own data. The draft policy cites these outputs rather than general claims. With the help of the campus disability service, the panel also reaches students who would not otherwise be asked how the draft affects tools they rely on. The panel records which level of involvement was offered, what the tests showed, and what changed in the policy as a result.
activities.f: Academic Integrity, Authorship and Course AI Policy
activities.gate: Mixed student and staff pairs read each output against what the assignment exists to teach, and the draft policy cites specific outputs rather than general claims.
activities.dl: A record of the involvement level offered, a saved set of assignment-test outputs with the pairs' readings, a draft policy that cites them, and a note of what changed.
activities.na: The panel can work from the instructor's account of each assignment's purpose and from published descriptions of chatbot capability, keeping the same involvement levels and record of changes.
activities.risk: Panel members use a free or institution-provided assistant after the orientation; assignment prompts contain no student data. Outreach through the disability service widens who is consulted.

activities.t: Setting an abstention rule before an infrared spectrum classifier meets compounds outside its training classes
activities.sum: Students who have completed a Python practical on infrared spectra arrive with a labeled library of infrared spectra for ortho-, meta- and para-substituted benzene derivatives, a nearest-neighbors classifier, and its accuracy over repeated held-out splits. The question now is what the classifier does with a compound that belongs to none of its three classes. Before any new measurement, each group writes an abstention rule: a threshold on neighbor distance, or on the share of neighbors that agree, below which the classifier's label is withheld and the spectrum is flagged for a chemist's reading. Groups justify the threshold from their held-out results, for instance from how far the least typical correctly classified test spectrum lay from its neighbors. They then measure two sets of samples: unknowns drawn from the three trained classes, and compounds the instructor chooses from outside them, such as mono- or trisubstituted rings. The classifier labels everything it is given; the rule decides what gets reported. Groups tabulate how often the rule withheld a correct label, let an out-of-class compound through, or caught one, and they write a short account of what a confident label from this model cannot show, such as a substitution pattern that is absent from the library. A closing revision asks each group to reset its threshold and explain which kind of error it chose to make less likely.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Groups write an abstention rule (a distance or agreement threshold below which the classifier's label is withheld and the spectrum goes to a chemist's reading) before measuring, then test it on in-class and out-of-class samples and revise it.
activities.dl: A written abstention rule with its rationale, a table of classifier labels and report-or-withhold decisions for in-class and out-of-class samples, and a revised rule with a statement of what a confident label cannot establish.
activities.na: Groups can assign the same spectra by hand from the diagnostic out-of-plane bending region and write the abstention rule as a reading protocol (when a spectrum is too ambiguous to assign), applying it to the same out-of-class samples.
activities.risk: Runs in the same free notebooks as the earlier practical, on lab computers; no account with an AI vendor is needed. All spectra are the class's own measurements, so no third-party data enters the tool.
