activities.t: Reading a newspaper-photograph classifier's errors as evidence about the historian's own categories
activities.sum: Here an image classifier's output is treated as an interpretation to be corroborated, never as evidence in its own right. A historian working with digitized public-domain newspapers trains a classifier on labeled photographs from the early twentieth century, following an openly reviewed lesson that moves through label counts, the choice of a metric, and per-label results, and relabels part of the set where the research question needs a category the dataset lacks. Before training, the historian writes down which categories matter and which boundaries already feel uncertain. Held-out results are then read label by label: overall accuracy is set aside where labels are imbalanced, and precision and recall are compared for each category. Misclassified images are pulled and sorted by hand into three piles: the model's mistake, an image the scheme cannot settle, and a labeling decision the historian would now reverse. The trained model is next run on unlabeled pages from a later decade or a different title, and any shift it suggests, such as a rise in one kind of photograph, is logged as a hypothesis. Each hypothesis counts only after the historian has read a sample of pages, including pages the model scored low, and found support in the corpus or in published scholarship. The resulting memo states what the classifier's sorting can and cannot establish, including that its categories were made rather than found.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The historian reads per-label precision and recall and the misclassified images as evidence about where the category scheme is unstable, and corroborates any pattern the model suggests in the unlabeled corpus by reading pages before it counts.
activities.dl: Per-label evaluation notes, a three-way sort of misclassified images, a log of corpus-level hypotheses with the reading that corroborated or rejected each, and a research memo on the category scheme.
activities.na: The historian can hand-code a stratified sample of pages with the same scheme, with a second coder, and record where coders disagree, which yields the same evidence about unstable categories on a smaller scale.
activities.risk: Runs in a free cloud notebook with a free account. Training and test images are public-domain newspaper photographs from a national library's openly released dataset, so no restricted material enters the tool.

activities.t: Seeing, thinking and wondering about a print-technique classifier's label and heat map
activities.sum: In a printmaking or art history course, each student spends time with one public-domain print and keeps the three lists of a see-think-wonder thinking routine: what they see, what they think it means, and what they wonder. Here the second list includes a judgment of technique, such as etching, engraving, woodcut or lithograph, tied to the visible evidence for it, for example the swelling of an engraved line or the broken edges of a woodcut. Only then does the instructor show what an image classifier makes of the same print. The instructor has trained the classifier with transfer learning on openly licensed museum images whose catalog records give the technique, held back a set of labeled prints to test it, and generated a heat map showing which regions most affected each label. Students set the label, its confidence and the heat map beside their own lists and sort the model's output: which parts correspond to something visible, which look like inference from features unrelated to technique, such as cropping, paper tone or a collection's photography conditions, and which raise a question. The heat map is read as a picture of the model's weighting, not as an account of technique. Discussion closes on what the label cannot establish, including anything that depends on the physical sheet, such as a plate mark at its edge, and each student turns one wondering into a question for a visit to the print room.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students complete their own see/think/wonder lists and a technique judgment before the label and heat map are shown, then sort the model's output into what it could have observed and what it appears to have inferred.
activities.dl: Each student's see/think/wonder lists with an evidenced technique judgment, an annotated comparison with the model's label and heat map, and one revised question for examining the physical print.
activities.na: Students compare their technique judgments with a classmate's and with the catalog record, then sort the classmate's reasons into observation and inference in the same way.
activities.risk: The instructor runs the model in a free notebook and projects or shares its outputs, so students need no account and do not use AI themselves. Training images are prints released by museums as public domain or CC0; the instructor confirms the release for each image.

activities.t: Two rounds of looking before checking machine-generated catalog metadata field by field
activities.sum: A cataloging team considering machine-generated metadata runs a small local trial on openly licensed e-books before deciding anything about its workflow. For each item, a cataloger first looks without any machine output, at the title page, verso, contents, preface and back matter, writing down ten details that bear on description and subject analysis, then looking again for ten more, the second pass aimed at what the first missed, such as a series statement, a translator, or a geographic focus that only the introduction reveals. The cataloger builds or confirms a record from those notes in the usual way. Only then does the team view what a metadata-generation model proposed for the same item, and each field is compared with the cataloger's record and marked as matching, differing in form only, or wrong. Tallied across the batch, the comparison shows which fields the model handles reliably, and the team sets this beside the Library of Congress report that structured fields such as title and author came close to its threshold for automation while subject and genre fell well short. The team also notes which second-pass details the model's subject proposals missed, since these often distinguish the item. A small batch cannot establish how the model performs on other kinds of material, and the team says so. The outcome is a recorded decision for each field, in which any cataloger can decline a machine suggestion and disputed subject or genre assignments go to a second cataloger.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Catalogers record observations of each item in two passes and build their own record, then compare machine-proposed values field by field and decide, for each field, whether output may be accepted with spot checks, must be reviewed every time, or is not used.
activities.dl: Two-pass observation notes and a record for each item, a field-by-field comparison table across the batch, and a written decision for each field: accept with spot checks, review every time, or do not use.
activities.na: The same two-pass looking and field-level comparison can be run between two catalogers' independent records for the same items, which gives the unit a baseline of human agreement per field.
activities.risk: Only openly licensed e-books are given to the model, so no licensed vendor content or patron data enters the tool; the trial uses a model the library already has institutional access to, or an open-weight model run locally.

activities.t: Weighing a simulated survey sample against the class's own pilot when choosing a research method
activities.sum: Groups in a research methods course prepare short accounts of case study, survey and experimental designs, then choose an approach for a question about study habits and course engagement, using rotating roles of questioner, arguer, supporter and summarizer so that every choice is argued and answered. Groups that choose a survey draft a short instrument of non-sensitive items. At this point the 'silicon sample' described in a published methodological guide for psychology enters as an option to evaluate rather than adopt: a group member, or the instructor, prompts a language model to answer the instrument as a set of simulated student respondents, recording the model, the date and the prompt. The class meanwhile completes the same items anonymously and voluntarily, which gives a small human pilot. Groups set the simulated distributions beside the pilot's, item by item, and run the guide's sensitivity check by rewording two items and reordering the instrument to see whether the simulated answers move in ways human answers would not be expected to. They then ask whose responses the simulation seems to reproduce, given what the guide reports about the populations language models over-represent. Each group finishes with a revised method choice that states what a simulated sample could legitimately do, such as stress-testing item wording, and what it cannot establish, such as how students at their own institution actually study.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Groups compare the simulated responses with an anonymous pilot of the same items in their own class, rerun the simulation with reworded and reordered items, and argue what a simulated sample can and cannot stand in for.
activities.dl: A side-by-side comparison of simulated and pilot responses, a sensitivity log of reruns with reworded and reordered items, and a revised method choice stating the uses and limits of a simulated sample.
activities.na: Groups can compare their pilot with responses predicted in advance by another group playing 'typical respondents', which raises the same question of whose answers a stand-in reproduces.
activities.risk: Only the survey items are entered into the model, never students' responses. The pilot is anonymous and voluntary with non-sensitive items; instructors may wish to confirm that a classroom pilot falls outside their institution's research review requirements.

activities.t: Arguing an early-alert controversy from a dropout model's held-out errors by student group
activities.sum: Over a topic cycle in a higher education or teacher education course, groups develop an argument about a live controversy: whether an institution should adopt an early-alert system that flags students predicted to leave. The evidence is a model the class can inspect. Using a browser-based machine-learning workflow, the instructor or the groups train a classifier on an openly licensed dataset of anonymized student records that includes enrollment outcomes, hold back a test set, and record overall accuracy. Following an open learning analytics handbook's account of predictive modeling, groups then break the held-out results down by the subgroups the dataset records, such as age at enrollment, scholarship status or attendance mode, and compute how often each subgroup's students were wrongly flagged or wrongly passed over. Each group also writes down what the outcome label actually measures and what it leaves out. Arguments are exchanged with another group for evaluation, the critique is discussed, and each member records the reasoning behind any change in the revised argument. The cycle ends with each group naming the challenge its revised argument answers better than its first version, and stating what the model cannot establish: why any particular student left, or whether a flag would lead to support that helps.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Groups build an argument for or against an early-alert system from the model's held-out error rates by subgroup, exchange it with another group for critique, and revise with recorded reasoning.
activities.dl: A subgroup error table from the held-out set, a first and a revised group argument with recorded reasoning for each change, and a statement of what the model cannot establish.
activities.na: Groups can work from the subgroup results reported in a published evaluation of an early-alert model, keeping the same argue, exchange and revise sequence.
activities.risk: The dataset is openly licensed and anonymized; no records from the institution are used. The workflow runs on a free public server with a free account, or the instructor can run it and share the outputs.

activities.t: Scoring a clinical risk model on its validation evidence before it enters a simulation scenario
activities.sum: Before a simulation scenario shows nursing students a risk score from a clinical prediction model, the faculty who will run it review the model in two parts. The first part adapts the 0–2 pre-deployment scoring that a published nursing-simulation framework applies to a chatbot's configuration, with domains drawn from current guidance on evaluating prediction models: whether the model was validated beyond the data it was developed on, how it was internally validated, its discrimination, its calibration, its performance across patient subgroups, and whether its intended population matches the scenario's patients. Faculty score each domain from the model's published evidence. The second part is a small local check. For each faculty-written synthetic case in the scenario bank, each reviewer first records the escalation decision an experienced nurse would make, and only then runs the model, whose coefficients or code are openly published, on the case values. Cases where score and expert judgment diverge are discussed one at a time: is the case unusual, is the patient outside the model's intended population, or does the case carry a cue the score ignores? Low domain scores and divergent cases point to revisions before students meet the scenario, for example presenting the score as one cue to question rather than as a decision. The review states in writing what the local check cannot establish, since a handful of synthetic cases says nothing about the model's calibration in real patients.
activities.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
activities.gate: Faculty score the model's published evidence on a 0–2 rubric, record their own expected escalation decision for each synthetic case before running the model, and decide how, or whether, its output appears in the scenario.
activities.dl: A completed domain rubric with scores and evidence notes, a case-by-case table of expert decisions and model outputs with discussion of divergences, and a written decision on how the score will appear in the scenario.
activities.na: Faculty can leave the risk score out of the scenario and teach escalation from vital signs and assessment cues alone, using the same synthetic cases.
activities.risk: Only synthetic, faculty-written cases are entered; no patient data is used. An openly published model can be computed in a spreadsheet or a free notebook.

activities.t: Revisiting a debate about intelligence after training an image classifier on the class's own photographs
activities.sum: A first-year seminar opens with a debate about what intelligence is, and the questions the debate raises are written down for later. In place of a visit to a demonstration center, the class builds something small. Each group photographs everyday objects for a sorting task the class agrees on, such as recyclable, compostable and landfill items from the campus waste stream, labels the photographs, and trains a convolutional image classifier in a free browser-based workflow, following an openly licensed tutorial. A share of the photographs is held back, and the group records how often the trained model labels them correctly. Groups then take a second set of photographs designed to probe the model: the same objects on an unfamiliar background, in poor light, partly hidden, or replaced by look-alikes. These results are set beside the held-out accuracy, and each group writes what the pattern of errors suggests the model learned, which may turn out to be backgrounds or colors rather than materials. The debate is then rerun with each position required to cite a specific observation from the class's models, and the original questions are revisited, along with how far one classifier can stand for other kinds of AI the students use, such as chat assistants or recommendation systems. The seminar closes with advice to developers that names a learning need or concern rather than novelty, and with a statement of what the classifier's accuracy cannot establish, such as whether it has any concept of recycling.

activities.na: Students can write explicit sorting rules for the same objects, test the rules by hand on the probe photographs, and bring the cases where the rules fail into the debate.

activities.t: Verifying acoustic species detections before they become occurrence records in a distribution model
activities.sum: An ecology lab that has deployed autonomous sound recorders across a study region wants occurrence records for a distribution model of one bird or amphibian species. A pretrained acoustic detector, of the deep-learning kind reviewed in the bioacoustics literature, labels candidate vocalizations in the recordings, each with a confidence score. Before any detection becomes an occurrence record, the researcher draws a sample of detections at several confidence thresholds, stratified by recording site and habitat, listens to each clip, and records an expert label; a second listener checks a subset. This yields precision at each threshold and shows whether errors cluster at particular sites, for example where a similar-sounding species or persistent noise is common. Following a published species-distribution workflow, the researcher then builds a presence-background distribution model twice, once from all detections above a default threshold and once from verified detections only, keeping thinning, background extent and spatially partitioned cross-validation the same for both. Comparing the two projections shows where unverified detections shift the predicted range, and the researcher checks whether those shifts fall in conditions the training data do not cover. Working notes record which threshold and verification rate the lab will adopt, and what the final map cannot establish: where the species is absent, or why it occurs where it does.

activities.gate: The researcher listens to a site-stratified sample of detections at several confidence thresholds, records expert labels, and compares distribution models built from verified and unverified detections.
activities.dl: A verification table of expert labels by confidence threshold and site, two distribution models built from unverified and verified detections with their evaluation results, and working notes on the chosen threshold and the map's limits.
activities.na: Occurrence records can come entirely from manual listening to a sample of recordings or from field surveys, run through the same distribution workflow at a smaller scale.
activities.risk: Uses the lab's own recordings and a freely available pretrained detector; clips that capture human voices are excluded or deleted before analysis to protect bystanders' privacy, and no third-party sound data enters a tool.

activities.t: Pre-lab audit of a manual-grounded lab assistant using students' own questions
activities.sum: Before a remote acid-base titration, first-year chemistry students each write three questions they expect to need answered during the experiment, phrased the way they would actually type them, including at least one about a safety step and one about a calculation. The instructor has already configured a document-grounded assistant for the lab: it indexes excerpts from the course's own laboratory manual, the procedure, and the safety notes, answers only from that material with references to the sections it drew on, and is set not to supply complete numerical answers. In a pre-lab session students put their questions to the assistant and open every section it cites. For each exchange they record whether the cited passage is the right part of the manual, whether the answer says what that passage says, whether the needed passage was never retrieved at all, and whether the assistant held to its limit on calculations or let a worked number through. Oddly worded questions and questions about steps the manual covers only briefly receive particular attention. Groups pool their records into a class tally that separates retrieval errors from answer errors, and the instructor reads the tally as evidence about both the assistant's configuration and the manual itself, revising either before the lab runs. During the experiment the assistant remains optional, and students carry their tallies with them as a guide to which kinds of question it handled well.

activities.t: Library staff chunk service documents for a retrieval assistant and log its failures by type
activities.sum: Library staff preparing a retrieval assistant for the library's own service documents, such as loan policies, room-booking rules, and interlibrary-loan procedures written by staff, begin by assembling a fixed set of questions patrons actually ask, drawn from desk logs with identifying details removed, and noting for each the passage that answers it. A generative assistant then breaks each document into short, self-contained topical chunks that name their subject. Staff read every chunk against its source paragraph and correct merged facts, dropped conditions, and wording the source does not contain. Both versions, the raw documents and the checked chunks, are indexed, and the question set is run against each. For every answer, staff open the passages the assistant cites and code what went wrong, if anything, using the seven failure points from an engineering study of deployed retrieval systems: the answer was never in the documents, the right passage ranked too low, it was retrieved but left out of the answer's context, it was present but not extracted, the format was wrong, the answer was too general or too specific, or it was incomplete. The team compares the two failure profiles, decides which documents need rewriting rather than re-chunking, and repeats the run after changes, keeping each coded log as a record of how the assistant behaved on the library's own material before it is offered to anyone.

activities.t: Checking a source-grounded answer to a pharmacology case for support and for the right kind of source
activities.sum: In a formative undergraduate pharmacology task, the instructor indexes a small source set in a document-grounded assistant: the instructor's own mechanism notes, openly licensed treatment guideline summaries, and public-domain product labeling where it is available. Students put an instructor-written case question to the assistant, such as whether a given anticoagulant suits an older adult with reduced kidney function, and save the answer with the passages it cites. They pick out the claims that bear on safety and ask two questions of each: whether the cited passage actually says what the answer says, and whether the passage comes from the kind of source the claim needs, with mechanism claims drawn from the course notes, product safety from labeling, and treatment choice from guidelines. A correct-sounding claim cited to the wrong kind of source is logged as a retrieval error, separate from a claim the passage does not support. Students then set the assistant's answer aside and work out the mechanism on their own, tracing how the drug's target leads to its intended effect, to its risks, and to what needs monitoring, and testing that reasoning against the patient's details. They revise the answer and add a short correction note naming what changed and which source or case detail justified it. The class compares logs to see whether retrieval errors cluster around particular questions or source types, a pattern the instructor can use to adjust the packet.

activities.t: Testing whether paper order changes an assistant's critique of a trainee's literature synthesis
activities.sum: A research trainee reads each paper for a short review closely, annotates it with questions and first interpretations, and writes a synthesis across the set before consulting any AI tool; the set is drawn from openly licensed articles. Only then does the trainee give an assistant the full text of all the papers directly in a single request, without building an index or a retrieval step, together with the synthesis, and ask it to identify omissions and misrepresentations. Because a study of long inputs reports that models use material placed in the middle less reliably than material at the start or end, the trainee runs the same request a second time with the papers in a different order, moving the paper the trainee considers most important from first position to the middle of the set. Every gap or misreading the assistant flags in either run is checked against the original text and marked as confirmed, already addressed, or not supported by the paper. The trainee then compares the two critiques: which flags appear in only one run, and whether those concern papers that sat in the middle. A short note records which confirmed gaps led to revisions and what the comparison suggests about relying on a single critique of a long input. The synthesis remains the trainee's own work throughout; the assistant's role is to point at places worth rereading, and no paper is cited that the trainee has not read.

activities.na: A peer who has read the same papers critiques the synthesis for omissions, and the trainee checks each comment against the papers in the same way.
activities.risk: Input-length limits differ between free and paid tiers; with shorter limits the trainee can supply fewer or shorter papers or use institution-provided access. activities.t: Testing an assistant's themes in an open management textbook before writing discussion questions
activities.sum: In an upper-level management course, the assigned reading is a set of sections from an openly licensed management textbook. Before any AI use, each student skims the sections and lists the three or four themes they expect to matter most. A document-grounded assistant that indexes the same sections is then asked for the major themes, with references to the passages each theme rests on. Students open every cited passage and decide whether it carries the theme or whether a single passing mention has been inflated into one. They also look for a theme from their own list that the assistant did not return, rephrase the request once or twice to see whether a narrower question retrieves it, and record whether the missing theme reflects a retrieval miss or a genuine difference in reading. Only themes that survive this check feed the next stage. In small groups students generate as many discussion questions as they can for each verified theme, treating none as unworthy at first, then sort and rank them and select the few the group will bring to class, each tied to a specific passage. A one-page summary in the student's own words accompanies the questions, and the class discussion proceeds from the student-written questions, with time set aside to compare which themes the assistant overweighted or missed.

activities.t: Editing an instructor-generated, citation-bearing text against the course readings
activities.sum: The instructor indexes the course readings that are openly licensed or instructor-written in a document-grounded assistant and uses it to generate a short text, perhaps six hundred words, on a topic the class has studied, asking for inline citations to those readings. Students receive the printed text and the readings; they do not use the tool themselves. Working as editors in a document with tracked changes, they audit the text sentence by sentence in two directions that the citation literature distinguishes. For every sentence that makes a claim, is it fully supported by the passages it cites? For every citation, does the cited passage support the sentence it is attached to, or is it merely on the same topic? Students tally both, so the text receives two simple counts alongside their comments. They then correct factual and theoretical errors, add context from the readings where a sentence has no support or the wrong support, and develop the argument with cases of their own. A closing paragraph describes the assumptions about class, gender, race, and ability that the original carried, including any that the readings themselves do not support. Before submitting, students compare their two counts with the instructor's own audit of the same text and write a few sentences on where their judgment differed and why. The marked-up, expanded text is the submission, read against the course readings and class discussion.

activities.t: Faculty build a closed course assistant and rate it with a typed question set
activities.sum: Participants in an accredited certificate in teaching and learning have already read an article unaided and compared their reading with a machine summary. In this unit each participant builds a closed course assistant, using a no-code builder that indexes documents they supply: openly licensed or self-authored readings, their own slides, and a course-information page with deadlines and policies. Before trying it, each participant writes a question set of perhaps twenty items in three types: questions about content in the readings, questions that require connecting two readings, and organizational questions about dates, submission, and policies. The questions are put to the assistant and the answers saved. Pairs then rate each other's answer sets independently, marking each answer as correct and supported, partly correct, or wrong, and noting whether the cited passage was the one a student would need. Partners compare ratings, discuss the answers on which they disagreed, and record why agreement came harder on open-ended content questions than on factual or organizational ones, if it did. Each participant summarizes how the assistant performed by question type, revises the documents or configuration where answers failed, and closes with a reflection on whether, and for which kinds of question, they would release such an assistant to their own students, and what students would need to know about its limits.
activities.f: Faculty and Staff Development
activities.gate: Participants write a typed question set, rate a partner's answer set independently, reconcile disagreements, and summarize performance by question type.
activities.dl: A configured closed assistant, a typed question set with saved answers, paired independent ratings with a reconciliation record, a by-type performance summary, and a reflection on release to students.
activities.na: Participants exchange course documents and answer each other's question sets from the documents alone, rating the findability and clarity of the materials instead.
activities.risk: Requires an institution-provided no-code assistant builder; only openly licensed or self-authored materials are indexed, and no student data is used.

activities.t: Tracing a famous quotation through a searchable corpus of the attributed author's public-domain works
activities.sum: Students choose a well-known quotation attributed to a writer or public figure whose works are in the public domain, and record whom it is usually credited to and where they have seen it. They then trace it through three channels. The top results of an ordinary web search give one answer. A document-grounded assistant, into which the librarian has indexed the attributed author's collected works from public-domain digital editions, gives another: students ask it where the words appear and save the passages it returns with their references. Because this kind of retrieval matches meaning rather than exact wording, it can return a passage that resembles the quotation in idea without containing it, so students check every returned passage with an exact-phrase search of the same text files and classify it as a verbatim match, a close paraphrase, a related idea, or nothing that supports the attribution. A passage the assistant presents as the source is never accepted on its word. Where nothing matches, students treat the absence as a finding to be tested rather than proof, searching a few distinctive words and checking letters or speeches the edition may not include. They finish with a verified or corrected attribution and a short account of what the search results, the assistant, and the primary text each said, including any passage the assistant offered that did not hold up.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students check every returned passage by exact-phrase search of the same files and classify it as verbatim match, close paraphrase, related idea, or no support for the attribution.
activities.dl: A verified or corrected attribution, a table of passages returned by the assistant with each one's classification, the exact-phrase search results, and a short account comparing the three channels.
activities.na: Students trace the quotation through web search, a quotation dictionary, and exact-phrase search of the public-domain texts, and compare the three answers with the starting attribution.
activities.risk: Works only with public-domain editions, so no copyrighted text enters the tool; the librarian prepares the index, and students need only access to it and to the text files.

activities.t: Transferring a public-domain painting's style onto a student photograph and tracing who made which part
activities.sum: Students choose a photograph they took themselves and two or three paintings in the public domain, which the instructor may tie to course themes, and run them through a neural style-transfer notebook that rebuilds the photograph so its content stays recognizable while its textures and colors follow a painting. Over several runs they change the balance between content and style and the network layers used, saving each output with its settings. For the result they find most interesting, they make an annotated map that attributes each visible feature: composition and objects to their photograph, brushwork and palette to the painting, and artifacts such as repeated textures or smeared edges to the optimization itself. Each student shares the final image beside its sources, labeled as a style-transfer output, together with the map and an account of the choices made. A group discussion then asks who authored the result: the student who chose and tuned, the painter whose manner was measured and copied, or the procedure. It also takes up what it means to imitate an artist's manner even when the work is in the public domain, how the tool's division of an image into content and style shapes what students notice, and when an artist or designer might use such a process or decline to.
activities.f: Co-Authoring with AI: Voice and Authorship
activities.gate: Students vary the content-style balance and layers, then map which features of the result come from the photograph, the painting, or the optimization.
activities.dl: A labeled style-transfer image shown with its source photograph and painting, a log of settings, an annotated attribution map, and the group's discussion notes.
activities.na: Students can make a hand-painted or collaged study of their photograph in a public-domain painter's manner and produce the same attribution map.
activities.risk: Only students' own photographs and public-domain paintings are entered; a photograph that shows an identifiable person is used only with that person's consent. The instructor can run the notebook for students without a suitable device. Shared outputs carry image descriptions.

activities.t: Predicting colors for public-domain historical photographs, then testing a colorization model's choices against documentary evidence
activities.sum: Building on readings about how image models produce statistically typical pictures, students select black-and-white photographs from public-domain collections, showing things such as uniforms, storefronts, vehicles, textiles or painted signs. Before any processing they write down the colors they expect a colorization model to assign and the colors they believe the objects actually had. Each student then colorizes the photograph twice, once with no guidance and once with a short text description, logging every prompt, saving every output, and labeling each as colorized. The research half follows. For each object the student looks for documentary evidence of its color, such as regulations, trade catalogs, paint or dye records, written descriptions from the period, surviving artifacts in museum collections, or early color photographs. Every color choice is marked as supported by evidence, contradicted by it, or not determinable, with the source cited. Groups compare these results with their predictions and across students working on similar subjects, noting where the model defaulted to modern or generic palettes, how skin and fabric were handled, and where a text description overrode the evidence. A shared document collects telling examples, and a debrief returns to the readings to ask what a colorized photograph adds to the historical record and what it takes away.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students research documentary evidence for each colored object and mark the model's choice as supported, contradicted or not determinable.
activities.dl: Written predictions, two labeled colorized versions with logs, an object-by-object evidence table with citations, and a shared group document of examples.
activities.na: Students can hand-tint a printed copy of the photograph from their predictions and run the same evidence check on their own color choices.
activities.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered, and every output is labeled as colorized. Evidence tables use named colors, which supports students with color-vision differences.

activities.t: Auditing generated card art for a global health trade game for nationality stereotypes before play
activities.sum: An instructor and teaching assistant building a classroom card game in which fifteen states trade resources and weather events that affect their populations' health generate the art for resource and event cards with a text-to-image model, aiming for generic images without identifiable people or places. Before the game reaches students, the card set is audited with the method of a published study of nationality stereotypes in generated images. The team first separates traits that can be seen in an image, such as clothing, housing, landscape and transport, from traits that cannot, and writes a short list of visible attributes that would amount to a stereotype for each region represented. A panel, which can include volunteers from a previous offering, annotates every card for those attributes without knowing which state it was generated for. The tallies are then compared across states: do one region's cards show dirt roads, crowding or traditional dress far more often than others, and do plain prompts pull certain states toward the same few images? Cards that carry a stereotype are regenerated with revised prompts, replaced with simple icons, or dropped, and each change is logged. When the game is played, students meet the change log in the debrief and discuss whether and how generic prompts still produced a patterned picture of the world's health.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: A blind panel annotates every card for listed visual stereotype attributes, tallies are compared across states, and flagged cards are revised, replaced or dropped.
activities.dl: An annotated audit of every card with tallies by state, a revised card set with generated images labeled, and a change log used in the students' debrief.
activities.na: The game can use icon-only cards or openly licensed photographs, and the same blind audit can be run on that set.
activities.risk: Students do not use AI. Generated images are labeled and depict no identifiable people or places; panel volunteers are not graded. Cards carry text labels so play does not depend on reading the images.

activities.t: Generating identity-label portraits in two languages and setting them beside archival portraits of the same categories
activities.sum: Groups with access to a second language, whether through a member who speaks it or a language the course teaches, pick a few identity labels that carry social or political weight, for example nurse, migrant worker or engineer, and record the assumptions commonly attached to each. For every label they write prompts in English and in the second language, and where that language marks grammatical gender, in a masculine form, a feminine form and a gender-neutral rephrasing, following the design of a multilingual benchmark study. They generate the same number of portraits for each version with one text-to-image platform, record the platform and settings, and label every image as generated. Each portrait is coded for perceived gender presentation, apparent age, setting and props by two coders, with disagreements noted rather than settled by guesswork. Groups then gather existing portraits of the same categories from openly licensed art-history, news and archival collections and code them the same way, so the generated sets can be compared with the visual history they may draw on. The analysis asks whether the language of the prompt shifted the images, whether neutral phrasing changed anything, and whether the generator repeats or intensifies typologies already present in the archive. Groups present their comparison and write a reflection connecting the tallies to the course's readings on faces and recognition technology.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Two coders per image record perceived gender presentation, apparent age, setting and props; tallies are compared across languages and with an archival set.
activities.dl: Double-coded portrait sets by label and language, a matching coded archival set, comparison tallies, a class presentation, and a written reflection.
activities.na: Groups can compare openly licensed archival and news portraits drawn from collections in two languages or countries, coding them the same way.
activities.risk: Generated faces show no real person; archival portraits come only from openly licensed collections and are never entered into a tool. Codes record perceived presentation only, and groups discuss the limits of coding gender from images.

activities.t: Training a paired image-translation model on the studio's own facade drawings and photographs, then critiquing what it invents
activities.sum: In an architectural design studio, students move from describing facades to building the data a model learns from. Each student photographs a set of campus and neighborhood facades from public streets, framing them straight on, and draws a matching label map by hand in which flat colors stand for wall, window, door, cornice and so on, following a legend the studio agrees. The pooled pairs become a training set for the paired image-translation notebook, which a technical instructor runs and adapts, setting aside some buildings the model never sees. The trained model then renders facades from label maps: first those of the held-out buildings, so its output can be set beside the real photograph, and then new label maps that students draw as design proposals. In studio crits each rendering is examined against the photograph and the label map, asking which elements the model reproduced, which it invented, such as mullions, ornament or weathering, and where it blurred a deliberate design move into a typical facade. Discussion also takes up how the class's own choice of buildings shaped what the model treats as normal. Every rendering is labeled as a model output, and students keep a log of the outputs they accepted and rejected, with reasons, which feeds the studio's discussion of authorship and accountability.

activities.t: Restoring the image of a water-damaged in-house manual page while marking every reconstructed region
activities.sum: A library unit's only printed copy of an in-house procedure binder, written by its own staff, has been water-damaged, and the photographs taken for digitization show stains, tears and faded diagram lines. Staff use an inpainting model to restore the page images so they can be read and reprinted, under rules that keep every generated detail identifiable. Before any processing, a staff member marks on each photograph the regions that may be filled, such as background stains, margins and broken lines in simple diagrams, and excludes every area containing text, numbers or labels, since the model would supply plausible characters that were never there. Text in damaged areas is instead transcribed by a person from the original page or marked as illegible. After restoration, the filled regions are saved as a separate mask layer, so anyone can switch between the original and the restored image, and a diagram that cannot be reconstructed with confidence is labeled as such rather than redrawn. Colleagues who actually perform the procedure then review each restored page against the damaged original and their own knowledge of the steps, confirming or rejecting each filled region. The archived version keeps the original photographs, the restored images, the masks and a processing note.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Staff mask which regions may be filled, exclude all text, and have the people who perform the procedure confirm or reject each filled region.
activities.dl: Restored page images with a separate mask layer of every filled region, human transcriptions or illegibility labels for damaged text, a staff review record, and a processing note.
activities.na: Staff can retype the binder and redraw diagrams by hand from the damaged pages, with the same illegibility labels and review.
activities.risk: Only the library's own in-house document is processed; manufacturer or other third-party manuals are not entered. The retyped text produced alongside the images makes the procedure available to screen-reader users.

activities.t: Asking an image generator to draw your data, then auditing its chart against a figure plotted from the data
activities.sum: In a short research-integrity workshop, researchers bring a small table of their own non-sensitive data and a description of the figure they intend to make from it. Each participant first asks a code-generation assistant for plotting code, reads it until they can vouch for every line, runs it, and saves the resulting figure with the code and the data source. Then, as a test rather than a production step, they give an image generator the same values and the same description and ask it to draw the figure. The two figures are laid side by side and the generated one is audited mark by mark: values that do not match the table, axis ranges and tick labels that were changed or invented, legend entries for series that do not exist, error bars that were never supplied, and lettering that reads plausibly but says nothing. Participants tally what they find and share examples. Discussion links the tally to publisher policies that treat generated or manipulated images in papers as misconduct, and to why a figure that can be regenerated from code and data can be disclosed and checked in a way a picture cannot. Each participant leaves with the reproducible figure, its code, and a disclosure statement for the delegated coding task, while the generated chart is labeled and kept only as a workshop specimen.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: The researcher compares every value, axis, tick label, legend entry and error bar in the generated chart with the figure plotted by code from the same table.
activities.dl: A code-plotted figure with its code and data source, a labeled generated chart, a mark-by-mark audit tally, and a disclosure statement for the coding assistance.
activities.na: Participants can audit an instructor-prepared generated chart against its source table and write the plotting code themselves.
activities.risk: Only the participant's own non-sensitive or synthetic data is entered, and the generated chart is never used in publication. Final figures carry alt text and the data table for screen-reader users.

activities.t: Keeping a student-drawn character consistent across a generated picture book and logging where it drifts
activities.sum: Pre-service teachers producing a short picture book for young readers begin by writing the story and drawing their main character themselves, in a few poses on plain paper, with a short list of features that should not change, such as the shape of the ears, the pattern on a coat, or a missing tooth. They then use an image generator that accepts a small set of reference images of a subject, supplying only their own drawings, and generate the scenes the story needs, saving every prompt and every unedited output. For each page they check the character against the feature list and log each drift: a coat that changes color, an extra finger, an age shift, a face sliding toward a generic cartoon style, or features that change when the setting changes. For each scene they decide whether to accept it, regenerate it, redraw it by hand, or cut it, and record why. Text and selected images are laid out into a draft book of about twelve pages, with the cover stating which images were generated from the student's drawings. The assessed product is the process portfolio of drawings, feature list, prompts, unedited outputs and drift log, together with a reflective essay on authorship, on what consistency means for a child reader, and on the university's AI guidance.
activities.f: Co-Authoring with AI: Voice and Authorship
activities.gate: Students log every drift in the character's listed features across pages and decide which outputs to accept, regenerate, redraw or cut.
activities.dl: Hand-drawn reference sheets and a feature list, saved prompts and unedited outputs, a page-by-page drift log, a draft picture book with labeled images, and a reflective essay.
activities.na: Students can illustrate every scene by hand, or trade reference sheets with a peer who illustrates them, and log drift the same way.
activities.risk: Only the student's own drawings are used as references; no real person's likeness or existing commercial character is entered. Students who do not draw can make cut-paper or collage references.

activities.t: Mapping where data goes during a training job in the institution's managed machine-learning environment
activities.sum: Graduate students in science and engineering who take a research-ethics course before submitting a proposal add a hands-on component to its unit on AI ethics. Individually or in small groups, they train and tune a small predictive model on a public-domain or instructor-supplied dataset inside the managed machine-learning environment that the institution's research computing group provisions for the class, following an open workshop's sequence of storage, notebooks, training jobs, tuning and resource monitoring. While they work, students draw a data-movement map: every place the data or a derivative of it is copied, which region it sits in, which institutional roles can read it, what persists after the job ends, and what the resource meter records. They then carry the map into the ethics case they chose, for example the misuse of personal data from a dating site, and ask what the same handling would have looked like if that case's data had passed through this environment. The written product is the data-management section of a mock research proposal. It analyzes the students' own workflow at the level of the underlying technology, the specific configured system and its use in a research project, and addresses anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness. A short comparison with running the same training on a laptop, where feasible, closes the section.

activities.t: Turning a business ethics privacy question on the institution's own licensed AI service
activities.sum: In a business ethics unit on technology, students finish the assigned readings and, before any AI use, draft their own responses to a pair of workplace privacy questions. They then put the same questions to the institution's licensed AI assistant, which they reach through campus sign-in under the institution's agreement rather than through a personal consumer account, cite the response, and judge how well it answered and what grade it would earn. The second half of the assignment turns the unit's questions on the tool itself. Using the institution's published description of its AI service, and the terms of the agreement where they are public, students work out what happened to what they just typed: whether it is retained and for how long, whether it may be used to train models, which institutional roles can see logs, and what a consumer version of a similar tool would have done differently. They evaluate that arrangement with the same ethical frameworks they applied in their written answers, and say whether their own answer to the privacy questions changes now that they are, in effect, the employees whose inputs are governed by an employer's contract. Answers, chatbot outputs and evaluations are shared with the course, and discussion extends to what students would require of a vendor in their intended careers.

activities.gate: Students write their own answers before using the assistant, grade its answer against theirs, and then establish from institutional documents what happened to their own inputs.

activities.na: Students can analyze the institution's published AI-service description and a consumer service's terms without using either tool, and answer the same privacy questions.
activities.risk: Students use institutional sign-in and need no personal account or payment. Students are asked not to enter personal information about themselves or others. Where the institution has not published service terms, the instructor might obtain a summary from the IT office.

activities.t: Evaluating a reference assistant grounded in the library's own documentation inside the institution's environment
activities.sum: A reference librarian who wants to know whether a document-grounded assistant could help answer the library's email questions adapts a published method for scoring a general chatbot on real reference questions, changing where the system runs and what it reads. Email questions the library received during a chosen period are collected, stripped of personal and confidential details, and sorted by type and by the effort level they demand. The library's systems partner configures a retrieval-grounded assistant inside the institution's own cloud environment, indexing only the library's public web pages and internal service documentation on hours, borrowing, interlibrary loan and access problems. Before any question is run, the librarian and the systems partner map every data transfer in the arrangement, from document ingestion to the query path, logs and retention, and confirm that question text stays within the institution's environment. Each question then goes to the assistant, and every answer is rated at three levels for how complete and how accurate it is and whether it points the user to further help, with accuracy checked by reference colleagues and a note on whether the answer cited a local page. The analysis pays particular attention to local, complex and access questions, the categories where the published evaluation found a general chatbot weakest. A short memo for library leadership addresses need, process, results, unintended outcomes and the cost of keeping the index current.

activities.gate: Librarians map every data transfer before testing, then score each answer on the rubric with accuracy confirmed by colleagues against current policies and pages.
activities.dl: A de-identified, typed question set, a data-transfer map of the assistant, rubric scores for every answer with notes on local citations, and an evaluation memo.
activities.na: The librarian can score the library's existing answer templates or FAQ pages against the same question set and rubric to find gaps in documentation.
activities.risk: No patron uses the assistant during the evaluation, and de-identified questions are processed inside the institution's environment. The work requires a systems partner with access to an institutional cloud tenancy.

activities.t: Scoping an enterprise assistant to instructor-authored files before it drafts discussion questions from public-domain readings
activities.sum: An instructor preparing an upper-division course on nature writing, built on public-domain and openly licensed readings rather than a textbook, uses the institution's licensed AI assistant to draft discussion questions, and first deals with a feature of enterprise deployment: the assistant can draw on any file the instructor's account can open. For many instructors that includes earlier students' submissions saved in cloud storage, colleagues' shared drafts and committee papers. Working with IT or library staff, the instructor builds a folder holding only the course readings, the outcomes document and their own lecture notes, and restricts the assistant to that folder where the tool allows it. A short test question about the course, read alongside the file references the assistant attaches to its answer, shows whether the restriction holds. The instructor then prompts iteratively for questions tied to named outcomes. Every question is checked twice: against the reading, for a page or passage it points to and for claims the text does not make, and against the files the assistant cites, so that any question drawing on something outside the folder is discarded and the gap reported to IT. Questions that fail either check are dropped or rewritten. The instructor tells students how the questions were produced and what the assistant was allowed to read, and shares the folder setup with colleagues.
activities.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
activities.gate: The instructor narrows what the assistant may read, tests that the restriction holds, and checks every question against the reading and against the files the assistant cites.
activities.dl: A scoped source folder, a recorded test of the restriction, a passage-checked and reference-checked set of discussion questions tied to course outcomes, and a short setup note for colleagues.
activities.na: The instructor writes discussion questions from their own reading of the texts, using the same list of outcomes.
activities.risk: Students do not use the assistant and nothing they have written is meant to enter it; the scoping step and reference check exist to keep earlier students' work out. Where the assistant cannot be restricted to the folder, earlier students' work may remain within its reach, so a course that needs to guarantee that no student text enters a tool can use the non-AI route. Only public-domain or openly licensed readings and instructor-written notes are supplied.

activities.t: Testing an enterprise-licensed and an institution-hosted model on accreditation evidence mapping against a preset threshold
activities.sum: An accreditation and assessment office that wants to know whether AI can help map evidence artifacts to accreditation standards tests the two deployments the institution has approved, rather than whichever tool is at hand. Staff first select nonsensitive artifacts that policy allows for the test, leaving out any candidate-authored work, and two experts code each one against the codebook independently and reconcile their differences; that reconciled coding is the reference. Before any model runs, the office sets the agreement level a deployment would need to reach before its labels could be used for anything beyond suggestions, following the practice of fixing an automation threshold in advance. The same artifacts and instructions then go to the institution's enterprise-licensed assistant and to an open-weight model the institution hosts on its own servers. The comparison matters for a practical reason. Some evidence the office routinely handles, such as samples of candidates' coursework, may be processed only on the hosted model under the institution's data policy, so the hosted model's accuracy on the test set decides whether AI has any role with those materials. Agreement with the expert coding is reported at the finer criterion level and the broader standard level for each deployment, and disagreements are reviewed one by one. The office records its decision, with the reasons, in its governance documentation.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Experts code first and reconcile, the office fixes an agreement threshold before any model runs, and every model label and disagreement is checked against the reconciled coding.
activities.dl: A reconciled expert coding of the test artifacts, a preset agreement threshold, criterion- and standard-level agreement figures for each deployment, a disagreement review, and a recorded governance decision.
activities.na: The office continues expert coding alone, which the test uses as its reference in any case.
activities.risk: Only nonsensitive artifacts the institution's policy permits for testing are used, with no candidate-authored work in the test set, and only within approved deployments; any later use with candidates' coursework is a separate governance decision. The hosted model requires institutional infrastructure; no one is asked to use a personal account.

activities.t: Checking a draft peer review on a local, offline model while the manuscript stays out of every tool
activities.sum: A faculty member who has drafted a review for a journal or conference wants a check on the review's own quality, but the review is part of a confidential process and many editorial policies prohibit sending reviews or manuscripts to outside AI services. Following an open course's appendix on running language models locally, the reviewer installs an openly available model on their own computer and works with the network connection switched off, after confirming that the venue's reviewer policy allows local use of this kind and noting how it would be disclosed if asked. Only the reviewer's own draft review goes to the model; the manuscript stays out of every tool. Drawing on the published design of a review-feedback pipeline, the reviewer runs three checks in turn: comments that are vague or generic, remarks that read as unprofessional, and a list of every question the review puts to the authors. The third check is completed by hand. The reviewer takes each listed question back to the manuscript and marks it as genuinely open or already answered, with the page. Each flag is treated as a suggestion, and because a local model is smaller than those the pipeline was built on, the reviewer also notes flags that are wrong or trivial. The reviewer then revises, or does not, and keeps a brief note of which flags led to changes.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The reviewer checks each flag and each listed question against the manuscript by reading it, decides whether to revise, and records which flags were wrong or trivial.
activities.dl: A revised review, a record of each flag with the reviewer's decision, a question list marked open or already answered with manuscript pages, and a note of false or trivial flags.
activities.na: The reviewer can apply the same three checks as a self-review checklist, or ask a co-reviewer to read the draft review where the venue allows.
activities.risk: Requires a computer able to run a small local model; the software and models are free. Local configuration alone does not prove that no data leaves the device, so the reviewer disables network access during the run. The manuscript, a third-party work, is never entered into any tool.

activities.t: Debriefing a hospital emergency simulation from transcripts kept under an institutional retention schedule
activities.sum: Faculty who run a role-differentiated hospital emergency simulation, in which each student takes one professional role in a hospital's response and answers in writing as the scenario escalates, host the scenario engine on the institution's managed chat service instead of a public chatbot. The institutional arrangement changes three things. Students sign in with their campus identity rather than a personal account. Each conversation is stored in institution-controlled storage under a retention period the program sets. And faculty can retrieve a student's transcript afterward. Before the simulation, students are told what is stored, who can read it, for how long, and how to request an alternative format. The faculty-configured scenario engine presents time-sensitive prompts across defined phases and ends with a role-specific debrief of its own. The faculty debrief then works from the stored transcripts. Each student's decisions are set against the scenario's escalation phases and the unit's emergency protocol, and students compare the engine's automatic debrief with the faculty one, marking where the engine praised a decision the protocol does not support or passed over a delay that mattered. Excerpts used in group discussion are shared only with the student's agreement and with names removed, and the retained transcripts are deleted at the end of the stated period.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Faculty and students analyze stored transcripts against the escalation phases and emergency protocol, and students contest the engine's automatic debrief.
activities.dl: Stored simulation transcripts, a faculty debrief built on them, each student's annotated comparison of the automatic and faculty debriefs, and consented, anonymized excerpts for group discussion.
activities.na: Faculty can run the scenario as a tabletop exercise, with a faculty member presenting the escalation prompts and a note-taker recording decisions for the debrief.
activities.risk: Campus sign-in replaces personal accounts and there is no cost to students. Students are told in advance what is stored and who can see it; excerpts are shared in group debrief only with consent, and retention follows the program's stated schedule.

activities.t: Testing what data minimization costs when IEP goals are drafted on an approved hosted service
activities.sum: Preservice and in-service special educators practice drafting individualized education program goals from fictional, instructor-written student scenarios, with an added question that their future practice will raise: how much of a student's information a goal-writing tool actually needs. For the first scenario each participant writes a goal unaided. For the second, they fill in a published structured goal template in two versions and submit each to the institution's privately hosted AI service, which the program has approved and which does not retain prompts. The full version supplies every field, including the scenario's invented name and disability identification. The minimized version replaces the name with a placeholder, omits the disability category, and keeps only the present level of performance, goal area, condition, behavior, criterion and time frame. Participants then rate all three goals, the unaided one and both generated ones, on six items of a published goal-rating instrument, which look at whether the behavior a goal targets can be seen and counted, serves the student's daily functioning, carries over to new settings, and can be taught by different team members across the day, and compare ratings with a partner. A short written reflection names which fields could be left out without weakening the goal, which seemed to matter, and which they would not enter into any tool, approved or not, when the student is real. The instructor gathers the field-by-field findings across the class and shares the pattern.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Participants write one goal unaided before any tool use, then rate all goals on the rubric and judge field by field what minimization cost.
activities.dl: An unaided goal, two generated goals from full and minimized templates, partner-compared rubric ratings for all three, and a reflection on which fields each goal needed.
activities.na: Participants can write the second goal twice by hand, once from the full scenario and once from the minimized fields, and rate all goals with the same rubric.
activities.risk: Only instructor-written fictional scenarios are used; no information about a real student enters any tool. The institution's hosted service uses campus sign-in and requires no personal account or payment.

activities.t: Building a small corpus from machine-transcribed handwritten letters and tracing how transcription errors move the counts
activities.sum: Students assemble a small corpus of handwritten letters from a public-domain digitized collection, saving each page image with a file name that carries the date and writer. Before any machine processing, each student reads and transcribes one page by hand, and that transcription becomes the reference for the page. The instructor or the students then send every page image to an image-reading model with a fixed transcription instruction and keep the raw output. As in the archival study the operation comes from, they compute character and word error rates on the hand-transcribed pages, run a second correction pass on a few pages, and measure whether it helped. The corpus is loaded into a web-based counting environment twice, once as raw machine text and once with the sample pages corrected, and students work through guided questions comparing the two: which frequent words change rank, which words that seem distinctive of a writer turn out to be misreadings, how spelling variants and abbreviations were silently modernized, and what a keyword-in-context search misses when one name is transcribed three different ways. Each claim students make about a writer's vocabulary is checked against the page image of at least one occurrence. The products are the error-rate table, the paired frequency tables, and a short account of which findings survive correction.

activities.gate: Students hand-transcribe sample pages to measure error rates, then compare frequencies and concordances built from raw and corrected text.

activities.t: Suggesting retention categories for scanned records with a document-reading model and comparing each suggestion with an archivist's decision
activities.sum: A university records unit testing whether a document-reading model could help sort a backlog draws on a published teaching case in which archivists compared machine classifiers with their own decisions. Archivists select a pilot batch of scanned records from the institution's own files, excluding anything containing personal or restricted information, and first assign each record to a category of the retention and disposition schedule themselves, without seeing any machine output. A staff member then gives the model each scanned record as a document, together with the schedule's category definitions, and asks for a suggested category, the passage or visual feature it relied on, and a statement when the record fits no category. The suggestions are tabulated beside the archivists' decisions. For each disagreement an archivist returns to the record and accepts, amends or rejects the suggestion, writing down the grounds and noting where layout, handwriting, stamps or attachments were misread. The team summarizes agreement by category, the kinds of records that went wrong, and whether the passages the model cited actually supported its suggestions. Retention decisions stay with archivists throughout, and the pilot report states whether the model suits a first sort, particular record series, or nothing at all, with the reasoning attached.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Archivists decide each record independently first, then accept, amend or reject the model's suggestion and record the grounds.
activities.dl: A table of archivists' independent decisions beside model suggestions and cited passages, a record of accepted, amended and rejected suggestions with grounds, and a pilot report.
activities.na: Archivists assign schedule categories by hand with a second archivist reviewing a sample, as in the reference condition of the parent case.
activities.risk: Only institutional records cleared for processing are used, in an institution-approved environment; restricted and personal records are excluded.

activities.t: Walking a site first, then testing an image model's segmentation of the street against field counts
activities.sum: Before designing for a site, architecture students walk the street in pairs, sketch the elevations, and record simple field counts at fixed points: trees, entrances, storefronts, parked cars, bus stops, and how much sky they can see. At the same points they take their own photographs from standing height, avoiding faces and license plates or blurring them. Back in the studio, they give the photographs to an image-understanding model and ask for segmentation masks and object locations, then compute what share of each image the model assigns to sky, vegetation, building facade, roadway and pavement, and how many entrances or trees it detects. These figures are set against the field counts and sketches point by point. Where the two disagree, students look at the mask itself and mark what went wrong: shadows labeled as road, glass facades read as sky, street trees merged with a park behind them, an entrance missed because it was recessed. Groups then decide which measures are reliable enough to include in the design brief, which need the field count instead, and which questions about the site neither source can answer, such as how the street is used at night. The discussion of model bias asks how these errors might relate to the kinds of streets represented in the model's training data.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students compare segment shares and detections with their field counts and sketches and mark mislabeled regions.
activities.dl: Field sketches and counts, segmentation masks with computed shares, a point-by-point comparison marking mislabeled regions, and a section of the design brief stating which measures were used and why.
activities.na: Students can estimate shares by laying a grid over printed photographs and counting cells, comparing the grid estimates with field counts in the same way.
activities.risk: Students use their own photographs taken from public streets, with faces and plates blurred. Pairs can divide walking and recording roles so students with mobility constraints can take part.

activities.t: Extracting DuPont inputs from a layout-heavy annual report by hand and with a document-reading model, then reconciling the two
activities.sum: Students analyzing financial statements work from an annual report the instructor has built as a PDF for a fictional company and laid out the way real reports are: income statement and balance sheet on different pages, a table continued across a page break, figures in thousands in one table and millions in another, a restated prior year in a footnote, and a chart that repeats some numbers. Each student first locates the needed figures, works out the three-part DuPont breakdown of return on equity, with its margin, turnover and leverage components, and writes an interpretation. They then give the same PDF to a document-reading model with an instruction to extract each input with its page and table, show every step of the calculation, and state its assumptions, such as whether average or year-end equity was used. Students reconcile the two analyses figure by figure. Each difference is traced to the page and classified as a misread layout, an unconverted unit, a missed restatement, a different but defensible assumption, or an error of their own. A 300-word reflection compares the two analyses and states which conclusions about the company hold under both. Because the report is fictional and instructor-written, an answer key exists, and the layout features can be varied from one term to the next.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students extract and compute by hand first, then reconcile every figure and step with the model's, tracing each difference to the page.
activities.dl: A hand-computed DuPont analysis and interpretation, the model's step-by-step extraction and calculation, a figure-by-figure reconciliation with classified differences, and a 300-word reflection.
activities.na: Students can exchange hand analyses with a partner and reconcile them the same way, using the answer key as the final reference.
activities.risk: The report is fictional and instructor-written, so no third-party filing is entered into a tool. The PDF is tagged for screen readers with tables marked up.
