activities.t: Asking an image-reading model to assess a documented nineteenth-century photographic hoax, with and without the caption
activities.sum: Each student chooses a documented photographic hoax from the nineteenth or early twentieth century whose images are in the public domain, such as the spirit photographs exposed in court in the 1860s, and researches how it was made and how it was exposed. They then test an image-reading model as a would-be verifier. In the first run the photograph goes in cropped of any caption or label, with a request to describe what is shown and say whether there are signs of manipulation. In the second, the same image goes in with its catalog caption. Students go through both responses one statement at a time and mark each as visible in the image, not visible, or supplied from elsewhere, paying particular attention to objects, attributes and relations the model describes that are not there, and to claims about the photographer or technique that appear only once the caption is given. A short in-class presentation compares the model's two accounts with the documented history of the hoax. Discussion follows on what was hardest to check, whether a model that recognizes a famous image is seeing it or remembering it, how this compares with earlier manipulation and its exposure, and whether and by whom image-reading tools should be relied on for verification.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students mark each statement in both responses as visible in the image, not visible, or supplied from elsewhere, and compare with the documented history.
activities.dl: Two model responses per photograph with a statement-by-statement mark-up, a short presentation comparing them with the documented history, and discussion notes.
activities.na: Students can compare two published descriptions of the same hoax photograph, one from its own era and one from a modern catalog, marking which statements are visible in the image.
activities.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered. Class-written verbal descriptions of each image let blind and low-vision students take part in the mark-up.

activities.t: Reading aloud an AI team member's pre-generated interpretation of a public overdose chart in an interprofessional case
activities.sum: In an interprofessional course, graduate students in nursing, pharmacy, social work and related programs prepare a community case about opioid overdoses and then work through it in small groups led by faculty. While preparing the facilitator guide, faculty give an image-reading model a public-domain chart of overdose deaths over time from a federal surveillance report, along with the case materials, and ask it, in the role of a health services team member, what the chart shows and what the community should do. Faculty choose readings that will be instructive in discussion, for example one that attributes a change in the trend line to a policy without evidence of cause, one that misreads an axis or a footnote about provisional data, and one that is careful and accurate, and they keep these unedited in the guide. During the session the facilitator projects the chart and reads the agent's interpretation aloud at set points. Teams test each claim against the chart and its data notes, saying which are supported, which go beyond the data, and which are simply wrong, and then decide what, if anything, from the agent's reading they would carry into their plan for the community. Students never use the model themselves. The groups then come together to compare findings and how they split the checking of the agent's contributions across their professions.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Teams test each claim in the agent's reading against the chart and its data notes, then decide what, if anything, to carry into their plan.
activities.dl: Team annotations of each pre-generated claim (supported, beyond the data, wrong) and a section of the team's plan stating what it took from the agent's reading and why.
activities.na: The facilitator can read instructor-written interpretations of the chart that contain the same kinds of overreach, presented as a colleague's view.
activities.risk: Students do not use AI; faculty generate the readings in advance. A table of the chart's values accompanies the projection for screen-reader users.

activities.t: Having an image-reading model narrate a student's hand-drawn methods diagram, then checking the narration against the paper
activities.sum: Working from the methods section of an assigned study alone, students sketch its procedure by hand as a diagram, showing the variables the researchers changed, the outcomes they recorded, the sequence of steps, the units sampled and the number of repetitions, with each element tied to the research question it addresses. Instead of asking a tool to describe the paper, they photograph their own diagram and give only the photograph to an image-reading model, asking it to narrate step by step the experiment the diagram depicts. Because the model has not seen the paper, its narration tests what the drawing actually communicates. Students lay the narration beside the methods text and mark every departure: a step the narration adds, a sample size it invents, two conditions it merges, an order it reverses, a control it misses. For each departure they decide whether the diagram was ambiguous, quoting the methods sentence the diagram was meant to show, or whether the model misread a clear drawing, which they also record. They revise the diagram to remove the ambiguities they own and photograph it again for a second narration. Submissions include both diagrams, both narrations with departures marked, and a one-sentence statement of the design the paper used. A drawing whose elements cannot each be tied to a sentence of the methods counts as unfinished.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students mark where the narration departs from the methods text, decide whether the diagram or the model is at fault, and revise the diagram.
activities.dl: An original and a revised hand-drawn methods diagram, two model narrations with departures marked and their causes attributed, and a one-sentence design statement.
activities.na: A partner who has not read the paper can narrate the diagram aloud, and the student marks departures the same way, as in the parent's partner comparison.
activities.risk: Only the student's own drawing is entered. Students who cannot draw by hand can build the diagram with shapes in any drawing software, and the model reads either.

activities.t: Captioning paired public-domain portraits with an attention model and examining what each gendered word attended to
activities.sum: The instructor selects pairs of public-domain portraits of sitters of comparable standing, such as a woman and a man who were both scientists, rulers or writers of the same period, and checks that each pair offers a meaningful comparison and that the assigned scholarship covers both sitters. Students first read the scholarship and note how it establishes each sitter's context and achievement. The instructor then runs the portraits through the caption model built in the visual-attention tutorial, which writes a short caption and records, for every word, the region of the image it attended to. Students receive the captions and per-word attention maps rather than using the model themselves. They examine the language of each caption, which words name the sitter, describe appearance, or suggest activity or status, and then check each gendered or status word against its attention map, asking whether the word rests on the person's face and body or on surrounding objects such as a book, a gown or a desk. They keep observations about these outputs separate from claims about the historical people, which come from the scholarship. Discussion moves through three levels, what attention-based captioning does in general, what this trained model took from its particular training images, and what follows from applying it to historical portraits, and considers whether the differences support a hypothesis about how those training images shape its descriptions and which further portrait pairs could challenge it. Students submit a short comparison quoting captions and attention evidence.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students compare captions for paired sitters and check whether gendered and status words rest on the person or on surrounding objects.
activities.dl: Captions and per-word attention maps for each portrait pair, a student comparison quoting both, and a stated hypothesis with the further pairs that would test it.
activities.na: Students can compare published museum catalog descriptions of the same portrait pairs, marking which words describe the person and which describe setting and dress.
activities.risk: Students do not use AI; the instructor runs the notebook and builds the caption model only from training images and weights whose terms permit classroom use, such as a public-domain captioned image set. Only public-domain portraits are entered as inputs, and class-written descriptions of each portrait support blind and low-vision students.

activities.t: Coding public-domain documentary photographs, then weighing a multimodal model's descriptions against the image and the original caption
activities.sum: Students in a visual research methods course draw a sample of documentary photographs from a public-domain government collection of the 1930s and 1940s, each with the original caption written by the photographer or project staff. Working from a codebook the class agrees on, each student first codes every photograph, recording people, activities, setting, material conditions and any theme they see, and notes where the original caption steers the reading. A multimodal model is then asked for a detailed description of each photograph and a few theme tags, as in the digital humanities project the operation comes from, but it is given the image without its caption. Students break each description into claims and rate them: visible in the image, a reasonable inference, an inference the image cannot support, or plainly wrong, such as people miscounted or objects that are not there. They also compare the model's tags with their own codes and with the photographer's caption, which carries its own framing of poverty and dignity. Pairs compare their ratings on the same photographs and discuss where they disagree. Students submit the model's analysis together with their own assessment of it, and a short note on whether such descriptions would help or mislead someone searching the collection.

activities.gate: Students code first, then rate each description claim for accuracy and overreach and calibrate their ratings with a partner.
activities.dl: Student codes for each photograph, the model's descriptions and tags, a claim-by-claim rating sheet, pair calibration notes, and a short note on use in collection search.
activities.na: Students can rate one another's written descriptions of the same photographs with the same four categories and calibrate in pairs.
activities.risk: Only public-domain photographs are entered. Class-written descriptions let blind and low-vision students do the rating with a partner.

activities.t: Pairing a deep-research agent's report with a rerunnable database search for each claim
activities.sum: A researcher assembling the evidence behind an argument breaks it into questions that each pose a single proposition data could settle, and groups them under the parts of the argument they support. For each question, a deep-research agent is asked to plan the task before it runs; the researcher saves the plan, notes what it leaves out, such as a population, a time window, or a type of study, and edits the request where the plan is too broad. The agent then searches, reads, and produces a report with references, which is saved with its run date. Because a generated report cannot be rerun to the same result, the researcher builds a second, independent channel for each question: a field-tagged search strategy in a bibliographic database, written out in full so that anyone can repeat it, with its date and hit count. Reference sets from the two channels are deduplicated by identifier and compared. The researcher records the overlap, the references found only by the agent, and the references found only by the database, and reads a sample from each group to judge whether they bear on the claim. Questions on which the channels diverge sharply are flagged, the researcher checks whether the literature behind them is recent, unevenly indexed, or dominated by preprints, and the divergence is reported as a figure alongside the synthesis rather than smoothed over.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher critiques the agent's plan before it runs, compares its reference set with a written-out database search, and reports divergence between channels as a measurement.
activities.dl: For each claim, an annotated research plan, the dated agent report with references, a written database search strategy with date and hit count, an overlap table between channels, and a divergence figure reported with the synthesis.
activities.na: The researcher runs the database channel alone, with a second bibliographic database as the independent comparison.
activities.risk: Deep-research modes are often limited to paid tiers; the database channel needs library database access. Only the researcher's questions enter the tool.

activities.t: Comparing a discovery system's AI research assistant with its standard search in a criminology source hunt
activities.sum: Each student takes a US city whose crime rate exceeds the national figure and, over three linked parts, accounts for it through a criminological theory. The data stage stays free of AI: students gather national and city crime rates and local unemployment and poverty figures from government statistical sources, documenting every source. In the source-discovery stage, students put their research question to the library discovery system twice, once to its AI research assistant, which returns a generated overview and a handful of sources, and once as a conventional keyword search they construct and record. They then compare the two in the way an academic library's adoption study did: how many sources overlap, what share of each list is actually about the city's crime and the theory, and whether the overview describes each source accurately, checked by reading each source's abstract against the sentence that mentions it. Students also note whether the overview presents its handful of sources as the answer or leaves the wider result list in view. From the combined, checked set they identify three arguments linking the theory to the city, with peer-reviewed sources and full citations, and submit both result lists with their comparison. The recorded keyword search remains the reproducible record of how sources were found; the overview is treated as one more claim about the literature. A recorded presentation follows, with feedback between parts.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Students compare the assistant's sources with a recorded keyword search, judge topical relevance, and check each overview sentence about a source against that source's abstract.
activities.dl: A documented data sheet produced without AI; the assistant's overview and source list; the student's recorded keyword search and results; an overlap, relevance, and summary-accuracy comparison; three theory-based arguments with sources; and a recorded presentation.
activities.na: Students who opt out use the conventional discovery search only, as the original assignment allowed, and compare two keyword strategies instead.
activities.risk: Uses the library's licensed discovery system through institutional login where the AI assistant feature is enabled; no personal or paid account is needed. If the feature is unavailable, the instructor can demonstrate it or supply saved outputs.

activities.t: Catching a planted contraindication in a web-grounded answer and weighing the pages it cites
activities.sum: Occupational therapy doctoral students preparing for fieldwork watch their instructor put an instructor-written patient case to a web-grounded assistant during a seminar and ask it for intervention suggestions, so that the answer arrives with inline citations to the pages it drew on. The instructor selects three suggestions, one of them chosen deliberately because it is contraindicated for this patient, and saves each with its cited pages. Students do not use the tool themselves. In small groups they first examine the cited pages for each option: who published the page, what kind of evidence it reports, whether it addresses a population like this patient, and whether it actually supports the suggestion attached to it. They then search the professional literature themselves for each strategy, recording their database searches so they can be repeated. For each option the group states whether it would accept it, amend it, or reject it, with the grounds, and identifies what in the cited pages made the unsafe option look plausible. The instructor, who knows in advance which option is contraindicated and why, checks the groups' evidence reviews against that reasoning. In a follow-on individual assignment, students generate interventions for a new case on their own and document the evidence behind each.

activities.gate: Students appraise each option's cited pages, run and record their own literature searches, and accept, amend, or reject each option with stated grounds.
activities.dl: A group appraisal of each option's cited pages, recorded literature searches, an accept, amend, or reject decision with grounds for each option, an account of what made the unsafe option plausible, and a follow-on individual intervention plan.
activities.na: The instructor presents three options from a published case with one planted unsafe option and a set of web pages of mixed quality, and students appraise them the same way.
activities.risk: The instructor runs the tool, so students need no account; the case is instructor-written and contains no patient data.

activities.t: Fact-checking a generated biography and the provenance of the pages it cites
activities.sum: Students receive, or generate for the occasion, a short biography of a well-documented figure in their institution's history, written by a generative search engine with citations to web pages. Choosing someone with local records, such as archives, yearbooks, or news coverage, means the checking can be finished. Students first work through the biography with lateral reading in the SIFT pattern, stopping on each claim, investigating, finding better coverage, and tracing it to its origin, and they correct the errors they find. A second pass turns to the cited pages themselves. A recent audit of generative search engines, by its authors' account, found that a meaningful share of cited pages showed signs of being machine-written, so students examine each cited page's provenance by hand: whether an author or organization is named and can be found elsewhere, whether the page reports anything first-hand or only restates other pages, whether its dates and details agree with the archival record, and what the page seems designed to get readers to do. They do not run detection software, and they record a page as unestablished rather than machine-written when its origin cannot be determined. The product is a corrected biography with a source table that marks each cited page as reliable, secondary, or unestablished, and notes which errors in the biography trace to which pages.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students fact-check each claim by lateral reading against local records, then examine each cited page's provenance, marking pages whose origin cannot be established as unestablished.
activities.dl: A corrected biography, a claim log with the evidence for each correction, and a source table classifying each cited page as reliable, secondary, or unestablished, linked to the errors it produced.
activities.na: Students fact-check a short web biography from an aggregator site with SIFT and assess the provenance of its sources in the same way.
activities.risk: Free-tier generative search engines suffice, and the instructor can supply a pre-generated biography. The subject should be a figure in the institution's public history, not a private individual.

activities.t: Regenerating AI search answers on news questions to map which outlets get cited
activities.sum: A media studies class chooses three or four current-affairs questions, such as a local policy dispute, a health story, and an environmental story, and each student puts one question to an AI search system several times: regenerating the answer within a session, asking again in a fresh session, and repeating a few days later. Where more than one system is available, the same question goes to each. Students record every outlet cited in every answer in a shared sheet, along with the date and system. The tally becomes the object of study. Groups count how many distinct outlets appear, what share of citations goes to the few most-cited outlets, and how much the set changes between regenerations and between systems. They compare their small sample with a large published study of AI search citations, which reported citations concentrated among a small set of established outlets and, by its author's measure, differences in the political leaning of cited outlets across providers. Students look up each frequently cited outlet in at least two published media-rating sources and note where the ratings disagree, rather than adopting a single verdict. The written analysis treats the answers' wording only in passing; its subject is which outlets the systems treat as worth citing, how stable that selection is, and what a reader who never clicks through would miss.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students tally cited outlets across regenerations, sessions, and systems, measure concentration and stability, and look up each frequent outlet's ratings in two published sources.
activities.dl: A shared citation tally by question, system, session, and date; concentration and stability measures; outlet ratings from two published sources; and a written analysis of citation patterns.
activities.na: Students tally the outlets on the first results page of two ordinary search engines for the same questions over several days and compare concentration the same way.
activities.risk: Free-tier AI search tools suffice; students without access can work from answers saved by classmates or the instructor.

activities.t: Editable Boolean strings beside generated answers in a team-taught engineering library session
activities.sum: A librarian and an engineering lecturer co-teach one session on generative AI and finding sources, each with a defined part. The librarian covers how answer engines and search-strategy assistants differ, the invention of sources that do not exist, and the coverage of what chatbots draw on; the lecturer states where AI use fits the discipline and where it does not, such as analyzing a specific product, where generic output falls short. Students then bring one research question and use it twice. They first give it to an assistant that translates a natural-language question into a Boolean search string, shown in full, editable, and run in the library's discovery system. Students read the string, change the terms, synonyms, and field limits they think are wrong or missing, rerun it, and save both versions with their result counts. They then put the same question to a generative answer engine and save its answer and sources. In pairs they compare what each route lets them inspect: the edited string can be rerun by anyone and its ranked results scanned, while the generated answer offers a synthesis whose path to its sources cannot be repeated. The lecturer reviews a sample of the edited strings for disciplinary vocabulary, and a short quiz on ethical use, on paper or online, closes the session.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Students edit the generated Boolean string, rerun it, save both versions with result counts, and compare what the ranked results and the generated answer each let them inspect.
activities.dl: The generated and edited Boolean strings with result counts, a saved generated answer with its sources, a paired comparison of what each route allows students to inspect, and a completed quiz.
activities.na: Students build a Boolean string by hand from a concept map of their question with the librarian, run it, and compare it with a peer's string for the same question.
activities.risk: Uses the library's discovery system; a free-tier general assistant can stand in for a purpose-built Boolean tool, and the quiz can be taken on paper.

activities.t: Rebuilding a web-grounded balanced scorecard from a company's own filings
activities.sum: Students in a strategic management course work with a named public company. The instructor, or each student, asks a web-grounded assistant to draft a balanced scorecard for the company with SMART goals in each perspective, citing the pages behind every figure and baseline. Students then trace each number twice. First they open the cited page and record what kind of source it is, whether the company's own annual report or regulatory filing, a financial-data aggregator, a news story, or something else, and whether the figure appears there as stated. Then they locate the same figure in the company's most recent filing, which they read directly rather than entering it into the tool, and note mismatches in year, unit, segment, or definition, such as a company-wide total presented as a single segment. Goals whose baselines cannot be traced to a primary filing are rebuilt from the filing, and goals that rest on invented figures are dropped and noted; an instructor following the assignment-design technique behind this record might weight catching such figures above presentation. The revised scorecard is set out in the form a strategy analyst would hand to a manager, with a source column pointing to the page of the filing for each baseline, and a short note on which kinds of cited pages carried the errors that were found.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students trace each figure to its cited page and then to the company's own filing, and rebuild or drop goals that do not hold.
activities.dl: A source-traced audit of each figure in the generated scorecard, a revised scorecard with a filing-page reference for every baseline, and a note on which kinds of cited pages carried errors.
activities.na: Students build the scorecard directly from the company's filings, then compare it with a classmate's version for the same company.
activities.risk: Free-tier web-grounded assistants suffice; the company's filings are read by students and never uploaded, and the instructor can supply a pre-generated scorecard.

activities.t: Using a model-drafted search strategy to trace a contested teaching claim to its evidence
activities.sum: Preservice teachers each choose a claim about teaching and learning that they believe and might one day act on, such as a claim about homework, class size, or matching instruction to preferred learning modes. Before searching, each writes the claim, a sentence on how strongly they feel about it and why, and their own list of search terms. A conversational assistant is then asked for one thing only: a search strategy for an education research database, with concepts, synonyms, and Boolean structure, but no sources and no verdict. Students run their own terms and the drafted strategy in the database, record each string exactly with its date and hit count, and compare what each retrieves, revising the strategy where the assistant's terms were too broad, missed the field's vocabulary, or quietly narrowed the claim. They then read the studies they select, and for each piece of evidence explain how it connects to the claim and what it cannot establish, look for a plausible competing interpretation, and revise the claim. The written trace keeps the student's opening reaction and the final judgment side by side, separating what they felt about the claim from what the evidence warrants in this context. The recorded strings remain the reproducible record of the search; the assistant never supplies evidence, only a draft of how to look for it.

activities.gate: Students write their claim, their reaction to it, and their own search terms first, then run, compare, and revise the drafted strategy and read the evidence themselves.
activities.dl: A claim with an opening reaction note, the student's and the assistant's search strings with dates and hit counts, a revised strategy, an evidence trace for each selected study, and a revised claim.
activities.na: Students build the strategy with a librarian or from the database's thesaurus, compare it with a peer's, and complete the evidence trace in the same way.
activities.risk: Requires library database access and any free conversational assistant; only the claim and search terms enter the tool.

activities.t: Checking a generated previsualization clip against a handwritten shot specification
activities.sum: Students in a cinematography course who have studied a single-shot film excerpt, noting whose view it adopts, how the frame is composed, the path and placement of the camera, the plane of focus and the lens, write by hand a half-page proposal for an original shot that works with the same variables. The proposal ends in a short shot specification: where the camera starts and ends, how it moves, what is in focus, and what the viewer should notice first. Only then does each student turn the specification into a prompt for a text-to-video generator, optionally attaching two or three of their own frame sketches as reference images, and generate a clip of a few seconds. The clip is treated as a test render of the written plan rather than as a finished shot. Alone or with a partner, students step through it frame by frame and mark each variable as delivered, approximated, contradicted or added, noting in particular camera moves the model introduced on its own, focus that drifts, and set dressing or figures the specification never asked for. A second generation with a revised prompt can show whether a missed variable responds to wording at all. In a closing critique, each student presents the specification beside both clips and says which decisions they would now hand to a camera operator, which they would rewrite, and what the comparison taught them about describing a shot precisely.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Students analyze a source excerpt and hand-write the shot specification before any generation, and the specification remains the standard the clip is judged against.
activities.dl: A handwritten shot specification, one or two generated test clips, a variable-by-variable compliance sheet, and a short critique statement.
activities.na: Students can shoot a rough phone previsualization with classmates or objects as stand-ins and run the same variable-by-variable comparison against the written specification.
activities.risk: Video generation is often limited on free tiers; the instructor might run generation from one departmental account using students' prompts. Only student-made sketches are used as reference images, prompts do not name or describe real people, and any clip shown outside class is labeled as synthetic.

activities.t: Frame-by-frame debugging of a generated clip of a scriptural scene against the passage
activities.sum: An instructor in a religious studies course chooses a short narrative scene from a public-domain translation of a sacred text and, before class, generates two brief clips of it with a text-to-video tool: one from a deliberately general prompt that only names the scene, and one from a prompt that restates the passage's own details. Students first read the passage closely and list what it actually specifies about setting, figures, objects, gestures and sequence. They then watch each clip at full speed and afterward step through it, logging every visible element as grounded in the passage, borrowed from later artistic tradition, historically out of place, or without any basis the class can find. Because the medium moves, the log also captures what happens between frames: a vessel that appears and vanishes, a figure whose clothing changes from one moment to the next, an inscription that dissolves into unreadable marks, actions shown in an order the text does not give. Groups propose a correction for each logged element, tied to a verse or to historical evidence about the period, and compare which kinds of departure the more detailed prompt reduced and which it left untouched. The discussion closes on what the clips suggest about the visual sources a generator draws on when it depicts a sacred narrative, and on how students would explain the difference between an illustration and an interpretation.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students log every visible element and every change between frames against the passage and course readings, then propose text-based corrections.
activities.dl: A shared element log for two clips, with each element classified and paired with a text-based correction, and a short group comparison of the two prompt conditions.
activities.na: The same log can be run on a published film or animated adaptation of the scene, viewed in class but not entered into any tool.
activities.risk: Only the instructor operates the generator; students need no account and enter nothing into a tool. The passage comes from a public-domain translation, the clips depict no real or living person, and they are labeled as synthetic when shown and are not circulated outside the course.

activities.t: Auditing synthetic-presenter openings for standardized-client cases against the case template
activities.sum: A veterinary communication faculty team that writes standardized-client cases from a fixed template, recording the owner's background, setting, language, household, the animal and the reason for the visit, adds a short video opening to selected cases. For each case the team writes the client's first statement and a handful of likely replies, then renders them with a synthetic-presenter tool, using one of the tool's stock presenters and stock voices so that no real person's face or voice is involved. Before any clip reaches students, two faculty members watch it against the completed template and sort every visible and audible feature into three columns: specified by the case, added by the tool without instruction, and in conflict with the case. Clothing, setting, accent, apparent age and the way worry or irritation is delivered are typical entries. Clips whose additions carry cues the team did not choose, such as signals of income or ethnicity, are regenerated with a different presenter or replaced by a faculty-recorded version. Students meet the approved clip as the client's opening in a communication lab, with all characteristics disclosed in the case history and the client labeled as synthetic, and then continue the encounter with a live standardized client or a peer. A short written reflection afterward asks what the synthetic opening conveyed and what only the live exchange did.
activities.f: AI-Generated Cases and Scenarios for Professional Learning
activities.gate: Faculty fix every client characteristic in the case template before generation and sort each clip's visible and audible features against it; students reflect on what the synthetic opening could and could not convey.
activities.dl: A set of approved synthetic client openings, a three-column portrayal audit for each clip, and student reflections comparing the synthetic opening with the live encounter.
activities.na: Faculty or trained standardized clients can record the opening statement on video, and the same template audit and student reflection apply.
activities.risk: Students do not operate any AI tool and need no account. Only stock synthetic presenters and voices are used: no photograph, likeness or voice of a real person is uploaded, no voice cloning is involved, and the tool is not used to infer or score emotion. Clips are labeled as synthetic in the case materials.

activities.t: Generated aerial footage of real and imaginary places checked against gazetteer and open map data
activities.sum: In an introductory world regional geography course, students who have read about toponyms and the study of place names receive a list that mixes real places, invented ones and literary landscapes. Working first in groups and without any generator, students check every name in an approved gazetteer, classify it as real or imaginary, and for the real places record coordinates and a few physical facts from open map and climate data: elevation range, coastal or inland setting, climate zone and typical vegetation. Each group then gives a text-to-video tool nothing but a place name and a request for a short aerial establishing shot, once for a real place and once for an imaginary one. The tool will usually return convincing footage in both cases. Students annotate each clip feature by feature, listing landforms, water, vegetation, settlement pattern, architecture and weather, and check every feature of the real place against their recorded data. For the imaginary place there is nothing to check against, so the annotation asks instead which real regions the footage seems to borrow from. Four source-evaluation questions, on plausibility, consistency with what is known, authority and the purpose a clip might serve, frame the comparison. Groups add their annotations to the class data table, and each student writes a short essay on what a persuasive clip of a place does and does not establish about whether the place exists or what it is like.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students classify each place with a gazetteer and record open geographic data before generating, then check each clip's features against that record.
activities.dl: A gazetteer-checked classification table, two annotated clips per group with feature-level checks, and a short essay on what generated footage establishes about a place.
activities.na: Students can compare stock or archival footage labeled with a place name against the same recorded data, or annotate published maps of literary landscapes, and write the same essay.
activities.risk: Only place names enter the tool, and prompts ask for landscapes without people. Clips are labeled as synthetic in the class table and are not posted elsewhere. Where generation is limited to paid tiers, the instructor can generate the clips from the class list so that students work only on the footage.

activities.t: Generating and revising an Engage-phase phenomenon clip, then deciding whether it belongs in the lesson
activities.sum: Pre-service Earth science teachers who are building a lesson on the 5E model use its Engage phase to test a generated video against what they know about geological processes. Each candidate chooses the phenomenon their lesson will open with, such as a meander cutting off into an oxbow lake or a dune migrating downwind, writes a short explanation of the process and its real timescale, and lists the misconceptions their future students are likely to bring. They then generate a clip of the phenomenon from a prompt and audit it against their explanation and a course geology text, looking at where erosion and deposition happen, how the water or sand behaves, and what the clip implies about time. Revisions are made conversationally, by instructing the tool to change the existing clip, and each instruction is logged with whether the clip changed as asked and whether the change made it more or less accurate. The candidate then decides whether to adopt the clip, adapt it with an on-screen caveat about compressed time, or reject it in favor of real footage or a stream-table demonstration, and writes a journal entry explaining the decision in terms of the misconceptions listed at the start. In seminar, candidates compare their decisions across phenomena and discuss which processes the generator rendered plausibly and which it did not.
activities.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
activities.gate: Teacher candidates audit the clip against their own process explanation and a geology text, log each revision instruction and its effect, and adopt, adapt or reject the clip on the basis of the misconceptions they listed beforehand.
activities.dl: A process explanation and misconception list, a generated clip with its revision log, an adopt, adapt or reject decision, and a journal entry justifying it.
activities.na: Candidates can audit openly licensed footage or a stream-table recording of the same phenomenon against the same explanation and misconception list, and make the same adopt, adapt or reject decision.
activities.risk: Only candidate-written prompts enter the tool. Generation and revision may require a paid tier; the instructor might run revisions from a departmental account using candidates' logged instructions. Clips used in teaching are labeled as synthetic.

activities.t: A class-built set of matched filmed and generated clips for practicing synthetic-video detection
activities.sum: Communication or first-year students who are learning to verify viral media build their own test set before they practice on anyone else's. Each student or small group records a few seconds of an ordinary campus scene on a phone, choosing subjects with no identifiable people, such as water in a fountain, traffic at a crossing or leaves moving in wind, and then writes a prompt describing that same scene for a text-to-video generator and produces a matching clip. The instructor gathers the clips, keeps the answer key, and shuffles them into a single class set. Once the set is assembled, students judge each clip as filmed or generated. For each one they first note their immediate reaction in a word or two and then, separately, the visual cue their judgment rests on and how confident they are. When the key is revealed the class tallies its own accuracy, looks for any tendency to accept generated clips as real, and sorts the cues into those that held up and those that did not. Students then apply the unit's fact-checking resources, including keyframe searches and checks for attached provenance information, to their own clips, where the true answer is already known. The debrief sets the class's results beside a published comparison of human and machine detection of generated faces in images and video, and asks what a class-built set of scenes can and cannot show.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students judge each clip as filmed or generated, recording their immediate reaction separately from the cue and confidence behind the judgment, then check against the answer key and practice verification methods on clips whose answer they know.
activities.dl: A shuffled known-answer clip set, individual judgment sheets separating reaction from cue and confidence, a class tally of accuracy and acceptance bias, and notes on which verification methods worked on known clips.
activities.na: The instructor can assemble a known-answer set from labeled, openly licensed synthetic and authentic clips, and students run the same judgment, tally and debrief without generating anything.
activities.risk: Clips show no identifiable people, and no likeness of any real person is generated. Generated clips are labeled as synthetic once the key is revealed and are not posted outside the class. Students without access to a generator can contribute the filmed half while a partner or the instructor generates the match.

activities.t: Logging each generated revision of a video abstract and reconciling the log with attached provenance data
activities.sum: A researcher preparing a short video abstract for an article builds the disclosure of AI involvement while making the video rather than afterward. Before any generation, the researcher writes the script, records their own narration, and notes what they expect the tool to do and what it should not do, such as depict data the article does not report. Explanatory visuals are generated from prompts and then revised through follow-up instructions to the same tool. Each instruction goes into a running log with the tool and version, the date, the instruction, what visibly changed, and whether the change touched anything the article claims. Any visual resembling a chart, a specimen or an instrument is checked against the article's own figures before it stays. Where the tool attaches provenance credentials to its output, the researcher opens the exported file in a credential viewer and sets the recorded actions beside their own log, noting what the credential records, what it omits, and what the log adds. The researcher closes with a short note on what they would do differently next time and a disclosure statement assembled from the log and the credential rather than from memory. A co-author or colleague can review the log against the final cut before the video is released.
activities.f: Academic Integrity, Authorship and Course AI Policy
activities.gate: The researcher scripts and narrates first, sets limits on what the visuals may depict, checks each revision against the article, and builds the disclosure from a contemporaneous log.
activities.dl: A video abstract, a contemporaneous revision log, a comparison of the log with the attached provenance record, and a disclosure statement drawn from both.
activities.na: The researcher can build the video from the article's own figures, slides and narration, keeping the same log of editorial changes and a disclosure stating that no generative tool was used.
activities.risk: Only the researcher's own script, narration and instructions enter the tool; published figures are not uploaded unless the researcher holds the rights, and no likeness of a real person is generated. Credential viewers are free to use; generation may require a paid tier. Synthetic visuals are labeled in the video's description.

activities.t: Deciding whether to air witness clips, some of them generated, during a simulated breaking-news event
activities.sum: A broadcast or multimedia reporting course that runs a fictional breaking-news event through three simulated press conferences adds a second stream of material to the exercise: short clips said to come from people at the scene. The instructor prepares them in advance. Some are filmed by staff who agree to appear, some are generated from prompts describing the fictional event, and no generated clip shows an identifiable real person. Students are told at the outset that the stream may contain synthetic material, but not which items. After each conference, students write an increasingly informed news update and, for every clip released so far, record whether they would air it, how they would attribute it, what corroboration they would seek, and what they would ask the official about it at the next briefing. The official, voiced by the instructor or by a conversational model the instructor configures, answers only from the scenario notes. Updates go through peer review, and students keep original and revised copies together with a provenance log for each visual. In the debrief the instructor releases the key, and the class compares its decisions with it and with documented forms of AI-generated material in recent election coverage, including satire that audiences took as fact, before discussing how a clip travels once a newsroom has aired it.

activities.gate: For each clip, students decide whether to air it, how to attribute it and what corroboration they would seek, and question the official about it; decisions are checked against the key in the debrief.

activities.t: Rehearsing dementia communication with a simulated agitated patient
activities.sum: Allied health and nursing students rehearse a bedside conversation with a conversational assistant that plays a hospital in-patient with dementia who has become agitated. Each student has already worked through the HELM learning object on communication, which sets out the means, reasons and opportunities a person needs in order to communicate and presents strategies for responding to agitation and recognizing how pain is expressed. The instructor writes the persona brief: an older adult on a general ward, a plausible unmet need behind the agitation, and replies that grow calmer or more distressed depending on what the student says. Students conduct a typed exchange of ten to fifteen turns, then annotate the transcript, marking where they addressed means, reasons or opportunities and where the simulated patient's distress rose. In the debrief, small groups compare annotated transcripts and note moments where the assistant responded in ways a person with dementia might not, such as following long multi-part sentences without difficulty. Those moments are logged as limits of the simulation and checked against the learning object and course references on dementia care.

activities.risk: Typed exchange works with a free-tier conversational tool; transcripts contain student-written text only and no patient information, and the HELM license is NonCommercial with attribution and site-specific conditions on modified versions.

activities.t: Critiquing a vision model's description of an oral biopsy image
activities.sum: Dental students ask a vision-capable model to describe a histology image of an oral mucosal biopsy and then critique that description against what an oral pathologist would report. The image is one the instructor owns or holds under an open license, and the instructor supplies a brief original history; no material from a published case archive is uploaded. Under supervision, students request a description at low and high magnification and a ranked differential diagnosis with reasons. They mark each statement as visible in the image, plausible but not verifiable from the image, or contradicted by it, and note where the differential passes over the duration of the lesion or the patient's risk history. As a companion reading, students open the University of Washington Case of the Month for April 2019 on its own site and observe how a withheld-diagnosis case moves from history and clinical findings through graded histology to a reasoned differential. The instructor's signed-out pathology report for the uploaded image is the key against which the model's description is checked, and the exercise remains educational, not diagnostic.

activities.t: Rating AI-written SBAR messages for a deteriorating patient
activities.sum: Students rate several AI-written SBAR messages about the same deteriorating patient and rewrite the weakest one; they use no AI tool themselves. Before class the instructor writes an original vignette, for example a postoperative patient with falling blood pressure and a rising respiratory rate, and asks a conversational tool for five versions of the nurse's call to the on-call physician. The set is left unedited, so it may include a message with no clear request, one that buries the assessment, and one that states findings not present in the vignette. In class, students open the AHRQ TeamSTEPPS SBAR tool page on the agency's site and read it as published. Working in pairs, they score each message for whether Situation, Background, Assessment and Recommendation are present, accurate to the vignette and usable by a clinician deciding quickly. Pairs compare scores, accept or reject each message as safe to send, and state the grounds. Each student then rewrites the lowest-rated message. The instructor's own rating of the set is shared afterward so students can see where their judgments differed.

activities.dl: A scored set of five messages with accept-or-reject decisions and one rewritten SBAR message.
activities.risk: Students need no account, device or tool beyond access to a public web page, and the specimen set can be printed; the vignette is invented and contains no patient data.

activities.t: Explaining a neurological localization to a why-asking assistant
activities.sum: After a self-quiz on one section of the neurological examination, medical students explain a finding they missed to a conversational assistant instructed to ask why at each step. The exam sections, patient videos and section quizzes come from the NeuroLogic Exam site, which students use as published on its own pages; no video or quiz text is uploaded to the assistant. A student who misjudged, say, a pronator drift or an abnormal pupillary response types an account of where in the nervous system the lesion lies and how the pathway produces the sign. The assistant does not supply the answer; it asks for the next link in the chain and, at the end, drafts a summary of what the student appears to understand and where the explanation stalled. The student corrects that summary, since the assistant may misstate anatomy or accept a flawed step, and submits the exchange with the corrected reasoning. The instructor reads the summaries before a small-group session and uses them to choose which localizations to revisit. Reasoning is checked against the site's anatomical descriptions and the course neuroanatomy text.

activities.gate: Each student writes their own account of where the lesion lies and how the pathway produces the sign, answers each why, and corrects the assistant's summary of their reasoning before submitting the exchange.
activities.dl: A why-chain exchange on one missed finding, with a student-corrected summary of the localization reasoning.
activities.risk: A free-tier conversational tool is sufficient; the site's videos are viewed in place, and its license (Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, with a bar on uploading videos to publishing or social platforms) is a reason nothing from it is uploaded.

activities.t: Scripting diagnostic test statistics from an instructor-written case
activities.sum: Medical students build a two-by-two table from an instructor-written patient vignette and direct a coding assistant to write a short script that computes sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from it. The vignette and its numbers are original to the course: a screening test result reported for a cohort, with biopsy confirmation as the reference standard. WebPath's Biostatistics Case Studies, in which pathology and laboratory findings become the data for a named calculation, suggested the kind of task; none of its cases or figures are used or entered into a tool. Students work the four statistics by hand before opening the assistant. They then request a commented script, read each line to see which cells feed which formula, run it, and compare its output with their hand calculation. Where the two differ, students determine whether the script transposed cells, the prompt described the table ambiguously, or their arithmetic slipped. A second run with prevalence changed shows which values move and which do not. The hand calculation and the instructor's worked key are the references for every figure the script returns.

activities.risk: A free coding assistant and a browser-based notebook are sufficient; the data are invented, and WebPath is all rights reserved, so its cases are neither copied nor entered into a tool.

activities.t: Spoken shift report to a voice assistant as oncoming nurse
activities.sum: Pre-licensure nursing students give a spoken shift report to a voice-capable assistant that plays the oncoming nurse and interrupts with questions. Students use the SBAR template their own program issues and a patient summary written by the instructor. The assistant is set up to behave as a busy colleague: it asks for a missing allergy, a last set of vital signs or what the student wants done, and it does not prompt for elements the student omits unless they bear on its next question. Each report lasts three or four minutes and takes place in the skills laboratory or at home before simulation day. Afterward the student reads the automatic transcript, marks which SBAR elements were delivered unprompted, which emerged only under questioning and which never appeared, and records a second attempt. The rehearsal sits at the practice stage of skill learning, ahead of faculty-observed handoff in simulation and on the unit. A QSEN strategy by Cari Granier, which pairs a handoff template with conversation scripts rehearsed before placement, is the idea behind the sequence. Transcripts are checked against the instructor's patient summary.

activities.t: Chatbot-gated clinical reasoning game on postpartum hemorrhage
activities.sum: Teams of nursing students work through an instructor-written postpartum case in which a conversational assistant acts as game master and releases the next piece of patient data only after the team types a clinically sound rationale. The instructor writes the case, the sequence of findings and the release rules, and gives them to the assistant as its instructions. A team that asks for the next clue without justifying its assessment priority, its estimate of blood loss or its choice of first intervention receives a graduated hint and no new data. The assistant may accept a weak rationale or reject a sound one, so each team keeps a log of every gate, the rationale offered and the ruling. In the debrief, teams compare logs, identify rulings they dispute, and settle them against the unit's obstetric hemorrhage protocol. The idea of locking each decision point of a hemorrhage case behind a challenge comes from a QSEN escape-game strategy by Linda Beaverstock and Vanessa Enloe; its puzzles and materials are not reproduced or entered into the tool.

activities.gate: Each team writes a clinical rationale at every gate, keeps a log of each rationale and ruling, and in the debrief identifies the rulings it disputes and settles them against the obstetric hemorrhage protocol.

activities.risk: One shared device per team and a free-tier tool or an instructor-configured course chatbot are sufficient; the case is invented, and typed team rationales are the only student text entered.

activities.t: Filling evidence-level gaps with an AI scholarly search tool
activities.sum: Nursing students acting as an evidence-based practice committee use an AI scholarly search tool to look for the levels of evidence missing from their shared matrix. Each student arrives with a clinical question already searched by hand in library databases and with the sources they appraised. The group pools these, sees which evidence levels are absent, and writes one guiding question per gap, such as whether any systematic review addresses the chosen nursing intervention. The same question is run in a library database and in the search tool. For every item the tool returns, students confirm that the article exists, open the full text through the library, and compare the tool's summary with the abstract and methods. Items that cannot be traced are logged and dropped; items that survive are appraised with the same instrument the group used by hand and added to the matrix with a note on how they were found. The committee framing and the expectation that a matrix span evidence levels follow, at the level of idea, a QSEN strategy by Elizabeth Murray; its parts, rubrics and files are not reproduced or entered into the tool.

activities.t: First-pass classification of skills-lab medication error reports
activities.sum: A pharmacy program's skills-laboratory committee uses its institution's private AI environment to make a first-pass classification of de-identified medication error reports logged by laboratory instructors over a year. Committee members write the coding scheme themselves from the categories on the program's own incident form, sorting each report by the stage of the medication process at which the error arose and by the contributing factors the instructor described. The assistant applies the scheme to each report and gives a one-line reason. Two faculty members independently code a sample of the same reports before seeing the assistant's labels, and disagreements among the three are reviewed in committee. The assistant may assign a stage the report does not support, so its labels are treated as proposals; faculty decide every final code. Counts by stage and by cohort then inform which laboratory sessions the committee revisits. The IUPHAR Pharmacology Education Project page on medication errors is read on its own site as the committee's reference for definitions and is not uploaded or reworded for the tool.

activities.t: Answering, then critiquing, an AI-drafted beverage survey
activities.sum: Public health students first answer a five-question beverage-consumption survey drafted by a generative AI tool and then critique it as an instrument. The instructor obtains the draft beforehand by asking a conversational tool for a short survey on sugary drink intake among college students and distributes it unedited, labeled as AI-drafted. After responding, students tabulate the class's answers and note where they hesitated: perhaps a recall period left undefined, response options that overlap or omit zero, a question that presumes consumption, or a term such as sports drink left open. Groups mark each item for leading wording, missing options and recall demands, and state what population the class sample could and could not represent. Each group then writes its own five-question survey, and groups rate one another's instruments alongside the AI draft before any are fielded with peers. Items from the Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System, which the CDC lesson Drink Up uses, serve as the comparison standard for question wording. Students use no AI tool at any point.

activities.risk: Students need no tool or account and the survey can be run on paper; peer surveying at a college may call for a check on local rules for class data collection, and the lesson plan is in the public domain with citation requested.

activities.t: A chatbot stakeholder in a mandatory vaccination community meeting
activities.sum: Students in a public health ethics session hold mixed community meetings on mandatory vaccination during a fictional outbreak, with a conversational assistant seated as an additional stakeholder. The structure follows the CDC lesson RAGE Outbreak: expert groups prepare the position of a public health officer, a healthcare professional, a concerned community member or a vaccine-hesitant parent, then re-form as mixed meetings that seek consensus. In this version the instructor briefs the assistant with a fifth role, for instance a small-business owner facing closure or a school superintendent, and each meeting puts its emerging consensus to it. The assistant argues its position and presses on the weakest point; the group answers with evidence before recording a decision. Students keep the transcript and mark which objections were sound, which rested on claims they could not verify, and which competing motives the assistant weighed or left out. The written recommendation that closes the lesson cites a source for every factual claim, including any the assistant introduced, and those claims are checked against public health agency guidance and the course readings on public health ethics.

activities.t: Testing a vision model's reading of a layered obesity map
activities.sum: Students build a county-level map of adult obesity with household income and physical inactivity layers, then give a vision-capable model a screenshot and ask what patterns it sees. The mapping sequence follows the CDC lesson on spatial analysis of obesity, adapted for undergraduates: the outcome layer comes first, the candidate explanatory layers are added one at a time, and students write their own hypotheses from the overlap before consulting the model. The model's reply is broken into separate claims. Students test each one against the county data table behind the map, accept, amend or reject it, and record the grounds. Claims about where values cluster can be checked directly; statements that low income causes obesity cannot be established from overlapping layers, and students label these as going beyond what descriptive epidemiology supports. The model may also misread the legend or name counties incorrectly, which the data table exposes. Groups close by comparing their hypotheses with the model's and listing what further study design would be needed to test a causal claim.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students produce a layered county map, their own hypotheses written before consulting the model, a claim-by-claim table marked accept, amend, or reject with grounds, and a list of what a causal test would require.
activities.dl: A layered map, a claim-by-claim table of the model's reading marked accept, amend or reject, and a short list of what a causal test would require.
activities.risk: Image upload may require an account or a paid tier, so a shared instructor account or group work can reduce barriers; the mapping platform and its data layers carry their own terms, and map interpretation by screenshot needs a text alternative for students using screen readers.

activities.t: Testing student-written dermatology items against a source-bound assistant
activities.sum: Veterinary students write original multiple-choice questions on skin presentations, with a separate explanation for every answer option, and then test them against a document-grounded assistant. The assistant is loaded only with openly licensed veterinary dermatology material chosen by the instructor. Each student drafts one five-option item on a presentation such as pruritus in a dog or alopecia in a cat and writes why each option is right or wrong before using the tool. The assistant then answers the item, argues the case for each distractor, and quotes the passage it relies on. Where it can defend a distractor from the source, the student decides whether the item is ambiguous or the assistant has stretched the passage, and revises the stem, the option or the explanation. Students record what changed and why. Option-by-option feedback is a format students meet in WikiVet's Dermatology Quiz, which they take on its own site for revision; none of its questions or feedback text is copied or entered into the assistant. Final items are checked by the instructor against the course dermatology references.

activities.t: Rehearsing an Initial Disclosure Meeting with an AI Patient
activities.sum: Residents rehearse the opening of an initial disclosure meeting with a conversational AI system playing the patient, and then score their own transcript before meeting a standardized patient. The instructor writes a new fictional adverse event in obstetrical care and the patient's bounded range of reactions, including confusion, anger and direct questions about what happened and what follows; the station materials of the published OSCE series are not entered into the tool. Each resident conducts the conversation in text, marks the transcript against the essential components of a disclosure meeting that the program teaches, and drafts the chart note recording what was said, together with a statement of whether an incident report is indicated. These three products correspond to the published series' stated objectives. A faculty member reviews the persona's replies for clinical accuracy and reads a sample of the notes against the transcripts. The rehearsal supplies a first concrete experience and a reflection on it; the standardized-patient encounter that follows is the second attempt, and the judgment of how the conversation felt to a person remains with that human encounter.

activities.t: Auditing Agent-Drafted Branches for a Resuscitation Scenario
activities.sum: Nursing students and a clinical instructor audit new decision branches that an agentic AI workflow has drafted for a screen-based cardiac arrest scenario. Working from an instructor-written brief built on the published scenario's objectives, namely recognizing arrest, activating the emergency response system, single- and multi-rescuer CPR, and SBAR communication, the agent carries out a chain of tasks: proposing decision points, writing the consequence of each choice, and drafting the SBAR exchange that follows. It also returns a log of the steps it took. Students receive the draft branches and the log, not the tool. In small groups they check each branch against the current resuscitation guidelines their program teaches, marking sequences that are out of order, consequences that are clinically implausible, and SBAR exchanges with missing elements. Each branch is labeled accept, amend, or reject, with the guideline passage cited. The instructor makes the final decision on whether any amended branch enters the teaching scenario, so the division of work is explicit: the agent drafts, students audit, and the instructor decides.

activities.gate: The group labels each drafted branch accept, amend or reject, cites the guideline passage behind each label, and writes the corrected version of every amended branch.
activities.dl: An audit sheet labeling each AI-drafted branch accept, amend or reject, with the supporting guideline passage and a corrected version of amended branches.

activities.t: What an Image-Only Reading of a Biopsy Misses
activities.sum: Pathology learners compare what a vision-capable AI model says about a renal biopsy micrograph, seen without any history, with what a pathologist reports for the same image. The class first reads a case from the University of Pittsburgh's online archive as published, by link, noting how its account moves from history and laboratory values through light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy before the diagnosis page is opened; nothing from that case is copied or uploaded. For the AI component the instructor supplies an instructor-owned or openly licensed micrograph with a known report. Students write their own description first, and list what a renal pathologist would perceive or decide here that the image alone does not hold, such as clinical context, stain selection and findings from other modalities. The model is then given only the image and asked to describe it and offer a differential. Students set its output beside their own description and the pathologist's report, marking statements supported by the image, statements not supported, and what required information outside the frame.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students write their own description first, list what a pathologist would need beyond the image, and mark each model statement as supported by the image, unsupported, or dependent on information outside the frame.
activities.dl: A three-column comparison of the student's description, the model's description and differential, and the pathologist's report, with each model statement marked supported, unsupported or dependent on information outside the image.
activities.risk: Only an instructor-owned or openly licensed image with no patient identifiers is uploaded, and the instructor can run the model once and share its output so that students need no account; images need text descriptions for accessibility.

activities.t: Eliciting Unannounced Concerns from an AI Home-Visit Client
activities.sum: Before working with a published unfolding case, nursing students practice a home-visit interview with a conversational AI system that plays an instructor-written fictional older adult, and then check what they managed to elicit. The persona is the instructor's own, a different person, setting and presenting problem from the NLN case of Red Yoder, and is written so that the stated reason for the visit is minor while further concerns of the instructor's own choosing, not those of the published case, surface only in reply to suitable open questions. No material from the published case is entered into the tool. Each student conducts the interview outside class and brings the transcript. Class time is spent taking the transcripts apart: pairs mark which questions opened a new concern and which closed one off, compare what each elicited with the instructor's persona sheet, and note replies in which the persona drifted from its brief. The class then turns to the published case, used by link as published, with the same attention to concerns that are not announced.

activities.t: Handoff Rehearsal with an AI Receiving Clinician
activities.sum: Advanced practice nursing students deliver a transition handoff to a conversational AI system playing the receiving clinician, and then compare their handoff with the one shown in a recorded simulation. After viewing the published video simulation, which follows an older adult with stroke from acute care to rehabilitation and from rehabilitation to home, each student writes and delivers a handoff for one of the two transitions. The assistant is configured from an instructor-written list of safety-critical items for that transition, such as swallowing status, fall risk, medication changes, follow-up arrangements and caregiver teaching, and asks only for items the student left out, with a general prompt first and a more specific one if the gap remains. A complete handoff therefore draws no questions, and the support recedes as omissions become fewer across attempts. Students keep the transcript, count the prompts they needed, and repeat the exercise for the second transition. Educator feedback and a class comparison with the recorded team's handoffs close the cycle, with attention to anything the assistant asked for that the instructor's list did not contain.

activities.dl: Two handoff transcripts, one per transition, with a count of the prompts the assistant needed to issue and a short comparison with the recorded team's handoff.

activities.t: Building Verified Clue Sets for a Drug-Name Puzzle
activities.sum: Pharmacology students build and exchange drug-name puzzles whose clinical hints are drafted by a document-grounded assistant and verified by the students against the source. The published daily game Drugdle is played as it stands, by link, as an example of recalling and spelling international nonproprietary names; none of its content is copied or entered into a tool. For the class-built puzzles, the assistant is limited to public-domain or openly licensed drug labeling and monographs chosen by the instructor. Each pair selects a drug from the course list and asks the assistant for a graded series of hints, from drug class down to a distinguishing adverse effect, each with the passage it rests on. The pair opens every cited passage, corrects or discards hints the source does not support, and logs the changes. Pairs then trade puzzles; the solving pair records a confidence rating before each guess and afterwards comments on any hint it found ambiguous or inaccurate. The instructor spot-checks the logs against the monographs.

activities.t: Testing AI-Proposed Plans Against a Global Health Case
activities.sum: Students in a global health delivery course test two AI-proposed program plans against the evidence in a published teaching case that the AI never saw. The instructor obtains the plans in advance by giving a conversational AI system a short, instructor-written general brief, to improve HIV voluntary counseling and testing at a district government hospital in a low-resource setting, and nothing from the case; the distributor's terms bar uploading the case to any AI tool, and students use no AI tool in the activity. Students read the Hinche case in the form those terms allow. In teams they map the stakeholders the case describes and take each AI plan apart, listing the assumptions it makes about staffing, financing, community health workers and local politics, and setting the case's evidence beside each one. Every element of a plan is marked accept, amend or reject, with the page of the case that grounds the decision. Teams present their amended plan, and the sequel case, also read as published, reports what happened two years later.

activities.dl: An annotated critique of two AI-proposed plans with each element marked accept, amend or reject against cited case evidence, and a team presentation of an amended plan.

activities.t: Comparing AI and Instructor Feedback on Practice Sutures
activities.sum: Veterinary students photograph their own practice cruciate sutures on a bench model and compare a vision-capable AI model's comments on the photographs with a clinical skills instructor's assessment of the same work. Students learn the pattern from the Bristol clinical skills booklet, consulted directly and unaltered; because the booklet is licensed without permission for derivatives, none of its text or photographs is uploaded, and the model receives only the student's own image and a request for comments on spacing, tension and knot security. Each student first writes a self-assessment. The model's comments are then sorted into three groups: observations the photograph can support, statements about things a still image cannot show, such as tissue tension or how the needle was driven, and remarks that conflict with the booklet. The instructor assesses the suture pad itself in the skills lab. Students set the three sources side by side, self, model and instructor, and note which feedback they would act on and why, with the instructor's in-person judgment standing as the measure of practical competence.
