activities.t: Sorting supported from unsupported claims about seed longevity
activities.sum: Students in an introductory biology course complete the Data Nugget on a long-running buried-seed experiment as published, building their own graph of germination across excavation dates and writing their own interpretation. Only after that work is handed in do they receive a one-paragraph explanation of seed longevity that the instructor obtained beforehand from a conversational model, using a short instructor-written question that contains none of the Data Nugget's text, table or images. No student uses an AI tool. Working in pairs, students sort each sentence of the printed paragraph into three groups: statements their own graph supports, statements that go beyond what the dataset can show, and statements the dataset contradicts. Sentences of the second kind often read as causal claims about why some species persist, which the germination counts alone do not establish. Each pair then writes a replacement for one overreaching sentence, stating what further evidence would be needed. The sequence places the students' own judgment ahead of the model's, so the paragraph is read as a second opinion against a position they already hold.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students produce their own graph and interpretation of the germination data before seeing the paragraph, and each pair sorts its sentences into supported, overreaching, and contradicted, rewriting one overreaching sentence with the further evidence it would need.
activities.dl: An annotated copy of the AI-written paragraph with each sentence classified and one sentence rewritten with a stated evidence requirement.
activities.risk: Students need no device, account or payment; the Data Nugget is used in print or on a password-protected course site as its permitted-uses page allows, and none of it is entered into an AI tool.

activities.t: Auditing a model's relabeling of a hand-drawn life cycle
activities.sum: After working through the published case on a foot dermatosis, students hold a hand-drawn parasite life cycle of their own making. In this activity each student photographs that drawing and gives the image to a multimodal model, asking it to name every stage shown, describe the route of transmission, and point out anything missing or mislabeled. The model sees only the student's drawing; no part of the case text is entered. Its reading may be accurate, may misidentify a stage, or may describe a different organism's cycle with equal confidence. Students list every correction and addition the model proposes and decide, item by item, whether to accept, amend or reject it, recording the page or figure in the course's parasitology reference that settles each decision. A revised drawing follows, with accepted changes in one color and the student's own corrections in another. Because the same cycle exists as a drawing, a verbal description from the model, and a reference figure, students can see what each form of representation leaves out, which becomes relevant when they draft the public-facing pamphlet the case ends with.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each student produces a revised life-cycle drawing that separates accepted changes from their own corrections, and a log deciding every model suggestion with the reference page or figure that settles it.
activities.dl: A revised life-cycle drawing with a decision log recording each model suggestion, the decision taken, and the reference figure that supports it.
activities.risk: Image upload may require an account or a paid tier on some services, so a shared instructor-run station or an institutionally provided tool keeps cost and account creation off students; only student-made drawings are uploaded, and the copyrighted case PDF is not.

activities.t: Testing a collision-theory explanation against the class's rate data
activities.sum: Students who have run the published practical on temperature and reaction rate arrive with their own table of temperatures and times and their own plot of the rate measure against temperature. Before any AI use, each group writes a short collision-theory account of the shape of its curve. A group member then gives a document-grounded assistant the group's data table only, typed in by the students, and asks for an explanation of the trend. The assistant often supplies a fluent account that includes general rules, such as the claim that rate roughly doubles with each ten-degree rise. Groups treat every quantitative statement in the reply as a prediction and test it on their own numbers, computing the ratio of rates across each ten-degree interval they measured. They also note anything the reply attributes to the data that the data cannot show, such as activation energy values or the behavior of individual particles. In a whole-class debrief the transcripts are taken apart side by side with the plots, and each group states which sentences of its original account it would keep, revise or drop.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: The group produces a transcript in which each quantitative claim is paired with its own calculated rate ratio, notes what the reply attributes to the data that the data cannot show, and decides which sentences of its original account to keep, revise or drop.
activities.dl: A marked-up transcript in which each quantitative claim is paired with the group's calculated value, plus a revised collision-theory explanation.
activities.risk: Only a small numeric table produced by the students is entered and no names are needed; one device per group is enough, and the practical's own safety and ventilation notes apply unchanged.

activities.t: Static reading versus runtime state on student-written code
activities.sum: This assignment follows the published debugging mystery, which students complete on its own terms and without AI, answering questions that can only be settled by watching a seeded program run. The follow-up turns the same idea on code the students wrote themselves. Each student takes a short earlier program of their own that uses a seeded random generator, chooses a seed, and writes five questions about its runtime state: the value of a variable on a given iteration, the order in which objects are created, the contents of a collection when a condition first holds. A coding assistant receives the student's source and the questions and answers from reading alone, without executing anything. The student then answers the same questions with breakpoints, conditional breakpoints and variable inspection. A comparison table records where the assistant's reading matched observation, where it diverged, and what in the code made static prediction hard, such as library-specific random sequences or aliasing. The debugger record, not the assistant's reply, is the evidence submitted, and the write-up states which kind of question each approach is suited to.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students write five runtime questions about their own seeded program, answer them with the debugger, and explain where the assistant's static reading diverged from observed state and which kind of question each approach suits.
activities.dl: A comparison table of predicted and observed runtime values with debugger screenshots and a short account of where static reading broke down.
activities.risk: Students paste only their own earlier code, never the published assignment's source; where a course prefers that student code not enter outside services, an institutionally provided assistant or an instructor-written sample program can stand in.

activities.t: Validating model-written scenes in a generative story program
activities.sum: In the published capstone, a text adventure calls a language model whenever the player walks into a scene that has no definition, so the model acts as a data source inside the student's program. This design keeps that assignment as published and adds a measurement layer around the model's contribution. Students write the opening scenes of a story of their own, and it is those student-written scenes that travel to the model. Where a campus offers an institutionally hosted language model, the course's calls run through it, so story text and logs stay inside campus systems and no student opens a personal account. Each student writes checks that test whether a returned scene has the structure the program expects and whether its exits refer to scenes that exist or can be generated. Every generated scene from fifty dead ends is logged, and the student tallies how many were malformed, how many broke continuity with the existing story, and how the program responded. The report feeds the assignment's own ethics reflection with figures from the student's run instead of general impressions.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Each student writes the story's opening scenes and the validation checks, logs every scene generated from fifty dead ends, and tallies malformed and off-story results with the program's response, so the ethics reflection rests on figures from their own run.
activities.dl: A set of validation functions, a log of fifty generated scenes, and a short report of malformed and off-story rates with examples.
activities.risk: Routing calls through an institutionally hosted model removes per-student cost and account creation and keeps logs on campus systems; the published materials name commercial services, so the hosting arrangement needs confirming locally before the term.

activities.t: Auditing an agent's cleaning of one's own field data
activities.sum: A researcher with a messy survey table of their own, with inconsistent species names, mixed date formats and stray whitespace, uses the Data Carpentry lesson's sequence as the yardstick for delegating the cleaning to an agent. The researcher first cleans a sample of a few hundred rows by hand in the lesson's manner, exploring with facets, filtering and sorting, transforming values, and exporting the recorded operation history. That history is a replayable statement of which decisions the researcher considers correct. An agentic tool is then given the full raw file and an instruction to clean it unattended and to keep a log of every change. The researcher compares the two records: row counts before and after, the set of distinct values in each categorical column, and each merge the agent made that the hand-cleaned sample did not. Merges of names that a field ecologist would keep separate, silently dropped rows, and dates coerced to a wrong format are listed with the rows affected. The outcome is a written statement of which steps can be delegated and which stay with the researcher, kept with the project's data documentation.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher cleans a sample by hand first, lists the agent's contested merges, dropped rows and wrongly coerced dates with the rows affected, and decides which steps can be delegated and which stay with them.
activities.dl: A delegation memo for the project's data documentation, listing the agent's contested decisions, the affected rows, and the steps the researcher retains.
activities.risk: Unpublished field data, which may include locations of sensitive species or sites, enters the agent, so a locally run or institutionally hosted tool and the terms of any data-sharing agreement need checking first.

activities.t: Competing explanations for a magnetic declination discrepancy
activities.sum: Each student finishes the published smartphone magnetometer exercise with personal values for total intensity, inclination and declination and with the agency reference values for the same location; the two sets rarely agree. This activity begins from that gap. Students first write their own best guess at its cause. They then describe their setup to a conversational model in their own words, including where they stood, what was nearby and how the phone was held, give it their calculated values and the reference values, and ask for three distinct explanations of the difference, each with a prediction that would distinguish it from the others. Typical candidates include nearby steel or wiring, an uncalibrated sensor, or a misjudged direction of geographic north. For each explanation the student designs one additional measurement, such as repeating the survey ten meters away or after recalibrating, carries it out, and reports whether the discrepancy moved as that explanation predicts. At least two explanations are eliminated or retained on the strength of the new data, and the student's original guess is revisited in the same terms.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Students produce their own first guess at the cause, an additional measurement designed and carried out for each explanation, and a report on which explanations the new data eliminate or retain, with the original guess revisited.
activities.dl: A short report presenting the three candidate explanations, the extra measurement designed for each, the new data, and the explanations eliminated.
activities.risk: The work needs only the student's own phone and a free text-based model; students describe their setup in words and are not asked to share precise home coordinates with the tool.

activities.t: Rebutting an AI advocate for shipping on schedule
activities.sum: Students read the first installment of the published engineering ethics case and record a private judgment on the engineer's decision. Before the class discusses it, each student rehearses the disagreement with a conversational model that plays a project manager arguing for release. The model is not given the case. It works from a short instructor-written brief set in a different industry, describing a product with a known intermittent defect, a fixed delivery date and a workforce whose jobs depend on the contract. The model presses the commercial and human reasons for release that the instructor has written into the brief. Students answer each turn with a specific technical point from the brief and name the canon of the professional code, or the ethical framework, on which the reply rests. Schedule, livelihoods and public safety each have a legitimate claim in the brief, and a reply that ignores one of them is easy for the model to exploit. Students submit the transcript marked with the objections they judged sound, then return to the published case and say whether their first judgment has changed.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students produce a private judgment on the case, rebuttals tying each reply to a technical point and a named code canon or framework, a marking of which objections they judged sound, and a statement of whether their judgment changed.
activities.dl: An annotated transcript marking which of the model's objections were sound, with each rebuttal tied to a technical fact and a named code provision or framework.
activities.risk: A free text-based model is sufficient; the published case is read at its own web address and is not pasted into the tool, and students who prefer not to use the model can pair with a classmate playing the manager from the same brief.

activities.t: Checking an AI climate summary against reviewed resources
activities.sum: The published classroom mixer gives every student a first-person account of a life affected by climate change, and reviewers of the activity note that it assumes basic climate knowledge. This follow-up supplies a way to examine that knowledge. After the mixer, each student writes, in their own words and without quoting the role card, one guiding question about the physical process behind the kind of impact their role concerned, such as how warming changes drought frequency or coastal flooding. The student puts the question to a search-enabled model and saves its summary and the sources it cites. Each factual sentence in the summary is then traced: students open the cited source to see whether it says what the summary attributes to it, and look for the same point in the reviewed resources of the CLEAN collection. Every sentence is marked as confirmed, corrected, or not traceable to any source, and the CLEAN record used is cited for each correction. Students post the checked summary for classmates, who comment on one tracing decision each. The posted version distinguishes the model's wording from the student's corrections.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students write their own guiding question, trace each factual sentence to its cited source and to reviewed resources, mark it confirmed, corrected, or not traceable, and cite the reviewed record behind each correction.
activities.dl: A checked and corrected climate summary with a sentence-by-sentence tracing table citing a CLEAN record for each correction.
activities.risk: The original mixer materials require a free account with their host and are used there as published; role-card text is not entered into the AI tool, and a free search-enabled model is sufficient for the follow-up.

activities.t: Reviewing AI-written lunar lander code by limiting cases
activities.sum: The PICUP lunar lander exercises build a simulation in stages and end by comparing a numerical result with an analytic solution the student derives. This adaptation places an AI-written program at the fuel-burn stage. Students first complete the constant-mass lander themselves and derive the vertical-descent solution with a constant burn rate by hand. A coding assistant is then asked, with a plain description of the physical model, for a simulation of a lander in a 1.6 N/kg field that burns fuel at 500 kg/s. Students review the returned code before running it. They check the units of every quantity in the update loop, the sign of the thrust term, whether mass is reduced before or after the acceleration is computed, and what happens when fuel runs out. They then run two tests. With the burn rate set to zero, the output is compared with their own constant-mass program. With the burn on, it is compared with their analytic solution over the same interval. Discrepancies are traced to specific lines. A class debrief collects the faults found across groups and discusses what the simplified model leaves out.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students produce their own constant-mass program and hand-derived analytic solution, a review of the returned code before running it, and explanations tracing each discrepancy in the two test comparisons to specific lines.
activities.dl: A code review listing each check, the two test comparisons with plots, and a line-level explanation of any discrepancy found.
activities.risk: A free coding assistant and any language already used in the course are sufficient; no student-written work is entered, and adapted materials carry the exercise set's attribution, noncommercial, share-alike terms.

activities.t: Building a counterexample to an AI claim about biased samples
activities.sum: Students put one question, in their own words, to a conversational model: does a biased sample always produce a misleading confidence interval? They save the reply. Models often answer with a confident generalization, sometimes hedged and sometimes not, and the replies collected across a class differ enough to be worth comparing. Students then open the published StatPREP activity and its Little App and work through it as written, with one added purpose: to find out whether the saved claim survives. Nothing from the activity is entered into the model. Using the app, each pair looks for a configuration that either supports or contradicts the model's statement and records the settings and the resulting intervals as evidence. Pairs who find a contradicting case return to the model, describe the result in a sentence of their own, and ask it to reconcile the two. The class then reads several first and second replies together, treating the model as one participant in the discussion whose statements are open to challenge. Each pair ends by rewriting the original claim so that it states the condition under which it holds.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Each pair records the app settings and intervals that support or contradict the model's claim and rewrites the claim so that it states the condition under which it holds.
activities.dl: A one-page record containing the model's original claim, the app settings and intervals that test it, and a rewritten claim with its condition stated.
activities.risk: A free text-based model is sufficient and the app runs in a browser; whether the hosted app is currently available was not confirmed, so that is worth confirming before class, and no activity text or app data is entered into the model.

activities.t: Running an AI-drafted gravimetric plan in a virtual lab
activities.sum: Students ask a conversational assistant to draft a procedure for a gravimetric determination of arsenic in water samples, then carry the plan out in the ChemCollective virtual lab, which is used as published by link. The request to the assistant is written by students in their own words from general analytical chemistry; the wording of the virtual lab problem is not pasted into the tool. A draft typically names a precipitating reagent and quantities, a filtering and weighing sequence, and the conversion from product mass to concentration. Students execute the plan as written at the virtual bench and record where it runs into trouble: too little reagent for complete precipitation, a step the bench cannot perform, a molar mass or mole-ratio slip in the final calculation. Restarting the experiment after a failed plan counts as a recorded result. The revised procedure, the masses the simulation returned, and a marked-up copy of the assistant's draft showing each instruction kept, changed or discarded are handed in together.

activities.t: Critiquing AI-generated particle pictures of water
activities.sum: After carrying out the hands-on water observations in the American Chemical Society lesson as published, pre-service teachers ask an image generator for a particle-level picture of what they saw and critique the result against their own observations. Each prompt is written in the participant's own words; no text or image from the lesson is entered into the tool. Generated pictures often show features worth examining: molecules spaced as widely as in a gas, particles that look fixed in place, no indication of attraction between molecules, or decorative shapes that do not correspond to water at all. Participants annotate a printed copy, marking each feature as consistent or inconsistent with what the water did, and then draw their own model by hand. A closing comparison sets the generated image, the hand drawing and a short written explanation side by side. Participants note what each mode shows that the others cannot, which misconception each could leave with a middle school learner, and what a teacher would say to accompany it.

activities.t: Auditing a coding agent's commits in a research repository
activities.sum: A faculty researcher gives a coding agent a bounded task in a copy of a project repository, such as refactoring a data-cleaning script on its own branch, and then reconstructs what the agent did from the version-control history alone. The setup follows the staged collision in the Software Carpentry episode on conflicts: the researcher edits the same lines of the same file while the agent works, so that bringing the two lines of work together produces conflict markers. The researcher resolves the conflict by hand, reading the log and the diffs to state, line by line, which change was the agent's, which was their own, and whose intent the merged version keeps. Analysis outputs are regenerated before and after the merge and compared. The product is a short reproducibility note kept in the repository and written as work in progress. It records the instruction given, the commits made, the resolution chosen and the checks run, so that collaborators and reviewers can see where automated edits entered the project.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher resolves the conflict by hand, states line by line which change was the agent's, which their own, and whose intent the merge keeps, and records the instruction, commits, resolution, and checks for collaborators.
activities.dl: A reproducibility note in the repository recording the agent's instruction, its commits, the hand-resolved conflict and the before-and-after output comparison.
activities.risk: Agentic coding tools are often paid and may transmit repository contents to a provider, so the exercise suits a copy of the repository containing no confidential, unpublished or human-subjects data.

activities.t: Questioning a grounded assistant about normalization in an opioid analysis
activities.sum: Students working through the Open Case Studies analysis of opioid shipments to rural and urban US counties first write their own answers to two questions the case raises: when shipment data call for normalizing, and how the way rural and urban groups are defined affects the result. Only then do they put the same questions to a document-grounded assistant loaded with the case study text, a use its license allows for noncommercial purposes with attribution. The assistant answers with passages it cites from the document. Students locate each cited passage, confirm that it says what the answer claims, and check the reasoning against their plots and against the Wilcoxon rank sum output they reproduced. Differences between a student's explanation and the assistant's are sorted into three kinds: the assistant found something the student missed, the student's account goes beyond the text, or the assistant's answer is not supported by the passage it cites. The annotated comparison is submitted with the reproduced analysis.

activities.gate: Students write their own answers on normalization and group definitions before asking, confirm each cited passage against the text and their reproduced analysis, and sort every difference into something they missed, something beyond the text, or an unsupported answer.
activities.dl: A written pre-answer, the grounded assistant's cited answers, and an annotated comparison sorting each difference, submitted with the reproduced analysis.

activities.t: Predicting hyperparameter effects in an age-prediction model
activities.sum: Learners following the Galaxy Training Network tutorial on age prediction treat the regression models they build as the AI under study. Having reproduced the tutorial's two analyses, an ElasticNet pipeline with feature selection on RNA-seq data and a gradient boosting regressor on DNA methylation data, each learner changes one element of a hyperparameter grid and writes down, before rerunning, what they expect to happen to the R2 score and why. The workflow is then rerun in Galaxy, and the new score table, parallel coordinates plot and predicted-against-true-age plot are set beside the prediction. Where the outcome differs from the expectation, the learner drafts an explanation in terms of the model: the regularization setting, the number of features kept, the number of estimators. A class session is given over to taking these discrepancies apart, with learners presenting their change, their prediction and their result. Parameter choices and scores go into a shared table, so the class can see how far results move across the grid and how they compare with the published work the tutorial refers to.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Learners produce a written prediction of how one hyperparameter change will move the score, made before rerunning, and their own explanation, in terms of the model, of any gap between prediction and result.
activities.dl: A prediction-and-result record for one hyperparameter change, with an explanation of the discrepancy, entered in a shared class table and presented in the debrief.
activities.risk: Galaxy runs in a browser on public servers that typically require a free account; the tutorial is CC BY 4.0 and its datasets are openly hosted, and reruns may queue at busy times.

activities.t: Checking AI search briefings on the South Napa earthquake
activities.sum: In the GETSI unit on the 2014 South Napa earthquake, each student researches one aspect of the event (seismology, faulting or damage) before a jigsaw. In this version the pre-class research is done twice: once with a search-oriented AI tool that returns a briefing with citations, and once by going to the sources the briefing cites and to agency and survey reports found independently. Students list the guiding questions for their aspect, record the tool's answer to each, and mark every claim as confirmed in the cited source, present in the source but altered, or not traceable. Magnitudes, dates, fault names and damage figures receive particular attention. In the jigsaw, each expert reports both the content of the briefing and how reliable it proved for their aspect. Groups then go on to the unit's GPS strain calculation for stations P198, P200 and SVIN, and compare their computed coseismic strain and recurrence estimate with any figures the briefings asserted.

activities.t: Ranking AI explanations of enzyme inhibition against a simulation
activities.sum: Students receive three short AI-written explanations of how competitive, uncompetitive and noncompetitive inhibition change a Lineweaver-Burk plot, and use the LearnChemE enzyme inhibition simulation, as published, to decide which statements hold. The instructor generates the explanations beforehand from a prompt of their own on standard Michaelis-Menten kinetics, keeping a set in which at least one explanation confuses two mechanisms or misstates which intercept moves. One explanation gives only the final pattern, while another reasons through which complex the inhibitor binds, so the set contrasts a bare result with a worked rationale. Students move the inhibitor concentration slider under each mechanism, switch between the direct and reciprocal plots, and note for every claim whether the slope and intercepts behave as described. Each explanation is ranked, the failing sentences are quoted and corrected, and every correction is tied to an observation in the simulation. No student uses an AI tool, and nothing from the simulation site is entered into one.

activities.t: Comparing AI-simulated survey answers with a community's own
activities.sum: Students in the InTeGrate unit collect natural hazard survey responses from their own social networks. Before opening the results, they ask a conversational assistant to answer the same survey questions as it expects residents of their community to answer, repeating the request several times to obtain a small set of synthetic respondents. The two sets are tabulated side by side: perceived likelihood of each hazard, self-rated knowledge, preparedness steps taken. Students look for patterned differences. The synthetic answers may cluster around a textbook view of risk, may favor hazards prominent in national coverage, or may flatten variation that the real responses show. Each difference is written up with a proposed source, such as training data that under-represent the region or a default toward generic advice, and with what the real data say instead. The comparison feeds the unit's second pass, in which students frame a research question from the full dataset. Only the survey questions, never respondents' answers, are entered into the tool.

activities.t: Testing AI-proposed modeling assumptions against rocket video data
activities.sum: Students track a rocket's launch frame by frame in the Tracker file from the Open Source Physics activity and obtain position-time data for the phase in which it speeds up. Before computing anything, each student writes down the assumptions they would make to turn a measured acceleration into a force. They then ask a conversational assistant what assumptions a simple model of the launch needs; it commonly proposes constant thrust, constant mass and negligible air resistance. Every proposed assumption is treated as a claim to test. A constant-thrust, constant-mass model predicts constant acceleration, so students check whether their velocity-time graph is linear over the tracked interval and how the fitted acceleration changes when the interval is shortened. Each assumption is accepted, amended or rejected with a reference to the data, and the student's own list is compared with the assistant's to see which considerations each had missed. The force calculation is then reported with the surviving assumptions stated and an uncertainty drawn from the scatter in the tracking.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Each student writes their own assumptions first, accepts, amends, or rejects each proposed assumption with reference to their tracked velocity-time data, and reports the force with the surviving assumptions and an uncertainty drawn from the tracking scatter.
activities.dl: A lab report giving the measured acceleration and inferred force, with a table of accepted, amended and rejected assumptions and the data supporting each decision.
activities.risk: Tracker and the activity file are free, and the handout is offered in English and Chinese; a free-tier assistant suffices, only general physics questions are entered, and adapted handouts carry CC BY-NC-SA attribution.

activities.t: Translating a galaxy research question into SQL with an assistant
activities.sum: In the SDSS Voyages Galaxy Color investigation, used as published, students frame their own question about galaxy color and draw a sample from the survey database with a query. Here the query is drafted by a coding assistant from the student's plain-language criteria: the student states the task, the region of sky, the kind of object, the brightness limits and the columns wanted, and explains what the sample is for. None of the activity's text is given to the assistant. The student runs the returned SQL in SkyServer and inspects what comes back, looking for stars admitted because no object-type condition was set, missing magnitude limits, or objects outside the intended region. Each defect is traced either to a gap in the plain-language request or to an error by the assistant; the request is revised, and the cycle is logged. When the sample matches the criteria, the student proceeds with the investigation as its page describes. The log of requests, queries and returned samples is submitted with the investigation's results.

activities.dl: A log of successive plain-language requests, the SQL each produced, and the defects found in each returned sample, submitted with the completed investigation.
activities.risk: SkyServer tools are free in a browser; the investigation is reached by link since no reuse license is stated, and the student's own criteria (not graded prose) are what enter the assistant, which may require an account.

activities.t: Questioning an AI-played stakeholder in a polio trial deliberation
activities.sum: While groups deliberate in the STEW lesson on choosing a study design for the 1954 polio vaccine field trial, taught as published, a conversational assistant plays one additional stakeholder who is not among the lesson's assigned roles. The instructor writes the persona brief from public historical accounts, for instance a county health officer anxious about enrollment, and runs the assistant on a projected screen; no lesson material is entered into the tool. Each group puts spoken questions to the persona about which design it prefers and why, and records the statistical claims it makes about randomization, comparison groups, consent and the number of children needed. Back in their own roles, groups sort those claims into sound, unsound and unverifiable, and decide whether any of them changes their recommendation. Because the persona argues fluently for its position, groups face a live opponent whose reasoning has to be examined on its merits before the lesson reaches its own conclusion. The sorted claims accompany each group's presented recommendation.

activities.t: Fine-Tuning a Small Model as a Corpus Lens
activities.sum: A humanities researcher with a bounded text corpus of their own, such as a run of digitized newspaper articles or a periodical's back file, fine-tunes a small, openly released language model on it and reads the generated text as evidence about the corpus, following the procedure of an openly licensed Programming Historian lesson. Before any training run, the researcher writes down their own reading of the corpus: the themes, recurring word associations and framings they expect, from close reading of a sample. The fine-tuned model is then prompted with short questions about the corpus's topic, and its outputs are read for recurring phrases and framings. Each interpretive observation is entered in a run log together with the prompt, the hyperparameters and the output file, and the log sits in the project's shared notes, visible to collaborators. Every pattern the model appears to surface is traced back to the corpus by keyword and concordance search; generated quotations and attributions are treated as model output, not as statements from the sources. Differences between the prior reading and the model-prompted reading are written up as questions for further archival work.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher decides which patterns the model appears to surface actually hold in the corpus, tracing each by keyword and concordance search, and treats generated quotations and attributions as model output, not as statements from the sources.
activities.dl: A reproducible run log pairing each interpretive observation with its prompt, settings and output, plus a memo of research questions arising from differences between the researcher's prior reading and the model-prompted reading.
activities.risk: Fine-tuning needs GPU access, usually through a cloud notebook account with usage limits or fees, and a corpus of copyrighted or sensitive material may not be suitable for upload to a hosted environment.

activities.t: Two Text Generators, One Public-Domain Source
activities.sum: Students choose a public-domain literary text, such as a poet's collected verse or a novel's opening chapters, and build two generators from it in a notebook: a Markov chain whose transition table they can inspect, and a small neural language model whose internal workings they cannot. A coding assistant drafts the scripts for both from each student's plain-language description. Students check the Markov script by hand-computing the transition counts for a ten-line sample and comparing them with the table the script produces, and they record any correction they had to request. With both generators running, they produce short passages at varied settings and write a stylistic commentary identifying which features of the source's voice (diction, meter, syntax, recurring images) each procedure retains or loses, quoting the source text for every claim. Passages worth keeping are assembled into a short piece with a note stating which lines came from which generator and which were edited by hand. The design takes only the general idea of comparing a statistical and a neural generator from a published creative-computing course; none of that course's assignment text is entered into a tool.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Each student hand-computes transition counts to check the Markov script, writes a commentary on which features of the source's voice each procedure retains or loses with a quotation for every claim, and attributes each line of the assembled piece.
activities.dl: A notebook with two working generators, a stylistic commentary quoting the source text, and a short assembled piece with a line-by-line note on what came from which generator or from the student's hand.
activities.risk: A browser-based notebook avoids local installation, though hosted notebooks and coding assistants commonly require accounts, and students without programming background may need paired work or a starter notebook.

activities.t: Correcting a Vision Model's Document Analysis
activities.sum: Students work with a scanned document from the National Archives catalog and the National Archives' Document Analysis worksheet for its type, whether written document, photograph, map, poster or cartoon. The worksheet's four-part progression (meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, use it as historical evidence) is put twice: once to a multimodal model that is given the scan and the worksheet questions, and once to the students themselves, who complete their own worksheet before seeing the model's. Pairs then go through the model's answers line by line against the scan and the catalog record. In the observation section they mark anything the model reports that is not visible on the document, and any misread date, name, stamp or handwriting. In the later sections they mark inferences the model has stated as observations and claims about context that the catalog record does not support. Each correction is recorded with the grounds for it, and each answer is labeled accepted, amended or rejected. The corrected worksheet and the list of grounds are the submitted work.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students produce their own completed worksheet before seeing the model's, then a line-by-line correction of its answers against the scan and catalog record, labeling each accepted, amended, or rejected with the grounds.
activities.dl: A corrected Document Analysis worksheet in which each of the model's answers is labeled accepted, amended or rejected, with the grounds for every correction.
activities.risk: The worksheets are public domain and free to copy, while individual archival documents may carry their own rights, so the scan chosen for upload is one the catalog marks as unrestricted; the instructor can run the model and distribute its answers so students need no account.

activities.t: Sorting the Claims in an AI-Written History
activities.sum: Students who have completed OER Project's Claim Testing lesson as published receive a one-page narrative of a historical episode from their course, such as the Columbian Exchange or the collapse of a particular empire, that the instructor has generated beforehand with a conversational model from an instructor-written prompt. No student uses an AI tool, and no part of the lesson's materials is entered into one. Working in small groups, students break the narrative into its separate claims and decide, for each, what kind of support it would need and whether the narrative supplies any. They then check a selection of the claims against the course textbook and assigned primary sources, recording where the narrative is supported, where it states something not found in the sources, and where it leaves out actors, regions or causes that the sources treat as significant. Groups compare their tables and discuss claims they classified differently. The product is a claim table with the evidence consulted and a short list of omissions, each tied to a source that documents what is missing.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Groups produce a claim table setting out the support each claim would need, what the textbook and primary sources show, and a list of omitted actors, regions or causes, each tied to a source.
activities.dl: A group claim table listing each claim in the narrative, the support it has or lacks, the evidence consulted, and a list of omissions tied to course sources.
activities.risk: Students need no account, device or payment because the narrative is distributed on paper or as a file, and only the instructor's own prompt enters a tool.

activities.t: Verifying Assistant-Proposed Sources for Letter Annotations
activities.sum: Students annotate a transcribed nineteenth-century letter from a public-domain digital collection chosen by the instructor, writing short researched notes on the people, places and terms it mentions. The design takes from a published archives exercise only the general idea of dividing research into small, separately checkable annotations; that exercise's letters and handouts are not used. For each annotation a student works two routes. A search-enabled assistant is asked what a named place, regiment or term refers to and returns an answer with linked sources; the student also searches library databases and newspaper archives for the same item. The student opens every source the assistant links, records whether it exists, whether it says what the assistant reports, and what kind of source it is, and then compares it with what the library search turned up. An annotation enters the final set only when its claims rest on a source the student has read. Alongside the annotated letter and bibliography, each student submits a verification log showing, per annotation, which assistant-supplied claims held, which could not be traced, and which the library sources corrected.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each student writes annotations whose claims rest on sources the student has read, with a bibliography and a log showing which assistant-supplied claims held, could not be traced, or were corrected by library sources.
activities.dl: An annotated letter with bibliography and a verification log recording, for each annotation, which assistant-supplied claims held, could not be traced, or were corrected by library sources.
activities.risk: Search-enabled assistants generally require an account and may limit free use, and some linked sources sit behind paywalls that library access can or cannot resolve; the letter is drawn from a public-domain collection so that no restricted archival image enters a tool.

activities.t: Testing a Chatbot's Grammar Rules Against the Data
activities.sum: Students first solve a published NACLO translation puzzle on their own, working from the competition PDF by link, so that they have the experience of deriving word order and word forms from a handful of translated sentences. The AI component then uses a different data set: six sentences in a constructed language written by the instructor, each with an English gloss. Because the language is invented, a model cannot draw on outside knowledge of it, and every rule has to come from the six sentences. Students paste this instructor-written set into a conversational model and ask it to state the word-order and affix rules and to show its reasoning. They treat each stated rule as a hypothesis, test it against all six sentences, and mark it confirmed, falsified or untestable on the data given. Where the model's reasoning names a step, students check whether the step follows from the sentences or from an assumption imported from English or another language. The write-up lists the rules that survived, the counterexample for each that did not, and the students' own corrected rule set, compared with the instructor's key.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Students produce a write-up of the rules that held against all six sentences, a counterexample for each rule that did not, and their own corrected rule set.
activities.dl: A write-up listing each rule the model proposed, its status against the data with counterexamples, and the student's own corrected rule set.
activities.risk: The published puzzle stays on the competition site and is not pasted into any tool; the constructed-language set can be run once by the instructor and the output shared, so students need no account.

activities.t: Generating an Image from a Couplet
activities.sum: After a class has read a poem through the Academy of American Poets' Teach This Poem lesson, used as published, students turn to a poem in the public domain and work with an image generator. Each student chooses one couplet, writes down what the lines literally name and what they leave unstated, and then enters only the couplet's words as the prompt. The generator returns several images. Students annotate one of them against the lines: which named things appear, what the generator added that the poem does not mention (figures, a season, a quality of light), and what in the couplet has no visual counterpart, such as sound, rhyme, negation or a shift in tense. Small groups place images from different couplets in the poem's order and discuss what a sequence of pictures does to the poem's argument. The lesson's own painting and song are not uploaded to any tool; the comparison is between generated image and poem text. Each student writes a paragraph of close reading that uses a specific mismatch between image and couplet as evidence for a claim about how the poem's language works.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making

activities.dl: An annotated generated image and a paragraph of close reading that argues from one specific mismatch between the image and the couplet.
activities.risk: Image generators often require accounts and limit free generations, so one shared classroom account or instructor-run generation is an alternative; students who are blind or have low vision need written descriptions of the generated images to take part in the comparison.

activities.t: Pressing a Chatbot on Responsibility for AI Harm
activities.sum: Students read the Ethics Unwrapped case on accountability for a fatal autonomous-vehicle crash as published and discuss it in class. For the written assignment they work with a conversational model on a different, instructor-written scenario, a hypothetical hospital triage system that misranks a patient, so that no case text is entered into a tool. Each student asks the model who bears responsibility and then presses it over several turns with objections drawn from the course readings on moral responsibility: that the operator lacked control, that the developer could not foresee the failure, that the system itself cannot be blamed. Students annotate the transcript, marking each point where the model's allocation of responsibility shifts and whether the shift followed from an argument or from the wording of the challenge. They sort the model's statements by the level they address: the underlying technology, the specific product, or its deployment in a setting. Claims the model attributes to philosophers are checked against the assigned texts. The submitted paper sets out the student's own allocation of responsibility and uses the annotated transcript as a foil.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Students press the model with objections from the course readings, mark where its allocation of responsibility shifts and whether argument or wording caused it, and argue their own allocation in a paper that uses the transcript as a foil.
activities.dl: An argumentative paper allocating responsibility in the instructor-written scenario, submitted with an annotated transcript of the exchange.
activities.risk: Students submit their own typed objections to a conversational tool, so an institutionally provided or free tier with clear data terms matters, and the hypothetical scenario keeps real persons and the published case text out of the tool.

activities.t: Annotating an AI Overview of Hindu Worship
activities.sum: Students read Harvard Divinity School's Religion in Context case study on online pujas as published, along with the sources it links. They then receive a printed overview of 'Hindu worship' that the instructor generated beforehand with a conversational model from a one-line prompt of the instructor's own; the case text is not entered into the tool, and students use no AI. Working in pairs, students annotate the overview sentence by sentence. For each sentence they note whether the case complicates it, citing the passage or linked source that supplies the missing setting, and whether it speaks of the tradition as a single uniform thing where the case shows variation by place, community or medium. They also note whose perspective the overview defaults to and which practitioners it leaves out. Pairs rate the overview against criteria the class has drafted for an adequate description of a living tradition, and compare ratings with another pair and with the instructor's. The product is the annotated overview and a rewritten paragraph in which each general statement is either tied to a specific context or removed.

activities.dl: An annotated AI-generated overview with case citations, a criteria-based rating, and one rewritten paragraph in which general statements are tied to specific contexts.
activities.risk: Students need no account or device because the overview is printed, and the case is read on the publisher's site so that no copyrighted case text is copied or entered into a tool.

activities.t: Auditing an Agent's Report on a Religious Community
activities.sum: Students delegate a bounded research task to an agentic deep-research tool: compile a sourced profile of one religious community in the region around the campus, such as a gurdwara, mosque association or Orthodox parish. The agent searches the web and returns a report with linked sources. Students then audit the report instead of using it. They reconstruct the agent's steps from its activity trace, open each source, and classify it by who is speaking: the community itself, another religious body, journalists, scholars, or a commercial directory. Using questions about whose voice is heard, whose is missing and who decided, they identify members of the community (by generation, gender, language, or lay and clerical standing) who do not appear in any source the agent chose. They mark sentences that describe a whole tradition where the source describes one congregation, and sentences that state a belief in the community's own voice without attribution. The AAR Religious Literacy Guidelines are assigned as background reading as published and are not entered into the tool. The audit memo ends with a list of sources a researcher would need to add.

activities.dl: An audit memo that classifies each source the agent used by speaker, flags overgeneralized and unattributed sentences, and lists the sources and voices a researcher would need to add.
activities.risk: Deep-research and agentic features are often limited to paid tiers, so one instructor-run report per community shared with the class is an alternative; the profile draws only on public web pages and names no private individuals.

activities.t: Voice Rehearsal Before a Language Exchange
activities.sum: Learners of French complete The Mixxer's lesson on meals as published and, before meeting their human exchange partner, rehearse the conversation aloud with a voice-mode conversational model. The model is given an instructor-written instruction to speak as a French-speaking peer and to talk about everyday meals; no lesson text is entered. Before the rehearsal each learner writes down what they expect to be able to say and what they expect a French speaker to say about meals. During the rehearsal they note expressions they lacked and any description of 'typical' French meals the model offers. They then hold the live exchange with their partner and afterward compare the two conversations: which expressions and corrections came only from the partner, which of the model's generalizations the partner's own account confirmed, qualified or contradicted, and how each interlocutor handled the learner's errors. Vocabulary and constructions taken from the rehearsal are checked against the course textbook or a dictionary before reuse. The written reflection closes with what the learner would prepare differently for the next exchange.

activities.t: Listening to a Position You Reject
activities.sum: Each student names a position on a public controversy that they reject and asks a conversational model to argue it in the voice of someone who sincerely holds it. Writing Commons' article on rhetorical listening is assigned reading in its published form; none of it is entered into the tool, and the analysis students write is in their own terms. Students read the model's argument and write an account of the reasoning and commitments from which the position makes sense to its holders, without rebutting it. They then tell the model their own view and record what happens: whether it holds the position, softens it or moves toward agreement with the student. Pairs who rejected opposite positions next exchange their own first-person statements and write the same kind of account of each other, then discuss the two experiences. The comparison centers on friction: what the model's readiness to accommodate made easier or left unpracticed, and what the classmate's presence required. Students check their account of the opposing reasoning against two published pieces by actual advocates of the position, noting what the model's version omitted.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students write accounts of the opposing reasoning from both the model's argument and a classmate's statement without rebutting either, compare the two listening experiences, and check their account against published advocates for what the model omitted.
activities.dl: Two written accounts of an opposing position's reasoning (one from the model's argument, one from a classmate's statement) and a comparison of the two listening experiences.
activities.risk: Students type their own views on a controversy into a tool, so topic choice stays with the student and a tool with clear data-retention terms or an institutional deployment matters; a printed model argument supplied by the instructor is an alternative for students who opt out.

activities.t: Predictions from Text or from Memory
activities.sum: Students read two nineteenth-century short stories in the public domain in installments: one widely anthologized, one obscure. At pauses the instructor has set, each student writes a prediction of what happens next, the textual clue it rests on and a confidence rating, before reading on. The same excerpts, up to the same pause, are given to a conversational model with a request for its prediction and its grounds. Afterward, students lay their predictions beside the model's and beside what each story actually does. For every model prediction they judge whether its stated grounds are present in the excerpt it was given or whether it refers to events, names or an ending the excerpt had not yet reached. The contrast between the famous story and the obscure one centers the discussion: where the model appears to recall a text it encountered in training, and where it reasons, as the students did, from foreshadowing, narration and genre. Students write a short note on what distinguishes inferring from a text and recalling it. The published lesson plan that suggested the format is not reproduced or entered into a tool.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students write their own predictions with a clue and a confidence rating before reading on, judge whether each of the model's grounds appears in the excerpt it was given, and write a note on inferring from a text versus recalling it.
activities.dl: A prediction sheet with clues and confidence ratings for both stories, annotated against the model's predictions, and a short note on inferring versus recalling.
activities.risk: Only public-domain story excerpts enter the tool, and the instructor can collect the model's predictions in advance and distribute them, so students need no account or device.

activities.t: Checking an AI-Written Label Against a Latin Epitaph
activities.sum: Students in a Latin or Roman history course receive a short museum-style label for a Roman funerary inscription, written by a general-purpose AI model, together with the inscription itself: a photograph, a transcription with expanded abbreviations, and a translation from an open-access epigraphic database. The instructor produces the label beforehand by giving a model only the database text, so no student uses an AI tool and no museum's teaching notes enter one. Pairs take the label apart sentence by sentence and sort each statement about the deceased into three groups: what the stone says outright (names, age at death, the dedicator), what follows from epigraphic convention (filiation or its absence, a freed person's formula, tribe, an opening such as Dis Manibus), and what the label supplies without support, which may include an occupation, an emotional bond or a social rank. Pairs then rewrite the label so that every inference is marked as one. The Ashmolean's teacher notes on death and burial inscriptions are linked as background reading on status, family and commemoration.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each pair sorts every statement in the label into what the stone says, what epigraphic convention implies, and what the label supplies without support, then rewrites the label so every inference is marked as one.
activities.dl: A sentence-by-sentence sorting sheet for the label and a rewritten label in which each inference is marked.
activities.risk: Students need no account or device beyond a way to view the photograph and database entry; a transcription and translation accompany the image for learners who cannot work from the photograph.

activities.t: Drafting and Testing Correction Rules After Text Recognition
activities.sum: A faculty member preparing a corpus of digitized sources works with a coding assistant to draft the correction scripts that follow automatic text recognition, and tests every rule before it touches the corpus. The researcher begins by hand-correcting a sample of pages to serve as ground truth and by listing the recurring recognition errors in the output: a long s read as f, broken ligatures, words split at line ends, confusions such as rn and m. For each error type the coding assistant drafts a regular expression or a short Python routine. Each rule is run on a second, held-out sample, and a log records every substitution with its surrounding line. The researcher reads the log and marks false corrections, which often include period spellings normalized away and proper names altered. Rules are kept, narrowed or dropped on that evidence, and the character error rate is computed before and after against the ground truth. The surviving rules, the log and the error rates go into the project's documentation of its correction method.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher hand-corrects the ground-truth sample, reads every logged substitution to mark false corrections, and decides which rules are kept, narrowed or dropped on that evidence.
activities.dl: A tested set of correction rules with a substitution log, before-and-after error rates, and a documented decision about the correction method for the corpus.
activities.risk: Recognition output from unpublished or rights-restricted archival material is subject to the holding institution's terms, so the error examples given to the assistant can be limited to short strings or to public-domain pages.

activities.t: Sourcing a Generated 'Period Photograph'
activities.sum: Students in a history methods course use an image generator to produce a plausible 'photograph' of a late nineteenth-century classroom and then treat the result as a candidate historical source. Beside it they place a public-domain photograph of a comparable scene, chosen by the instructor from a national library's online collection, with its catalog record. For both images students fill in the same sourcing sheet: maker, date, place, who commissioned it and why, physical format, and how it reached the collection. For the library photograph each line is answered from the catalog record. For the generated image the lines stay empty or can be answered only with the student's own prompt and the date of generation. Students then look at what the generated image does contain, which often includes dress, furniture or poses drawn from different decades, and note what it suggests about the pictures the model was built from. No real, named person is depicted. A short written comparison states what makes a photograph usable as evidence. The Digital Inquiry Group's lesson on evaluating photographs is linked as a published companion.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students complete the same sourcing sheet for both images, note details in the generated image drawn from different decades, and write a comparison stating what makes a photograph usable as evidence.
activities.dl: Two completed sourcing sheets and a short written comparison of what each image can and cannot serve as evidence for.
activities.risk: Image generators often require an account and may limit free use, so generation can be done once by the instructor or in groups; both images need text descriptions for students who cannot view them.

activities.t: Structured Academic Controversy with a Source-Bound Paraphrase Check
activities.sum: Students work in teams of four, split into two pairs, on a contested historical question, each pair holding a set of public-domain documents that supports one assigned position. One pair presents; the other restates what it heard without rebutting, and the presenters confirm the restatement. At that point the listening pair types its restatement into a document-grounded assistant that has been loaded only with the team's document set. The assistant marks any statement it cannot locate in the presenting side's documents and quotes the nearest passage. Both pairs go to the documents and accept or contest each mark, recording their grounds; the assistant may miss a fair paraphrase or treat a reasonable inference as an addition, and those cases are part of what the team settles. Roles then reverse. In the last phase the pairs set aside their assigned positions and write either a consensus statement or a statement of where they still disagree, with each sentence keyed to a document.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: The team produces the restatements, a decision with recorded grounds to accept or contest each mark against the documents, and a consensus or disagreement statement with every sentence keyed to a document.
activities.dl: A log of accepted and contested flags with reasons, and a team consensus or disagreement statement keyed to the documents.
activities.risk: A short typed restatement by students enters the tool, so a campus-licensed or no-login grounded assistant on one shared device per team limits account and privacy demands.

activities.t: Three Transcriptions of One Civil War Letter
activities.sum: Students transcribe a passage from the facsimile of one of the three letters that Lot Sabine Willard, a first lieutenant in the 11th Illinois Cavalry, wrote to his family in March and April 1862, working from the handwriting alone. A vision-capable model is then given the same facsimile image and returns its own transcription. Students set three versions side by side: their own, the model's, and the typeset transcription published by the Newberry. Every point of disagreement goes into a table with a proposed explanation, which may be a letterform, an abbreviation, a line break, or the model's tendency to modernize spelling or supply a word that makes the sentence read smoothly. Students then return to the central question of the Newberry activity, how Willard's attitude toward battle changes across the three letters, and note whether any disputed word bears on that reading. The handwritten original remains the reference; the typeset text is treated as an expert reading that can itself be questioned.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students transcribe the passage from the handwriting alone, explain every disagreement among the three versions, and note whether any disputed word bears on how the writer's attitude toward battle changes across the letters.
activities.dl: A three-column transcription table with an explanation for each disagreement and a short note on whether any disputed reading affects the interpretation of the letters.
activities.risk: The site states that digitized images may be used for any lawful purpose subject to the Newberry's Rights and Reproductions Policy; image upload usually requires an account, and students who cannot read the facsimile can work from the two typed versions.

activities.t: Mapping Current AI Commentary onto a 1929 Radio Debate
activities.sum: Students who have worked through the National Humanities Center's lesson on the 1929 magazine debate over commercial radio, used as published, turn to present-day commentary on generative AI and ask which arguments return with each new medium. No AI tool is used; AI is the subject. The instructor supplies two recent, openly readable opinion pieces, one welcoming generative AI and one objecting to it. Students name the kinds of argument they found in the 1929 essays in their own words and build a chart that sets those against the claims in the two current pieces, quoting a line for each cell. Some cells fill easily and others stay empty, and the class discusses both. A last column asks a question drawn from the idea that a technique fades from view once it is routine: which worries about radio are no longer noticed because radio became ordinary, and which claims about AI concern things that may become similarly unnoticed. Students write a paragraph on one argument with no counterpart in the other period.

activities.gate: Students name the 1929 argument types in their own words, set them against the two current pieces with a quoted line for each cell, and write a paragraph on one argument with no counterpart in the other period.
activities.dl: A comparison chart with quoted lines and a paragraph on one argument that has no counterpart in the other period.
activities.risk: The lesson is free to read online and is used by link, and the opinion pieces are chosen from sources without a paywall so that no student needs a subscription.

activities.t: Rehearsing Judges' Questions Before an Ethics Bowl
activities.sum: In the week before an in-class ethics bowl, each team rehearses its position with a chatbot that plays a judge and may only ask questions. The team works on an instructor-written case and drafts its own outline: the stakeholders, its answer to the case question, and its reasons. The outline goes to a general-purpose chatbot with an instruction to respond only with questions about assumptions, consistency and overlooked parties, and to offer no position or verdict of its own. The team answers aloud or in writing and keeps the transcript. Afterward members sort each question into one of three groups: it exposed a real gap in the position, it was already answered in the outline, or it rested on a misreading of the case. The team revises its outline in response to the first group only and says why the other questions were set aside. The bowl itself runs with human presenters, respondents and judges, and the PLATO lesson plan for an in-class ethics bowl is linked as the published guide to that format.

activities.gate: The team produces its own outline of stakeholders, answer and reasons, sorts each question by whether it exposed a real gap, was already answered, or misread the case, and revises only for real gaps, saying why the rest were set aside.
activities.dl: An annotated transcript sorting the chatbot's questions into three groups, and a revised position outline.
activities.risk: A team's outline enters the tool, so one shared login or a campus-licensed chatbot per team limits individual account requirements, and a human questioner can stand in for teams that opt out.

activities.t: Writing Consent Terms for a Synthetic Voice
activities.sum: Students listen to a short synthetic voice clip of a consenting speaker, placed beside a real recording of the same person, and write the consent and disclosure terms they would require before such a clip could be made or shared. The instructor prepares the clip in advance with a voice-generation tool, using the instructor's own voice or that of a colleague who has agreed in writing, so students use no AI tool. Groups first map the people with a stake in a cloned voice: the speaker, family or an estate, listeners, the tool's provider, and performers whose work depends on their voice. They then look at the clip at three levels, the underlying technology, this particular artifact, and the settings in which it might be used, from a course announcement to a performance released after a speaker's death. Each group drafts terms covering scope, duration, labeling, withdrawal of consent and use after death. activities.t: Question-Only Assistant for a Scripture Analysis Draft
activities.sum: Students in an introductory course on Judaism, Christianity and Islam draft a short analysis of one assigned scripture passage and revise it in response to an assistant that may only ask questions. The passage comes from the Hebrew Bible, the New Testament or the Qur'an in a public-domain or openly licensed translation. The student gives a document-grounded assistant the passage and the draft; the assistant is configured to ask, for each interpretive claim, where in the passage it is anchored, and to offer no interpretation or rewriting. Students answer by quoting a verse or phrase, or by recognizing that a claim rests on later tradition, a commentary or the textbook instead of the passage. They revise and attach a note on which questions led to a change, which they set aside, and any point at which the assistant drifted into supplying a reading of its own. The exchange is ungraded and comes before instructor feedback; grading stays with the instructor. Later papers in the course are written with fewer rounds of questions or none.

activities.t: Ordering in French with a Voice Assistant as Server
activities.sum: First-year French learners who have studied the food chapter of Français interactif hold a spoken role-play in which a voice-capable assistant plays a server in a French restaurant. The instructor writes a short menu and a role card that tells the assistant to stay in character, speak at a beginner's pace and avoid correcting the learner. Each learner orders for two people, asks about one dish and changes one item, and the session transcript is saved. In pairs, learners go through their own lines in the transcript and check partitive articles, expressions of quantity, forms of prendre and boire, and questions with inversion against the chapter's grammar pages. They also compare the assistant's lines with how servers and customers speak in the chapter's restaurant and interview videos, noting phrasing that sounds scripted or unlike those speakers, and places where the assistant let an error pass without comment. A class debrief collects the most frequent errors and the points where the simulated server and the filmed speakers differed.

activities.t: One Request, Three Ways: Testing a Chatbot's Uptake
activities.sum: Language learners write the same request in the target language three ways (blunt, hedged and indirect or ironic) and send each version to a chatbot in a separate conversation to see how it is taken. The situation is one the instructor sets, such as asking a neighbor to turn down music or asking a professor for an extension. For each version the learner records the wording, what was meant, and what the chatbot's reply shows it understood: whether it treated the hint as a request, registered the irony, or answered the literal words. Learners then put the same three versions to the instructor or another proficient speaker and record how that person says each would land in the setting described. The two sets of responses are compared. Discussion turns on where the chatbot's sense of politeness and directness follows target-language convention and where it appears to follow a different default, often that of English. The CASLS InterCom issue on pragmatics is linked as background reading on the gap between what is said, meant and understood.
activities.f: Style, Genre and Language Through AI Imitation
activities.gate: Each learner writes one request bluntly, with hedging, and indirectly or ironically, records what each version meant, and sets the chatbot's uptake beside a proficient speaker's account of how each would land in the stated setting.
activities.dl: A three-row record of wording, intent and uptake for the chatbot and for a proficient speaker, with a short comparison.
activities.risk: Chatbots vary in quality across languages and free versions may be weaker in less widely supported ones, so one shared demonstration account can replace individual accounts.

activities.t: Following an AI Search Tool's Citations to Their Origin
activities.sum: Students in a college writing course pick one factual claim from a recent opinion piece and ask an AI search tool whether the claim is accurate, then follow every source the tool cites back toward its origin. Only the claim, restated as a question in the student's words, goes into the tool. For each citation the student opens the page and keeps going until reaching the report, dataset or statement the information began with, entering one of four results in a trace log: the source says what the tool reported, it says something narrower or different, it does not mention the claim, or it cannot be opened. Students then look for the same claim once more through the library's databases and news indexes without the tool, and add what that search finds. The finished log supports two verdicts written in a short memo: one on the claim in the opinion piece, and one on how closely the tool's answer matched its own cited sources. The Writing Spaces activity on moving through information networks is linked as a published companion.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each student follows every cited source to the report, dataset, or statement where the information began, records one of four results for each, searches the library without the tool, and writes verdicts on the claim and on the tool's answer.
activities.dl: A citation trace log and a short memo giving a verdict on the claim and on the search tool's report of its sources.
activities.risk: Some cited sources sit behind paywalls, so library database access and a log category for sources that cannot be opened are part of the design; free tiers of AI search tools may limit the number of queries.

activities.t: Reading the Campus Assistant's Terms Beside the Course Policy
activities.sum: First-year writing students read the data and use terms of the assistant their campus licenses alongside the course AI policy, and then check what they read against the tool's behavior.
