activities.t: Accepting or Rejecting an AI's Cuts to One's Own Paragraph
activities.sum: Students take a paragraph from their own draft that they judge to be wordy, ask a chatbot to revise it for concision, and then decide on every cut the chatbot made. The original and the revision are set side by side and each change is numbered. For each one the student records a decision (accept, amend or reject) and a reason, with attention to what the cut did besides shorten the sentence: a qualification removed, an emphasis moved, a term replaced by a near-synonym, or a sentence rhythm flattened into something that no longer sounds like the writer. The student then assembles a final version from the accepted and amended changes. Before working on their own paragraphs, the class rates two revisions of a sample paragraph written by the instructor and compares its ratings with the instructor's, since concision allows more than one acceptable result. The Purdue OWL's exercises on eliminating wordiness are linked for further practice with their own answer pages and are not entered into any tool.

activities.t: Testing an AI Cultural Generalization Against eHRAF Evidence
activities.sum: Students in a cross-cultural methods course receive a short AI-written claim that two cultural traits tend to occur together, for example that societies with a given marriage practice also show a given residence pattern, and treat it as a hypothesis to be tested against ethnographic evidence. The instructor produces the claim in advance with a conversational model and distributes it on paper together with the prompt that generated it; students use no AI tool. Working from the published Cross-Cultural Correlation Study assignment, used as it stands by link, they restate the claim in testable form, assemble their comparison sample in eHRAF World Cultures, and judge the strength of support in the way that assignment specifies. A closing section of the paper returns to the AI claim: which societies fit it, which do not, and whether its wording reflects a default vantage point, such as English-language sources or one region standing in for humanity. The claim is checked against primary ethnographic passages cited by page, not against the model's own elaboration.

activities.t: Second-Coding an AI's Codes for Afterlife Beliefs
activities.sum: Students act as second coders alongside a document-grounded assistant that proposes codes for beliefs about the afterlife in ethnographic passages. They begin with HRAF's published Religion exercise, completed by hand as it stands, which gives practice in reading an ethnographic excerpt for a specific trait. The AI stage uses different material: the instructor loads a set of public-domain ethnographic accounts into a grounded assistant along with an instructor-written codebook, and no text from the HRAF exercise or the eHRAF database enters the tool. Each student codes the same passages independently and records those codes before seeing the assistant's. The class then computes simple percent agreement between human and machine coding, and pairs resolve each disagreement by quoting the sentence in the account that supports one code over the other. The assistant may assign a code that the quoted passage does not support, or may read a moral judgment into a plain description; such cases are logged with the passage as the deciding reference. The log of resolved disagreements feeds a short memo on what the codebook left ambiguous.

activities.t: Adding a Local Judicial Independence Decision with AI Search
activities.sum: Students use an AI search tool to locate a recent court decision on the independence of judges or prosecutors from their own jurisdiction, then verify it before it joins class discussion. The UNODC exercise on judicial decisions and documents is used as published for the shared discussion; this design adds a locally sourced case beside it. Each pair writes its guiding questions before searching: which court, which period, what kind of interference is alleged. The search tool returns candidate decisions with summaries and links, and it may cite a case that does not exist, misstate a holding, or attach a real citation to the wrong court. Pairs trace each candidate to the official reporter or the court's own website, read the decision itself, and keep a log showing which details in the AI summary matched the text and which did not. The verified decision is presented with a one-page brief and two discussion questions written by the pair. Nothing from the UNODC page is entered into the tool; the queries are the students' own.

activities.t: Questioning an AI Stakeholder in an AI Governance Simulation
activities.sum: During CFR Education's Regulating AI simulation, run as published, the student council questions a conversational assistant that plays one outside stakeholder, such as an AI developer's policy director or an allied government's envoy. The stakeholder brief is written by the instructor; no text from the simulation is entered into the tool, and the instructor operates the assistant on a shared screen while council members pose questions aloud. The assistant answers in role, and its replies are treated as one voice in the room whose contributions are open to challenge, not as a source of record. A student recorder enters each substantive claim on a stakeholder map with one column for interests and one for evidence. After the session, small groups sort the recorded claims: supported by the case's background materials, supported by another citable source, or unsupported. The council then deliberates and advises on the policy options the case presents, noting which stakeholder claims influenced the recommendation and on what evidence. Because the simulation concerns AI governance, the debrief can also take up what it meant to consult an AI system about its own regulation.

activities.t: Correcting an AI Reading of a 1917 Political Cartoon
activities.sum: Students ask a vision-capable model to interpret a political cartoon from early 1917 and then correct its reading using period documents. The activity sits beside CFR Education's Zimmermann Telegram simulation, which is used as published; the cartoon given to the model is a public-domain image the instructor draws from a library or archive collection, so that no file from the simulation is uploaded. Before prompting, each student writes a brief interpretation of their own: figures, symbols, caption, likely target. The model's reading is then set beside it. The model may misidentify a figure, miss a visual convention of the period, or explain the image with events that had not yet happened when it was drawn. Students mark each statement in the output as supported by the image, supported by a dated primary source, anachronistic, or unsupported, citing the documents they read for the simulation and the archive's catalog record. The corrected reading is brought into the cabinet deliberation as evidence of how the question of neutrality looked to the public at that moment.

activities.t: Checking Voting Barriers Against a Current State Election Code
activities.sum: After completing David Price's three voting simulations, students ask whether the barriers their character met would apply in their own state today. Each student carries a voting profile through the electoral settings in the published resource, ending with the Jim Crow-era election. The sequence then moves from that distant case to a near one. Students load the current text of their state's election code, a public legal document, into a document-grounded assistant and ask which provisions bear on a voter in their profile's circumstances: registration deadlines, identification, absentee eligibility, polling hours. The assistant answers with references to sections of the uploaded code. It may cite a section that says something narrower than its summary, or overlook a relevant provision. Students open each cited section, read it in full, and record whether the answer holds, noting the statute's effective date and any matters the code leaves to county practice. The product is an annotated profile listing each barrier, then and now, with the statutory section that governs it or a note that the assistant's claim was not found in the source.

activities.t: Comparing a Simulated Coalition with the Actual Agreement
activities.sum: After negotiating a governing coalition in Colin Brown's Germany simulation, run as published, students use an AI search tool to find out what an actual coalition agreed. The simulation supplies the experience of bargaining under constraint; the search stage supplies a real case to set beside it. Working in their negotiating teams, students ask a search-oriented assistant for the coalition agreement that followed a recent German federal election, the parties' pre-election positions in two or three policy areas, and which party received which ministries. The queries are the students' own, and the simulation's character sheets are not entered into the tool. The assistant returns summaries with links; it may blur manifesto pledges with agreed text or attribute a concession to the wrong party. Teams follow each link to the agreement itself, to party documents, or to reporting from established outlets, and correct the summary where needed. The debrief sets two tables side by side, the class's negotiated trades and the verified real ones, and considers what a simplified model of bargaining includes and what it leaves out.

activities.t: Auditing an AI Argument About Korematsu
activities.sum: Students audit an AI-written argument about Korematsu v. United States, separating what it reports from what it asserts. The instructor generates the argument beforehand by asking a conversational model whether the ruling was justified and distributes the printed output; students use no AI tool. The session sits beside Annenberg Classroom's wartime civil liberties lesson, which is used as published. Each student reads the argument once and notes an initial reaction, agreement or unease, before any checking. Pairs then mark every sentence as description of the ruling, opinion about it, or a blend, and check each descriptive sentence against Executive Order 9066 and the majority and dissenting opinions, all public-domain texts. Findings may include a quotation that does not appear in the opinion, a dissent's reasoning attributed to the majority, or a confident claim about later legal history that the documents cannot settle. Pairs compare their sentence-level judgments with another pair's and with the instructor's marked copy, discussing where a first reaction and a checked judgment came apart. The audited copy, with page references, is the product.

activities.t: Ranking an AI Theory of Change Among Student Drafts
activities.sum: An AI-drafted theory of change is placed, unlabeled, among students' own drafts, and the class ranks them before learning which is which. The program being modeled is a short fictional description written by the instructor, for instance a campus peer-mentoring scheme; J-PAL's Chicago summer employment case is used afterward as published, and none of its text is entered into a tool. Each group drafts a table linking the program's activities to the changes it is expected to produce. One further table comes from a conversational assistant given the same description and operated by the instructor. All tables are anonymized and ranked against criteria the class has agreed: whether each link states an assumption, whether each outcome could be measured, and with what data. After the reveal, students put questions to the assistant about why it chose particular links. Its table arrives as a finished product; the reasoning behind it has to be drawn out and may not hold up under questioning. The class then turns to the published case and works through it by hand, without AI, carrying the same criteria forward.

activities.t: Simulating Selection Bias with a Coding Assistant
activities.sum: Students use a coding assistant to build a simulated dataset in which the true effect of a program is known, then watch two evaluation methods disagree about it. The idea of estimating one program several ways comes from J-PAL's Happiness on Tap case, which is read as published; its data and text are not entered into the tool. Students describe in their own words a hypothetical program that households choose to join, and ask the assistant for R or Python code that generates household records in which better-off households are more likely to enroll. They set the true effect themselves. The assistant then writes code for a simple comparison of participants with non-participants and for a comparison under random assignment. Because the data are synthetic, runs can be repeated, reset, and altered: stronger selection, smaller samples, a different effect. Students read every line of generated code, confirm that the simulated selection mechanism is the one they specified, and check that the randomized estimate recovers the effect they set. A short report explains the gap between the two estimates in terms of comparison groups and assumptions.

activities.dl: A commented simulation script and a short report explaining why the two estimates differ and by how much under varied settings.

activities.t: Cross-Checking a Grant's Power Analysis by Simulation
activities.sum: A faculty researcher preparing a grant proposal for a cluster-randomized study uses a coding assistant to write a simulation-based power analysis and reconciles it with an independent calculation. The researcher first settles the design inputs from pilot data and the literature: expected effect size, outcome variance, number and size of clusters, intracluster correlation, anticipated take-up. A formula-based calculator or hand calculation gives a first answer, recorded before the assistant is consulted. The assistant is then asked for commented R code that simulates the design many times and reports the share of runs that detect the effect. The two answers may differ, because the code may ignore clustering, mis-specify the variance, or treat take-up differently from the formula. The researcher traces each discrepancy to a line of code or an assumption and documents the resolution. J-PAL's power calculations exercise informs the choice of design features to vary; none of its text or parameters is used. The reconciled figure, the code, and a note on how it was checked go into the proposal's methods section and data-management record. No participant data enter the tool.

activities.t: Voice Practice Intake with an AI Client
activities.sum: Students conduct a spoken practice intake interview with a voice-enabled AI model playing a client, then code their own transcript for interviewing behaviors. The client is a fictional profile written by the instructor, with a presenting concern, a reason for reluctance, and details the client offers only if asked in an open way. Georgia State's intake interview case study video is viewed as published before the session; nothing from it is entered into the tool. Each student speaks with the AI client for about ten minutes and exports the transcript. Working from the course's interviewing text, students mark each of their own turns as open question, closed question, reflection, or interruption, and note where the client's answers narrowed or widened in response. The AI client may be more forthcoming and more patient than a person at a first agency contact, and the debrief names those differences. The rehearsal is positioned as preparation for a later interview with a trained human role-player or field supervisor, where human assessment takes place. A coded transcript and a paragraph on two exchanges the student would handle differently are submitted.

activities.t: Hand-Checking an AI-Coded Population Pyramid
activities.sum: Students build one population pyramid by hand and a second with a coding assistant, then verify the coded one against their own arithmetic. The hand stage uses public age-and-sex counts for one country from United Nations population estimates or a national statistical office: students work out cohort shares and draw the pyramid on graph paper. Population pyramids are a general demographic technique; Population Education's Power of the Pyramids lesson, which also teaches them, informs this design at the level of idea only. For a second country, students download current counts and ask a coding assistant for a script that computes cohort percentages and draws the pyramid. The script may use the wrong denominator, such as each sex's total in place of the whole population, reverse an axis, or merge the oldest age groups. Students recompute three cohorts by hand, compare them with the plotted values, and read the code to locate any discrepancy. With both pyramids verified, they write a comparison of the two shapes and what each suggests about past fertility, mortality, and migration, stating which inferences the counts support and which would need other data.

activities.risk: The census data and a browser-based notebook are free; the hand-plotted stage needs only graph paper, and the coded figure carries alt text or a data table for readers who cannot use the image.

activities.t: Checking AI-Written Hominin Narratives Against Cranial Measurements
activities.sum: Students in a biological anthropology lab test AI-written accounts of human evolution against the cranial measurements they have taken themselves. The measuring is done first, using the Smithsonian-listed skulls lab as published, with casts or photographs of ape, modern human, and fossil hominin crania. Before class the instructor asks a conversational model for short evolutionary narratives about the same species, working from an instructor-written prompt that names the taxa only; nothing from the lesson is entered into the tool. Each student pair receives a printed narrative and marks every sentence as supported by their tabulated values, contradicted by them, or beyond what cranial features can show, such as claims about behavior, diet, or direct ancestry. Pairs then compare markings and trace disagreements back to the measurement table. Model output of this kind often states inferences with the same confidence as observations, and the sentence-level sorting makes that difference visible. A closing discussion gathers the sentences placed in the third category and considers what further evidence, such as postcranial remains or dated strata, would bear on them.

activities.risk: Students use no AI tool or account; the narrative is distributed on paper or as a file, and photographs can stand in for casts where a cast collection is not available.

activities.t: Auditing an Assistant-Written Script for Earthquake Data Preparation
activities.sum: Students in an introductory GIS or geoscience course map recent earthquakes from public USGS records, and a coding assistant writes the script that prepares the download for import. The source exercise has students clean and reformat the catalog by hand in a spreadsheet; here that stage becomes an audit. Students describe the needed transformation to the assistant, run the script it returns, and then inspect the result before any mapping: the record count is compared with the original download, latitude and longitude columns are checked for order and sign, and the handling of missing magnitudes or depths is traced in the code. They ask the assistant to explain its reasoning for each operation and annotate where the explanation and the code diverge. Only the audited file goes into the GIS software, where students map the distribution, overlay plate boundaries, and commit to a prediction about where earthquakes occur relative to those boundaries. The report includes the script, the audit notes, the maps with scale and orientation, and the tectonic interpretation.

activities.gate: Students check the script's output against the original download before mapping, annotate where the assistant's explanation and its code diverge, and commit to their own prediction and tectonic interpretation from the maps.
activities.dl: A report containing the assistant-written script, the audit notes, the processed data file, maps with scale and orientation, and a tectonic interpretation with predictions.
activities.risk: The earthquake records are public and contain no personal data; the design needs access to a coding assistant and GIS software, and the source material's noncommercial share-alike terms apply to any adapted handout.

activities.t: Interviewing a Simulated Bystander in a Fictional Dilemma
activities.sum: Learners in an international humanitarian law or human rights course question a chatbot that plays a bystander at the moment of decision in a fictional incident the instructor has written. The scenario, set in an invented town during an armed conflict, stops where the character has to choose whether to help a stranger at personal risk. In small groups, learners interview the character about what it fears, what options it sees, and whom it believes responsible, then record the reasons it gives. Each learner privately ranks those reasons from most to least credible before the group works toward a shared ranking, and the gaps in the story surface where people and the model filled in details differently. The class then turns to the documented bystander accounts in the ICRC exploration, read as published and never entered into the tool, and compares the simulated reasoning with what real people in those accounts faced and did. Discussion considers which obstacles and risks the simulation left out, softened, or resolved too easily.

activities.dl: A group ranking of the simulated bystander's stated reasons with a short written comparison to one documented account.
activities.risk: One shared instructor or group account is enough, since the interview can be run from a single screen; the scenario is fictional, so no real person's story is entered into a tool.

activities.t: Questioning a Treaty-Grounded Assistant on Minimum Recruitment Ages
activities.sum: Learners studying the law on child soldiers put questions to a document-grounded assistant that holds only the treaty texts the instructor has loaded, such as the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions and the Convention on the Rights of the Child with its Optional Protocol on armed conflict. The assistant answers questions about minimum ages for recruitment and participation in hostilities and cites the article it relies on. Before asking, each pair writes its own guiding questions and its own reading of one provision, so that there is a prior position to compare. Every cited article is then opened in the official text and checked: whether the wording matches, whether the obligation is framed as taking all feasible measures or as a prohibition, and whether the instrument applies to states, to armed groups, or to both. Pairs chart where the instruments set different ages and where the assistant merged them. The ICRC exploration on child soldiers is used alongside as published; its materials are not loaded into the tool.

activities.t: Critiquing an Assistant's Estimate of Relational Contact Effects
activities.sum: Students in a political behavior or research methods course ask a data-analysis assistant to estimate whether relational voter contact raised turnout, using a synthetic contact-and-turnout table the instructor has built. The table is constructed so that volunteers chose whom to contact, which means contacted and uncontacted voters differ before any contact occurs. Each student first writes a short analysis plan naming the comparison group and the threats to inference they expect. The assistant is then asked for an estimate and for the code behind it, and students compare its approach with their plan: which voters it compared, whether it adjusted for prior turnout, and whether its written summary claims a causal effect that the design cannot support. Because the instructor knows the effect built into the data, the class can see how far each estimate lands from it. The topic follows a Harvard Kennedy School case on relational organizing in Ohio, which is cited as background; no case text or data is used or entered into the tool.

activities.gate: The student writes an analysis plan naming the comparison group and expected threats before asking, then a critique judging which voters the assistant compared, whether it adjusted for prior turnout, and what causal claim the design supports.
activities.dl: A written critique setting the student's own analysis plan beside the assistant's code, estimate, and summary, with a judgment on what the data can support.
activities.risk: The dataset is synthetic, so no voter records or personal data are involved, and the design does not require students to buy the case.

activities.t: Updating a Published Case Timeline with AI Search
activities.sum: Students who have read a published Harvard Kennedy School case on flood protection at New York City's East River Park use an AI search tool to assemble the public record of the project since the case was written. The case is read as purchased, by each student, and none of its text is entered into the tool; queries are written from the students' own knowledge of the project's name and location. Each team asks the tool for developments in a stated period and receives a summary with linked sources. Every link is opened, and an item enters the shared timeline only when the team has found the claim in a city agency document, court filing, council record, or dated news report and has recorded a working link to it. Claims the team cannot trace are logged separately with the wording the tool used. The finished timeline is set beside the case's account of participation and transparency, and teams note which later events bear on the questions the case raises.

activities.gate: Each team builds a timeline in which every item rests on a public record it found and linked, logs the claims it could not trace in the tool's own wording, and notes which later events bear on the case's questions.
activities.dl: A sourced timeline of the project after the case date, with a separate log of AI-reported claims the team could not trace to a public record.

activities.t: Debating Deference to a Moderation Classifier in Role
activities.sum: Students playing The Oversight Board microgame, used as published under the Reacting Consortium's membership and permission terms, take on one added question: how much weight the Board gives to an automated classifier. Before the session the instructor writes a small set of sample political posts, some in more than one language or dialect, and runs them through an openly available toxicity classifier, recording the score for each. The game's own case materials are not entered into any tool. Factions receive the posts and scores on paper and argue in role for accepting, amending, or overriding each automated call, giving grounds a Board member could record. The set is built to include near-identical posts that receive different scores, so players meet the question of patterned error directly. The Board then votes on a short rule for when human review is required. In the debrief, students step out of role and compare the reasons they gave with public documentation of how such classifiers are trained and where their scores have been reported to vary across groups of speakers.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Students produce in-role arguments for accepting, amending, or overriding each automated score, and the Board's own rule for when a classifier decision requires human review.
activities.dl: An in-role argument on each automated call and a Board-adopted rule stating when human review of a classifier decision is required.

activities.t: Coding a Multi-Agent Deliberation for Group Decision Phenomena
activities.sum: After reading the open Noba module on the psychology of groups, student teams watch a multi-agent AI system deliberate and code the transcript with the module's concepts. Each team starts a run from an instructor-written brief in which several agents, each given different pieces of information, have to agree on a decision such as choosing among three candidates for a grant. The agents exchange messages, and the system returns the full transcript with its final choice. Teams code each turn using the module's definitions: whether shared information is repeated while unshared information goes unmentioned, whether positions move toward a more extreme version of the initial lean, and whether signs associated with groupthink, such as pressure toward agreement, appear. Class time is spent taking the transcripts apart instead of rerunning them. Teams compare codings and consider where the vocabulary of human groups fits the agents' behavior and where it does not, since the agents have no need to belong and no status to protect. The module's discussion questions on groups students have belonged to supply the human comparison.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Teams produce a turn-by-turn coding of the transcript against the module's definitions and an account of where the vocabulary of human groups fits the agents' behavior and where it does not.
activities.dl: A turn-by-turn coded transcript of the agents' deliberation with a short account of where group-process concepts did and did not apply.
activities.risk: Multi-agent runs can consume paid usage, so a single instructor-run transcript shared with all teams is a lower-cost variant; the brief contains no student data.

activities.t: Screening Study Designs During a Literature Review
activities.sum: A faculty researcher sorting articles for a literature review uses a document-grounded tool to extract, for each study, the four things the Noba Statistical Thinking module asks of any article: the research question, how participants were selected, the summary results, and the strength of the evidence. The module's closing task is written for students critiquing one article; here it becomes a screening protocol applied across a set of open-access or licensed PDFs that the researcher is permitted to upload. For a subset of articles the researcher reads the methods section and fills in the four fields before querying the tool, which gives a baseline for judging its extractions. Each tool answer is then checked against the methods section, with particular attention to whether random sampling and random assignment have been conflated, since that distinction governs whether a study supports generalization, causal conclusions, both, or neither. Disagreements are logged by type. The resulting evidence table records, for every article, the extracted fields, the page checked, and whether the entry was corrected.

activities.risk: Publisher licenses and library terms govern whether full-text PDFs may be uploaded to a third-party tool, so the set is limited to open-access articles or an institutionally hosted environment.

activities.t: Rehearsing a Co-Facilitation Dilemma with Simulated Group Members
activities.sum: Social work students practicing group facilitation rehearse a response to a critical incident with a chatbot that plays several members of a youth group, in a scenario the instructor has written. The scenario is original, with its own group, setting, and incident, and is built around a moment when a member's culturally grounded action meets a group norm and the co-facilitators read it differently. The IASWG case Somali Boys Group is read as published and is not entered into the tool. Students type their intervention, the simulated members react, and the exchange continues for a few turns. The debrief has two parts. Students review their facilitation choices against group-work concepts such as norms, inclusion, and co-leader communication. They then read the transcript for what the simulation assumed about the young people it voiced, marking flattened or stereotyped responses and noting whose knowledge would be needed to judge them. The published case is the comparison for how a practitioner with cultural knowledge read a moment of this kind.

activities.gate: Students produce their own typed interventions and a transcript annotated for their facilitation choices and for the flattened or stereotyped responses the simulation gave, with a note on whose knowledge would be needed to judge them.
activities.dl: A role-play transcript annotated for facilitation choices and for the cultural assumptions the simulation made, with a short reflective commentary.
activities.risk: The scenario is invented and no client or case material is entered; students who share the background of the simulated members may find the portrayal uncomfortable, so an observer role or a different scenario can be offered.

activities.t: Testing an AI Explanation of Shooting Hotspots Against Maps
activities.sum: Sociology students compare an AI-written explanation of why fatal shootings cluster in certain urban neighborhoods with the evidence in public interactive maps. Students first complete the TRAILS mapping activity as published, locating areas of concentrated fatal shootings and viewing the same areas on maps of inequality, segregation, and criminal justice disparities. The instructor separately obtains a one-page explanation from a conversational model, using a general question that contains nothing from the activity, and distributes it on paper. Students begin by writing down their first reaction to the text and whether it sounds right. They then go through it claim by claim, marking statements the maps can support, statements about individual motives or character that area-level data cannot support, and statements that move from spatial overlap to cause. Legends, units, and data years are checked wherever the text cites a pattern. In discussion the explanation is treated as one more reading open to challenge, and students compare their first reactions with what the checking showed.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Each student marks which claims in the explanation the maps can support, which assert individual motives the area-level data cannot carry, and which move from spatial overlap to cause, and notes how that checking compared with their first reaction.
activities.dl: A claim-by-claim annotation of the AI-written explanation with a short note comparing the student's first reaction to the result of checking.
activities.risk: Students use no AI tool or account, and the maps are public; the subject is fatal violence in named neighborhoods, which some students may know personally, so advance notice of the topic is a consideration.

activities.t: Comparing Human and Vision-Model Accessibility Audits of a Route
activities.sum: Students studying the social model of disability compare their own audit of a travel route with one produced by a vision-capable model. The TRAILS virtual field activity, used as published, has students travel a route from the position of a wheelchair user and record barriers and supports. For the AI component, students work with a different route documented in their own photographs of campus or in openly licensed street-level imagery, so that no part of the published activity or its mapped imagery is uploaded. The model is asked to list barriers and supports visible in each image. Students set its list beside their own and classify the differences: features both found, features only one found, and things a still image cannot show, such as a door's weight, a curb ramp blocked at certain hours, or how staff respond to a request for help. The last category carries the discussion toward nonmaterial factors. Students also consider whose experience would be needed to settle disagreements and what the exercise itself, done by people imagining a wheelchair user's position, cannot convey.

activities.gate: Students audit the route themselves, classify each difference from the model's list as found by both, found by only one, or not visible in a still image, and consider whose experience would be needed to settle disagreements.
activities.dl: A side-by-side comparison of the student's and the model's barrier lists for one route, with a classified account of the differences and of what images cannot show.
activities.risk: Student photographs avoid identifiable people and private property; image upload often requires an account, and students with mobility-related experience are not asked to disclose it or to serve as the class's authority.

activities.t: Modeling a fishery from a team's own catch records
activities.sum: After playing the Fishbanks simulation as published, each team works with the log it kept during play: fleet size, where its ships fished, and catch in every round. A coding assistant in a shared notebook helps the team write a small stock-and-flow model of a fishery, with one stock, a regrowth term and a catch that depends on fleet size. The model is kept deliberately plain, a few lines the team can read aloud, because the aim is to see the feedback structure, not to reproduce the simulation's internals, which the team has no access to. Teams adjust two or three parameters until the model's catch curve roughly follows their own record, then use it to test a rule they propose themselves, such as a fleet cap or a per-round quota, and observe whether the stock recovers. Each line of generated code is annotated with what it represents in the fishery. In the debrief, teams set their plots side by side and discuss where the simple model departs from what happened in play, and what the delay between overfishing and falling catch did to their decisions.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each team annotates every line of the model with what it represents in the fishery, proposes and tests its own policy rule, and accounts for where the simple model departs from what happened in play.
activities.dl: Each team submits an annotated notebook with its fitted model, one tested policy rule, and a short account of where model and play diverge.
activities.risk: Only the team's own play log and student-written prompts enter the coding tool; a free notebook environment suffices, though access to the simulation itself follows the publisher's terms.

activities.t: Auditing an AI-drafted due diligence memo on FTX
activities.sum: Students in a financial accounting or ethics course receive a two-page due diligence memo, written by a conversational AI tool at the instructor's request, that recommends a private investment in FTX as of early 2022. The instructor produces the memo from a short prompt of their own, without giving the tool any part of the MIT Sloan case, and labels it as AI-drafted. Students read the case as published and annotate the memo sentence by sentence with four marks: supported by the case, contradicted by the case, not addressed by the case, and knowable only in hindsight. A second pass looks at what the memo leaves out, working through the incentives of employees, regulators, investors and customers and noting which of them the memo never questions. Before discussion, each student rates the memo against the course's criteria for a due diligence document, covering evidence, governance, related-party exposure and audit quality, and then compares that rating with the instructor's. Discussion centers on the gaps between ratings and on what a reader in early 2022 could have asked for.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each student produces the four-mark annotation of the memo against the case, a list of the stakeholders and questions the memo never raised, and a rating against the course's due diligence criteria.
activities.dl: Each student submits the annotated memo with a criteria-based rating and a list of the questions the memo did not ask.
activities.risk: Students need no AI account; the case is read from the publisher's page, and the memo is distributed as a labeled handout in an accessible format.

activities.t: Testing a single-cause answer against a causal loop diagram
activities.sum: Before opening the Boeing 737 MAX 8 case, each team asks a general conversational assistant, in the team's own words, for the single root cause of the two crashes and saves the reply. The assistant answers from its general training; nothing from the case document is pasted into it. Teams then read the case as published and sort candidate causes on a fishbone diagram under headings they choose, such as design, schedule, cost, oversight and communication. The fishbone is redrawn as a causal loop diagram, with each arrow tied to a page of the case, so that reinforcing pressures become visible. The saved answer is placed on the diagram: teams mark which loop it sits in and which loops it leaves out. In a second exchange, a team describes one omitted loop in its own summary and asks the assistant to defend or revise its answer, then judges whether the revision rests on reasons or simply agrees. Teams present the diagram alongside both exchanges and state where their account and the assistant's still differ.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Teams produce a fishbone sort under headings they choose, a causal loop diagram with every arrow tied to a page of the case, and a statement of where their account and the assistant's still differ.
activities.dl: Each team presents a page-referenced causal loop diagram with the two saved AI exchanges located on it.
activities.risk: A free general assistant is sufficient; the case is read from the publisher's page and is not uploaded, and teams can share one account so that no individual sign-up is needed.

activities.t: Pitching an innovation measurement plan to a skeptical physician
activities.sum: Students who have read Yale's Design at Mayo raw case rehearse a pitch with an AI assistant playing a senior physician who doubts that a design lab's results can be measured. The persona brief is written by the instructor from general knowledge of physician-led organizations; no page, video or document from the case site is given to the tool. Each student drafts, in their own words, a one-page plan for how an in-house innovation center might show clinicians what its work has achieved, then pitches it in a text or voice exchange. The simulated physician raises objections about clinical time, patient outcomes and what counts as evidence, and the student revises the plan after each one. The topic is bounded and the student does the talking. Afterward, students sort the objections in their transcript into those that match something they found in the case materials and those that are generic, and note any objection a physician in the case would likely raise that the simulation never did. Class debrief compares the sorted lists and the revisions they prompted.

activities.gate: Each student produces a measurement plan in their own words, its revisions after each objection, and a sort of the simulated physician's objections into those grounded in the case and those that are generic, noting any the simulation missed.
activities.dl: Each student submits the transcript, the revised measurement plan, and the sorted list of objections.
activities.risk: Students' own draft plans enter the tool, so an institutionally approved assistant suits this design; the case site's terms prohibit reposting, and no case material is uploaded.

activities.t: Checking a scaling model against one new region's evidence
activities.sum: After reading Yale's SELCO Foundation raw case, teams test its scaling question on a region the case does not treat. Each team picks a region and writes guiding questions about what a decentralized energy program there would depend on: who lends to rural households, who repairs equipment, which agencies and local organizations are active. An AI search tool is used to answer those questions from current public sources, working only from the team's own queries; nothing from the case site is entered. For every answer, the team opens each cited source and logs who published it, when, in what language, and whether it says what the tool's summary reports. The log has a column for where a source sits: local organization, national agency, international funder, or press. Teams then look at the balance, since results may lean toward English-language and funder-published material, and where a member reads a regional language, one query is repeated in it for comparison. The closing memo states which of the foundation's building blocks would likely transfer and which evidence is thin.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each team writes its own guiding questions, logs who published each cited source and whether it says what the summary reports, and writes a memo on which building blocks would likely transfer and where the evidence is thin.
activities.dl: Each team submits a source log and a transfer memo that separates sourced findings from gaps in the available evidence.
activities.risk: Only student-written queries enter the search tool; free search-oriented tools vary in how many queries they allow, and the case is read on the publisher's site without reposting.

activities.t: Classifying a second industry from AI-gathered market shares
activities.sum: This follow-on to Ezra Pugh's team-based exercise on fast food market structure moves teams to a second industry whose data they assemble themselves. Teams first complete the original task: from one set of market shares, each commits to an answer pairing a market-structure classification with a position on antitrust action, and defends it. Each team is then assigned another industry, such as domestic airlines or ride-hailing, and writes down the classification it expects before searching. An AI search tool is asked for current market-share figures. Every figure goes into a table with its source, date, unit (revenue, units or users) and market definition, and the team opens each source to confirm the number appears there. A figure is accepted, amended or rejected, with the reason recorded; figures that cannot be traced are dropped. With the verified table, the team makes the same kind of paired choice and defends it to the class, explaining where its prior expectation changed and how the market definition it adopted affects the classification.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Teams produce their expected classification before searching, a market-share table with a recorded reason for accepting, amending, or rejecting each figure, and a defended classification and antitrust position built on the figures they confirmed.
activities.dl: Each team submits a verified market-share table with accept, amend or reject decisions and a defended classification and antitrust position.
activities.risk: Free search-oriented tools are sufficient and only team-written queries are entered; some industry reports sit behind paywalls, so library databases may be needed to confirm a figure.

activities.t: Two labor-market models rank the mall's stakeholders
activities.sum: Teams first complete Michael Levine's team-based activity on a shopping mall split between two cities with different minimum wages, ranking six stakeholders from most negatively to most positively affected in the short run and the long run. A conversational assistant is then given the openly licensed scenario and asked for two rankings of the same stakeholders, one reasoned from a competitive labor-market model and one from a monopsony model, with the assumptions behind each stated. Teams lay the three rankings side by side. Where the orderings differ, they name the assumption doing the work: how responsive employment is to the wage, whether an employer sets wages, whether shoppers and workers cross the city line. The scenario leaves details open, so teams also list what the assistant filled in without being told and what they filled in themselves. Each assumption is tested against the facts the scenario actually gives and against the textbook's two models. Whole-class discussion moves from the rankings to which assumptions the class finds better supported and why.

activities.gate: Teams rank the stakeholders themselves first, name the assumption behind each difference among the three rankings, list what the assistant and they themselves filled in, and test each assumption against the scenario's facts and the textbook models.
activities.dl: Each team produces a three-column comparison of rankings with the assumption behind each difference and a note on which assumptions the scenario supports.
activities.risk: A free assistant is sufficient and only the openly licensed scenario text is entered, with attribution retained; teams can share one device.

activities.t: Plotting average against marginal driver recruitment cost
activities.sum: Students begin with Louis Vayo's short exercise on driver-recruitment advertising, choosing by hand among four strategies from two small samples of per-driver cost, and write one sentence on why. That choice is made without any tool, since deciding between average and marginal reasoning is the thinking the exercise is about. Students then ask a coding assistant for a short script that simulates two advertising platforms whose cost per additional driver rises as more drivers are recruited, and that plots average cost and marginal cost for each. The script arrives as a finished product. Students turn it into a reasoned one by annotating each line with what it means economically: which variable is the last driver's cost, where the running average is computed, what the rising-cost assumption is. They change the rate at which costs rise and find the point at which a choice based on averages picks the more expensive platform at the margin. Each student returns to the original four options and states whether the plot changes or confirms the first answer.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Each student chooses among the four strategies by hand and says why, annotates each line of the script with its economic meaning, finds the crossover point, and states whether the plot changes or confirms the first answer.
activities.dl: Each student submits the annotated script, two plots, and a short statement relating the crossover point to the original choice.
activities.risk: A free browser-based notebook with a coding assistant is sufficient; students enter their own prompts and the openly licensed figures, and plots need text descriptions for screen-reader users.

activities.t: Comparing an AI price forecast with a classroom pit market
activities.sum: A class runs the Economics Network's hand-run pit market as published, with one addition: a forecast made by a conversational assistant before trading and kept sealed until afterward. The instructor writes the buyer values and seller costs for the session's card decks, gives that list to the assistant, and asks it to predict the price range, the number of trades, and how prices will move from round to round, with reasons. Students trade without seeing the forecast, since a prediction shown in advance could steer the prices they ask for. After the last round, the forecast is displayed beside the transaction prices the class recorded. Students separate the forecast into two kinds of statement: those that follow from the deck by arithmetic, which they recompute by drawing the supply and demand steps, and those that are claims about how people behave, which only the class data can test. Discussion turns to which behavioral claims held, which did not, and what would differ had traders read the forecast first. A second session with a new deck lets students write their own forecast.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students separate the forecast's arithmetic claims from its behavioral claims, recompute the arithmetic from supply and demand steps, test the behavioral claims against the class's own transaction prices, and later write their own forecast.
activities.dl: Students produce a marked-up forecast separating arithmetic from behavioral claims, with each claim compared to the class's transaction record.
activities.risk: Only the instructor uses the AI tool and only instructor-written card values are entered; the experiment needs open floor space, so seated trading is an option for students with limited mobility.

activities.t: Testing an AI account of a bank failure
activities.sum: After a class has run the Economics Network's computerized bank-run experiment as published, students receive a one-page explanation of a recent bank failure written by a conversational AI tool from the instructor's own prompt. The handout is labeled as AI-written, and no handbook material was given to the tool. Students already hold two things to test it with: the conditions under which the Diamond-Dybvig model produces a run, and their own session's record of when patient depositors withdrew early. They mark each claim in the explanation as one the model accounts for, one their class data illustrates, one that lies outside the model (interest-rate losses, uninsured deposit concentration, social media speed), or one with no support they can find. Factual statements about the bank are looked up in the public post-failure review issued by the relevant regulator. The class meeting is spent taking the experiment apart alongside the handout: where the explanation uses the language of panic, students ask whether their own early withdrawals were panic or a reasonable response to what others were doing.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Each student marks every claim as accounted for by the model, illustrated by the class data, outside the model, or unsupported, and writes a paragraph on what the model and the class data each explain about the failure.
activities.dl: Each student submits the marked explanation with a short paragraph on what the model and the class data each explain about the failure.
activities.risk: Students use no AI tool; the experiment itself requires networked computers or a lab as described on its page, and the handout and regulator review are provided in accessible formats.

activities.t: A vision model's reading of a customer setting
activities.sum: Students working on a venture idea photograph a place where their intended customer meets the product or service, such as a counter, a shelf or a waiting area, framed without identifiable people. Following Glenn Fajardo's d.school exercise, each uploads the photo to a vision-capable assistant and asks what makes the scene interesting, then what story the objects in it might belong to. The replies are saved as a numbered list of observations. Students then go back to the same place with a notebook and no device in hand. For a set period they check each observation against what is in front of them, marking it confirmed, refuted or not visible from where they stand, and add what the photograph could not carry: sound, waiting time, who speaks to whom, what people do with their hands. The written comparison names one detail the assistant drew attention to that the student had missed and one thing only being there supplied. In class, students state which observations changed their sense of the customer's situation.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Students produce a return visit's direct observation, marking each saved observation confirmed, refuted, or not visible, and their own record of what the photograph could not carry, such as sound, waiting time, and who speaks to whom.
activities.dl: Each student submits the photo, the saved AI observations marked confirmed, refuted or not visible, and a list of what only direct observation supplied.
activities.risk: Photos exclude identifiable people and private premises need the owner's consent; a free multimodal assistant is sufficient, and students without a nearby site can use a campus service point.

activities.t: Scripting and voicing an observation walk for a venture
activities.sum: Students who have taken the d.school's Inspiration Walk, an audio-guided solo walk, write and voice one of their own for a venture challenge they are working on. Each student plans a short route with a few stopping points and scripts spoken prompts that direct a listener's attention at each one, tying what can be seen there to the challenge. A text-to-speech tool turns the script into an audio track with pauses long enough to look and write. The author listens through first, checking pacing, pronunciation of place names, and whether any instruction is unclear when heard instead of read. A classmate then takes the walk with earbuds and a notebook. The author reads the classmate's notebook and marks which prompts produced an observation and which produced nothing or confusion. Weak prompts are rewritten and the track is voiced again, which takes minutes, so a second classmate can test the revision in the same week. The group debrief compares prompts that worked across different routes and what each listener noticed that the author had not expected.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Students produce the route, the spoken prompts for each stop, and a revised script based on which prompts yielded observations in a classmate's notebook, with a note on what changed and why.
activities.dl: Each student submits two versions of the script and audio track with the test listeners' notebooks and a note on what was revised and why.
activities.risk: Listeners need a phone and earbuds; a transcript, an indoor or step-free route, and a seated version keep the walk open to students with hearing or mobility constraints, and free speech tools may cap track length.

activities.t: Auditing a research agent's map of a problem space
activities.sum: Teams choosing a venture problem first build the d.school's six-layer map by hand, posting notes for how their topic shows up as data, technologies, products, experiences, systems and implications. The same topic is then handed to a research agent, a tool that plans and runs a multistep web investigation from one instruction, with a request to populate the six layers and cite a source for every entry. The agent's report comes back as a second map. Teams audit it before using any of it. Where the tool exposes its plan and the pages it visited, the team reads that trail and notes what it searched for and what it skipped. For each entry in the data and systems layers, and a sample from the others, a team member opens the cited source and tags the note verified, plausible or unsupported. Verified notes are merged into the hand-built map in a second color; unsupported ones are set aside with the reason. The team then words its own challenge from the merged map and marks which layer, and whose notes, that choice rests on.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Teams build their own six-layer map by hand, tag each audited entry as verified, plausible, or unsupported against its cited source, merge only verified notes, and word their own challenge, marking which layer and whose notes it rests on.
activities.dl: Each team submits a merged two-color map, an audit table of the agent's entries and steps, and a worded challenge statement.
activities.risk: Multistep research modes are often limited or unavailable on free tiers, so an institutional license or one instructor-run report per team may be needed; only the team's topic statement is entered.

activities.t: Checking an AI budget memo against a campaign table
activities.sum: Students first work Geoff Fripp's Marketing ROI Made Simple exercise by hand from the publisher's worksheet, as published. The AI component uses a different table that the instructor writes for the class: a fictional retailer, its own product and margin, and a quarter of campaign results with spend, units and revenue. That instructor-written table is loaded into a document-grounded assistant, which is asked for a one-page memo recommending where next quarter's budget goes, with return on marketing investment shown for each campaign. Students receive the table and the memo together. They recompute every return figure by hand and check whether the memo's numbers were calculated on gross margin or on revenue, since the two give different rankings. Each sentence of the memo is then marked as traceable to a cell in the table, as an inference the table permits, or as a statement with no basis in it, such as a claim about audience or seasonality. The course rubric announces that unsupported statements carried into a student's own final recommendation lose marks, and students write that recommendation last.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each student recomputes every return figure by hand, marks each memo sentence as traceable to a cell, an inference the table permits, or without basis, and writes their own budget recommendation last.
activities.dl: Each student submits the recomputed table, the sentence-by-sentence marked memo, and a short budget recommendation of their own.
activities.risk: Only the instructor-written table enters the tool, and the instructor can run it once for the class; the published worksheet is used by link, not uploaded, and its solutions are members-only.

activities.t: Auditing chatbot borrowing advice against hand-computed costs
activities.sum: Small groups in a personal finance or introductory accounting course audit a printed piece of chatbot advice about how to pay for a purchase. The instructor writes a short scenario of their own, a fictional renter facing a car repair bill with three ways to finance it, each with a stated rate, fee and term, and beforehand collects a conversational assistant's recommendation on that scenario. Groups begin without the printout: they compute the monthly payment and total cost of each route by hand or in a spreadsheet and settle on their own ranking. The printout is then handed out. Each sentence of the advice is labeled as informing the borrower of a consequence, steering toward one choice, or narrowing the options, and every figure in it is recomputed from the scenario's terms. Groups mark where the advice ignores a stated constraint, such as the renter's monthly budget, or supplies a number the scenario does not contain. The FDIC module's own borrowing-comparison activity is run as published, on paper, earlier in the session; none of its text goes into an AI tool.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Groups produce their own cost comparison and ranking before seeing the advice, then an annotated copy in which every sentence is labeled and every figure is recomputed from the scenario's terms.
activities.dl: Each group produces an annotated copy of the advice with every sentence classified and every figure recomputed, beside its own cost comparison table.
activities.risk: Learners need only paper or a spreadsheet; no accounts are required, no personal financial information is used, and the scenario is fictional.

activities.t: Loan interview role-play mapped to lender criteria
activities.sum: Learners in a consumer finance or financial counseling course sit on the applicant's side of a loan interview conducted by a conversational assistant. The instructor writes a one-page file for a fictional applicant with a mixed record: steady income, little savings, one old collection account. The assistant is set up as a loan officer and asks whatever it judges relevant; each learner answers in character from the file for about ten minutes and saves the transcript. In the debrief that follows, pairs tag every question the assistant asked with the lender criterion it serves (capacity, capital, or credit history and character) and list what a human underwriter would have asked that the assistant did not. They also mark any place where the assistant stated a lending rule or approval threshold, and check those statements against the course text and current regulator guidance. The FDIC module's application-review activity and its self-assessment worksheet are used as published, on paper, before the role-play, so learners have already applied the criteria from the lender's chair. No module text and no personal financial information enters the tool.

activities.dl: Each pair submits an annotated interview transcript with questions tagged by lender criterion and a list of gaps and checked rule statements.

activities.t: Sorting one's own negotiation moves after a role-play
activities.sum: After a two-party contract negotiation role-play, students write up their own moves from memory: opening offer, concessions, questions asked, information shared or held back, and the terms agreed. Those notes, and nothing from the licensed role materials, are loaded into a document-grounded assistant limited to the uploaded text. The assistant sorts each recorded move into positional or interest-based bargaining and quotes the line of the notes it relied on. Negotiating pairs then go through the sorted list together and accept, amend or reject each label, writing a one-line reason whenever they overrule the tool. A move the assistant reads as positional may, in the pair's account, have been a test of the other side's alternatives, and that disagreement becomes material for the class debrief. The instructor's debrief handouts and the published teaching themes remain the reference for what the categories mean. The simulation itself (Sally Soprano I, from the Program on Negotiation) is purchased and run as published, with one licensed copy per participant; students are told to keep confidential role instructions and figures out of their notes.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Each negotiating pair accepts, amends, or rejects every label the assistant gave its moves, writing a one-line reason for each overrule grounded in what the move was meant to do.
activities.dl: Each negotiating pair produces a sorted list of its own moves with every label accepted, amended or rejected and a reason for each overrule.
activities.risk: Only student-written notes are uploaded, and the simulation's per-participant license means its role materials stay out of any tool; a restricted or institutionally provided document assistant keeps the notes from wider reuse.

activities.t: Enumerating multi-party deal packages with a coding assistant
activities.sum: Students in a negotiation or public policy management course test claims about a multi-party deal by having a coding assistant enumerate every possible agreement. The instructor writes an original scoring scheme for a fictional siting dispute: five issues, a handful of options on each, a private point value for every party, and a supermajority rule for approval. After the class has negotiated a scored multi-party simulation, each team asks the assistant for a commented script that lists all packages in the instructor's scheme, computes each party's score, and flags which packages clear the approval rule and which are Pareto-efficient. Before trusting the output, teams score three packages by hand from the scheme and compare. They then use the enumeration to examine statements made in debrief, such as 'no better deal existed' or 'one party could block anything', and write what the script cannot show: why a party that gains on paper may still hold out. Harborco is run as published under its per-participant license; its role sheets and point values are never typed into the assistant.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Teams hand-score three packages to check the script, test two debrief claims against the enumeration, and write what the script cannot show, such as why a party that gains on paper may still hold out.
activities.dl: Each team submits the commented script, its three hand-scored packages, and a short memo testing two debrief claims against the enumeration.
activities.risk: A free coding assistant and a browser-based notebook suffice; the scoring scheme is instructor-written, so no licensed simulation content enters the tool.

activities.t: Coding a transcribed video negotiation for process moves
activities.sum: Pairs negotiate a short cross-border licensing deal over video conference, record it with both parties' consent, and run the recording through a speech-to-text tool that labels speakers. The scenario is two pages written by the instructor, so nothing proprietary is spoken into the recording. Each student corrects the machine transcript against the audio, noting where overlapping talk, accents or product names were misheard or assigned to the wrong speaker. On the corrected transcript, pairs code a small set of process moves: who proposed the agenda, when the first number was put on the table, interruptions, and questions about the other side's interests. Counts and time stamps go into a one-page profile of the session. Students then re-record only the first three minutes with a changed opening and compare the two transcripts. The exercise is preparation for Ren the Robot, a Program on Negotiation simulation designed for video conference, which is licensed per participant and run as published, without recording or transcription. Its listed themes of agenda-setting and the effect of the video medium indicate what the practice round attends to.
activities.f: Workplace Communication and Career Readiness
activities.gate: Each student corrects the machine transcript against the audio; each pair codes its own process moves into a one-page profile with counts and time stamps and compares the original opening with a re-recorded one.
activities.dl: Each pair submits a corrected, coded transcript, a one-page process profile, and a comparison of the original and re-recorded openings.
activities.risk: Recording requires each partner's consent and a stated retention period; transcription accuracy often varies by accent and audio quality, which the correction pass records, and a conferencing platform's built-in or institutionally licensed transcriber avoids sending recordings to a third party.

activities.t: Reconciling assistant-written difference-in-differences code with a spreadsheet result
activities.sum: Students complete a published policy-evaluation project twice: once unaided in a spreadsheet, following the project's own walk-through, and once with code written by a coding assistant. The project is CORE's Doing Economics Empirical Project 3, used as published by link; its text and data file are not given to the assistant. Instead, each student describes the calculation in their own words (group means before and after a policy, and the difference between the two changes) and asks for a short R or Python function. The function is first run on a twelve-row table the student invents, where the answer can be worked out by hand. Only then is it run locally on the project data. Students place the two sets of results side by side and trace every mismatch to its cause: a filter applied differently, missing values dropped silently, groups defined another way. A short memo records what matched, what did not, which version was right, and how the student knows. The spreadsheet result, built step by step, is the reference throughout.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each student describes the calculation in their own words, tests the function on an invented table worked by hand, traces every mismatch against their own spreadsheet result, and records which version was right and how they know.
activities.dl: Each student submits the function, its test on an invented table, a side-by-side results table, and a reconciliation memo.
activities.risk: Free coding assistants and free R or Python environments suffice; the project's text and data are not uploaded, in keeping with its NoDerivatives license, and code runs on the student's own machine or a campus notebook service.

activities.t: Testing a vision model's reading of Lorenz curves
activities.sum: Students who have drawn Lorenz curves and calculated Gini coefficients by hand or in a spreadsheet give their finished chart to a vision-capable model and ask it to read the chart back. The curves come from Doing Economics Empirical Project 5, completed as published; only the student's own chart image is uploaded, with the coefficient values left off. The model is asked which country or year is most unequal, to rank the rest, and to estimate each Gini coefficient from the picture. Students compare those answers with their calculated values and sort the discrepancies: curves that cross and so cannot be ranked by eye, a legend misread, an estimate given to two decimals from a chart that cannot support it. They then redraw the chart once (different colors, direct labels, or a table beneath) and repeat the request to see whether the reading changes. A half-page note states what the chart conveys that the single coefficient does not, and the reverse. The calculation precedes the upload in every case, so the model's reading is tested and never used as the answer.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Each student calculates the Gini coefficients before uploading, sorts the model's misreadings against those values, redraws the chart once to see whether the reading changes, and writes what the chart conveys that the single coefficient does not, and the reverse.
activities.dl: Each student submits the original and redrawn charts, a table of the model's readings beside calculated coefficients, and a half-page note on chart versus coefficient.
activities.risk: A free vision-capable chat tool suffices; only the student's own chart is uploaded, and a text table beneath the redrawn chart also serves readers who use screen readers or have color vision differences.

activities.t: Comparing language-model agents with class public goods data
activities.sum: After a class has played a public goods game and analyzed its own contributions beside published experimental data, the instructor shows what a group of language-model agents did under the same kind of rules. Before the session, the instructor writes a plain statement of a standard public goods game (endowment, multiplier, group size, ten rounds, with and without a punishment option) and has a small agent workflow play it several times, saving each agent's stated reasoning and contribution per round. Students receive the run logs and a chart of average contributions. They plot the agents' path against their class data and against the published cross-country results they worked with in Doing Economics Empirical Project 2, which is used as published. Working from the logs, groups classify the agents' stated reasons, note whether contributions decay as they did among people, and write down what the agents' behavior appears to assume about other players. The discussion treats the agent run as a simplified model: where it departs from human data, and what in its setup or training text might account for that. Students use no AI tool themselves.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Groups produce a chart setting the agents' contributions beside their class's and the published data, a classification of the agents' stated reasons, and an account of where the agent run departs from human data and why.
activities.dl: Each group produces a three-series chart of agent, class and published contributions with a one-page account of where the agent run departs from human data and why that might be.
activities.risk: The instructor runs the agents and distributes logs, so students need no accounts or paid tools; the cost of repeated agent runs falls on the instructor or department, and class contribution data are shared only in anonymized form.

activities.t: Checking a model's backward induction on a hand-drawn game tree
activities.sum: Students draw the extensive form of a two-stage leader and follower quantity game on paper, photograph it, and ask a vision-capable model to solve it by backward induction while explaining each step. The payoffs are ones the instructor sets for the course, written on the board; the tree is the student's own drawing. The model's reply is treated as a worked example under examination. Students check that it has read each payoff from the photo correctly, that it starts from the follower's decision nodes, that each comparison uses the right player's payoff, and that the path it names follows from those comparisons. Errors are annotated on a printout. Pairs then put a second question to the model: why might a real follower choose the lower-payoff response after an aggressive leader move? They compare its answer with what their classmates did when the class played such a game. EconPort's Stackelberg classroom experiment is run as published beforehand; its instructions and screens are not uploaded. The hand solution each student completes first is the key the model is checked against.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students draw their own game tree, solve it by hand first, and mark every misread payoff, misplaced comparison, or unsupported step in the model's solution; pairs then weigh its account of follower behavior against what classmates did.
activities.dl: Each pair hands in its game tree, its own hand solution, and an annotated printout of the model's step-by-step solution with errors marked.
activities.risk: A phone camera and a free vision-capable chat tool are enough, and pairs can share one device; students with handwriting or motor differences can draw the tree in any diagram tool and upload that image.
