activities.t: Adding chatbot alternatives to a whole-system map
activities.sum: Design or entrepreneurship teams build a whole-system map of a product on a wall with sticky notes (components, life-cycle stages, people, connected systems), set priorities from an estimated life-cycle assessment and business needs, and brainstorm at every node, following VentureWell's Whole System Mapping exercise. This version adds a second round of ideas from a conversational assistant after the team's own. Once the unaided brainstorm is on the map, one member reads the node list to the assistant and asks for one alternative design decision per node, plus one proposal for removing a part of the system altogether. The assistant's ideas go up on notes of a different color. Teams compare the two colors: which nodes only the humans touched, which assumptions the assistant reversed that the team had taken for granted, and which of its proposals rest on claims about materials or processes that nobody has checked. Every idea, from either source, is then scored in the team's decision matrix against the priorities set earlier, and the team records the trade-off that rules each shortlisted idea in or out.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: The team produces its own brainstorm at every node before the assistant's round, scores every idea from either source against the priorities it set earlier, and records the trade-off that rules each shortlisted idea in or out.
activities.dl: Each team produces a two-color system map, a decision matrix scoring ideas from both sources, and a record of the trade-off behind each shortlisted idea.
activities.risk: One free chat account per team is enough and only a node list is entered; the exercise is adapted under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so adapted handouts carry attribution and the same license, and separately credited images on the source page are not reused.

activities.t: Sourcing salary and rent assumptions for a cash-flow projection
activities.sum: Students build a multi-year personal budget projection for an early-career scenario of their choosing, and the work centers on where each input number comes from. A search-oriented assistant is asked for an entry-level wage, typical rent, and a tax estimate for that occupation and place, with links. Students open every link. Each figure goes into an assumptions register with four columns: the value the assistant gave, the value found at the cited page, the publishing body and date, and a decision to keep, replace or drop. Figures the cited page does not contain are replaced from a government wage or housing series located through the library. The projection is then built in a spreadsheet from the register alone, with rows labeled in the income-statement terms the course later applies to a venture. Students may use a fictional graduate instead of their own plans. The approach of meeting business finance terms first through a personal projection follows a published lesson on TeachingEntrepreneurship.org, which faculty can consult directly; its materials are not reproduced or uploaded here.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The student produces an assumptions register giving, for every figure, the value supplied, the value at the cited page, the publisher and date, and a keep, replace or drop decision, then builds the projection from the register alone.
activities.dl: Each student submits an assumptions register with a keep, replace or drop decision for every figure and a multi-year projection built only from the register.
activities.risk: Free search assistants and a spreadsheet suffice; the option of a fictional graduate means no student is asked to disclose personal plans, family finances or expected income.

activities.t: Prompt and change log for an app-builder assignment
activities.sum: Entrepreneurship students who are building a small web application with an AI app builder keep a structured log of the build and use it to compare two ways of working. The surrounding assignment can be the one published on TeachingEntrepreneurship.org, used as written by link; this record describes only the log and the comparison. Every prompt is entered with what the builder changed, what stopped working, and what the student did next. Midway, each student builds the same feature twice: once from a single long request that leaves the builder to plan and act, and once in small requests with a check after each. Both versions go to a classmate for a ten-minute user test with three set tasks. The log then records, for each version, which tasks the tester completed, which defects appeared, and how many corrections the student had to make by hand or by further prompting. A closing page, shared with the class as work in progress, states which claims about the app the student has confirmed by testing and which rest only on the builder's own description of what it made.
activities.f: Prompting as a Practiced Skill
activities.gate: Each student keeps the prompt-and-change log, compares two builds of one feature through a classmate's user test, and states which claims about the app testing confirmed and which rest only on the builder's own description.
activities.dl: Each student submits a prompt-and-change log, user-test results for the two builds of one feature, and a one-page statement of confirmed and unconfirmed claims about the app.
activities.risk: App builders often cap free use and require accounts, so build quotas, an institutionally provided option or shared team accounts need settling in advance; students are advised to keep personal data out of test applications.

activities.t: Interviewing a simulated non-reader stakeholder before drafting
activities.sum: Before drafting a workplace recommendation report, each student identifies people who will be affected by the decision without ever reading the document, and interviews one of them in simulation. The student writes a short brief in their own words: the organization, the decision under consideration, and the chosen stakeholder's position, for example a night-shift employee affected by a scheduling change. A conversational assistant plays that person and the student asks about concerns, constraints and what a fair outcome would look like. Afterward the student sorts the assistant's statements into three groups: concerns that match what the student knows of the actual setting, concerns that sound plausible but would need confirming with a real person, and generic remarks that could apply anywhere. Only the first two groups feed the draft, and the second is listed as open questions for the report's author to pursue. A revision memo names each change made because of a non-reader stakeholder. Purdue OWL's stakeholder worksheet is completed as published, on paper, before the interview; the worksheet itself is not uploaded or reproduced.
activities.f: AI in the Writing Process: Invention, Feedback and Revision
activities.gate: The student writes the brief, sorts the stakeholder's statements into matched, needing confirmation, and generic, lists open questions for a real person, and writes a revision memo naming each change made for a non-reader stakeholder.
activities.dl: Each student submits the sorted interview transcript, a recommendation report draft, and a revision memo naming changes made for non-reader stakeholders.
activities.risk: A free chat tool suffices; briefs describe a fictional or anonymized organization so that no employer's confidential details or coworkers' names are entered.

activities.t: Drafting a committee postmortem from its own records
activities.sum: A department committee that has finished a project, such as a curriculum revision or a new internship program, writes its postmortem report with an institutionally hosted, document-grounded assistant working over the committee's own records. Agendas, minutes, the project timeline and the shared message thread are loaded into the hosted environment. The assistant drafts the factual sections (what was decided when, who was assigned what, which deadlines moved), citing the document and date behind each statement. Members read the draft against the records and against their own recollection, correcting entries and adding what was never written down: the hallway agreement, the objection nobody minuted. Those additions are marked as member-supplied. Judgments about what worked, what did not, and what to do differently are written by the members themselves in a meeting, and the assistant is not asked for lessons learned. The report ends with action items, each with an owner. Purdue OWL's guide page on postmortem reports is consulted as published for the genre's purpose and its question areas; the page is read by members and is not loaded into the tool.

activities.gate: The committee writes its own judgments of what worked, what did not, and what to do differently, adds the agreements and objections the records never captured, and assigns an owner to each action item.
activities.dl: The committee produces a postmortem report with a cited chronology, member-supplied additions marked as such, member-written judgments, and owned action items.
activities.risk: Committee records can include personnel matters and student names, so they stay in an institutionally hosted environment under campus data rules, and members agree beforehand on which threads are loaded.

activities.t: Testing Peer-Evaluation Weighting Rules on Synthetic Ratings
activities.sum: A program committee responsible for project courses decides how peer ratings will adjust individual grades drawn from a shared team grade, and uses a code-capable assistant to see what each candidate rule does before adopting one. Following Karen Moore's account of weighted peer evaluation, in which a rating counts for more when the rater worked directly with the person rated, committee members write two or three weighting rules in plain language. They also write a synthetic rating set for an invented twelve-person team with shifting subgroups, so no student data is involved. The assistant turns each rule into a short script, runs it on the synthetic set, and tabulates whose share of the grade rises or falls under each scheme, with a plain average included for comparison. Members recompute a sample of the adjustments by hand in a spreadsheet and read the script against the written rule. The discussion that follows concerns the tension between group and individual grading and how much weight novice raters' judgments can carry.

activities.gate: The committee writes the candidate weighting rules and the synthetic team, checks a sample of the script's adjustments by hand and the script against each written rule, and chooses the rule, stated in plain language, that will adjust individual grades.
activities.dl: A committee memo that states the chosen weighting rule in plain language and attaches the comparison table and the hand-checked sample calculations.

activities.t: First-Pass Grouping of Statistics Journals for a Teaching Inquiry
activities.sum: An instructor of a first-year statistics seminar studies a semester of weekly student journals as evidence of how the class reasons about quantitative concepts, with a document-restricted assistant doing a first pass over the full set. The course follows the cycle Michele DiPietro describes: students write a weekly entry in response to a structured prompt, the instructor comments and returns it, and the set is read together for class-wide misunderstandings. At the end of term, with the approvals and student permissions the institution requires, the instructor de-identifies the entries and loads them into an institutionally hosted assistant limited to that corpus. The assistant proposes groupings of recurring misconceptions, for example treating a sample proportion as a population value or reading correlation as cause, and quotes the entries it assigns to each. The instructor opens every quoted entry, rejects groupings the wording does not support, recodes a sample unaided, and records where the two passes differ. The checked groupings inform the next cycle of prompts and a write-up of the inquiry.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The instructor opens every quoted entry, rejects groupings the wording does not support, recodes a sample without the tool, and records where the two passes differ.
activities.dl: The instructor produces a verified codebook of recurring statistical misconceptions with quoted journal evidence and a short methods note on where the assistant's pass and the unaided pass differed.
activities.risk: Student writing enters a tool, so the design assumes an institutionally hosted environment, de-identified entries, student permission and whatever ethics review the institution requires for studying course work.

activities.t: Comparing a Hand-Drawn Argument Map With an AI Map
activities.sum: Students in an introductory philosophy course map a short argument by hand, then compare their map with one a conversational assistant produces for the same passage. The task borrows the structure of Mara Harrell's paired tests: questions about the components of a brief argument, ending in a student-drawn argument map, with parallel versions built on different content. Here the passages are public-domain texts, such as a paragraph from Hume's Enquiry, and each student commits to a map on paper before opening the tool. The assistant is asked to identify the conclusion, the premises and the inferential links, and its output is redrawn in the same format. Students mark every node or arrow where the two maps differ and, for each, either defend their own reading or revise it, citing the sentence in the passage that settles the matter. A later round with a new passage of parallel structure repeats the comparison. The assistant's map is treated as one participant's reading, open to challenge, and both maps answer to the text.

activities.gate: Each student commits to a hand-drawn argument map before opening the tool, then defends or revises their reading at every point where the two maps differ, citing the sentence in the passage that settles it.
activities.dl: A pair of argument maps for one passage with each point of difference marked and a written defense or revision tied to a sentence in the text.
activities.risk: Only public-domain passages are entered, a free conversational tool is sufficient, and an instructor-run demonstration on a shared screen can stand in where students lack accounts.

activities.t: Logging Image-Generator Use in a Design Process Book
activities.sum: Design students who use an image generator during ideation record each use in the process book they keep across a project. The process book, as Dan Boyarski's account describes it, is a semester-long record of how a project developed, read by faculty alongside the finished work and used in progress conversations. In this version every generated image that enters the project gets an entry: the prompt as typed, a print or thumbnail of the output, the decision to keep, alter or discard it, and a caption of a sentence or two stating what the image contributed and what the student changed. Hand sketches, references and material tests sit on the same spreads, so the book shows where generated imagery entered the sequence and where it did not. At progress conversations student and instructor read the entries against the project brief and against the tool's saved history. Students who decline the generator keep the same book without those entries. The book is read alongside the final piece, not in place of it.

activities.gate: Students produce a process book that records, for every generated image entering the project, the decision to keep, alter, or discard it and what they changed, alongside their own sketches, references, and material tests.

activities.t: A Group Reading of Dewey Beside an Assistant's Selections
activities.sum: Teacher candidates read a one-page excerpt from John Dewey's 1897 essay 'My Pedagogic Creed', a public-domain text, using the NSRF Text Rendering protocol as published, and then compare the group's charted selections with selections made by an assistant limited to the same page. The protocol is followed from the linked document without modification; nothing from it is entered into the tool. Once the group's chart is on the wall and its discussion has closed, the facilitator gives the assistant only the Dewey excerpt and asks it to choose the passages it finds most significant and to say why. The assistant's choices are posted beside the group's. Participants discuss what each set foregrounds, which lines both chose, and which of the group's choices came from classroom experience the assistant had no access to. Each assistant selection is checked against the page to confirm it is quoted exactly. The unaided reading comes first by design, so the comparison shows what the tool selected and passed over, and its reading stays open to challenge like any participant's.

activities.gate: Teacher candidates produce their own charted selections from the excerpt before the assistant is consulted, and identify which of their choices came from classroom experience the assistant had no access to.
activities.dl: A paired wall display of the group's selections and the assistant's, with a short written note from each participant on what the two sets foreground differently.

activities.t: Setting a Committee's Root-Cause Analysis Beside an AI's
activities.sum: A program assessment committee works through a shared problem, for instance that few sections submit student work samples for the annual program review, using the NSRF Hidden Issues protocol as published, and afterward sets its own analysis beside one from a conversational assistant. The protocol is run from the linked document, unmodified, and none of its text goes into the tool. When the committee's charts are complete, a member gives the assistant only the one-sentence problem statement the group wrote and asks for its own account of underlying causes. The reply is printed and posted. Members mark which of the assistant's causes also appear on their charts, which are generic to any institution, and which of their own depend on local knowledge the assistant did not have: staffing patterns, the submission system, a past decision. Each cause the committee keeps, from either source, is tied to evidence someone in the room can name. The committee accepts, amends or sets aside the assistant's suggestions and records its grounds before deciding next steps.
activities.f: Faculty and Staff Development
activities.gate: The committee completes its own root-cause analysis first, ties each cause it keeps to evidence a member can name, and records its grounds for accepting, amending or setting aside each of the assistant's suggestions.
activities.dl: The committee produces an annotated comparison of its own causes and the assistant's, with a recorded decision and grounds for each suggestion kept, amended or set aside.
activities.risk: Only a one-sentence, committee-written problem statement with no names or records is entered, and one member's access to a conversational tool is enough for the session.

activities.t: Diagnosing Handwritten Math Errors Before an AI Does
activities.sum: Teacher candidates diagnose error patterns in handwritten arithmetic and then compare their diagnoses with a multimodal assistant's reading of the same pages. The work samples are written by the instructor: multi-digit subtraction and fraction addition completed by hand with consistent errors built in, such as subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in every column or adding numerators and denominators straight across. Candidates first record, for each sample, the error pattern and what it suggests the student understands. A photograph of each page then goes to the assistant with a request to identify the errors and their likely cause. Candidates tabulate where the assistant misread the handwriting, named a slip where there was a pattern, or matched their diagnosis, and check both against the instructor's key. The exercise precedes the IRIS case study on identifying and addressing student errors and its linked resources, which are used as published by link; no IRIS material is given to the tool. Discussion turns on what a diagnosis requires beyond a correct answer: knowledge of how learners arrive at a procedure.

activities.dl: A comparison table for each work sample listing the candidate's diagnosis, the assistant's diagnosis, the key, and a note on any mismatch.
activities.risk: The pages are instructor-written, so no child's work is photographed or uploaded; image upload may require a signed-in account, and an instructor demonstration can substitute.

activities.t: Weighing AI Function Hypotheses Against A-B-C Records
activities.sum: After completing the IRIS A-B-C analysis activity as published, teacher candidates ask a conversational assistant for alternative hypotheses about the function of the behavior and test each against their own observation records. The IRIS handout and video are used unchanged by link and are not given to the tool; what candidates enter is a typed version of the antecedent, behavior and consequence notes they wrote themselves, with no names. The assistant is asked what functions those records could be consistent with and what further observation would distinguish among them. Candidates sort the replies: hypotheses their recorded entries support, hypotheses that would need data they did not collect, and hypotheses that rest on details not found in their notes. For each they cite the entries that bear on it. They then keep, amend or reject their original hypothesis and write a paragraph giving the grounds. In debrief the class compares which suggestions were declined and why, and what a single short observation can and cannot establish.

activities.t: Rehearsing a Difficult Parent Conference by Voice
activities.sum: Teacher candidates rehearse a parent conference aloud with a voice-capable assistant playing a parent who disagrees with the school about how to respond to his child's classroom behavior. The conference follows the class's reading of the IRIS case 'He Just Needs a Little Discipline', used as published by link. The persona is not taken from that case: the instructor writes an original role brief, with a different family, grade and history, in which the parent holds a firm view that the child needs stricter consequences and is wary of the school's recommendations. Each candidate speaks with the assistant for about ten minutes while a peer observes and takes notes. The transcript is saved. Afterward the candidate marks the turns where they acknowledged the parent's position, where they explained the school's concern, and where the conversation stalled, and the observer says how the exchange came across to a listener. A second attempt follows the debrief. The assistant's replies are treated as rehearsal material, and statements made about behavior support are checked against course readings.

activities.t: Claim, Support, Question on an AI Answer About Learning Styles
activities.sum: Students in an educational psychology course examine a printed AI answer to the question of whether matching instruction to students' learning styles improves achievement, using Project Zero's Claim, Support, Question routine exactly as published. The instructor generates the answer beforehand with a conversational model and distributes it on paper with the prompt that produced it; students use no AI tool. Working in small groups with the routine open by link, they take the answer one assertion at a time and document on chart paper what the routine asks for, keeping to the support the answer itself supplies and not what they already believe about the topic. Assertions the answer leaves unsupported are flagged. Groups then turn to the assigned research reviews and mark each flagged assertion as supported, contradicted or not addressed by that literature, with page references. The closing discussion compares charts across groups: where the answer's confident wording ran ahead of its support, and which of the groups' questions the readings could not settle either.

activities.t: A Disassembled Device Read by Students and by AI
activities.sum: First-year engineering students take apart a small mechanical device, such as a retractable pen or a hand-crank flashlight, and compare their own account of its parts and purposes with a multimodal assistant's labeling of a photograph of the pieces. Teams first work through Project Zero's Parts, Purposes, Complexities routine as published, by link, with the object in hand, and commit their map to paper. They then lay the components out, photograph them, and ask the assistant to name each part and state what it does. The routine's text is not entered into the tool; the assistant sees only the students' photograph. Teams annotate the reply against the physical object: parts misidentified, parts merged or missed, and purposes the assistant could not infer from an image, such as a spring's preload or the feel of a detent. Where the team and the assistant disagree, the object is reassembled and operated to settle it, and a manufacturer's diagram is consulted where one exists. The comparison shows what handling a mechanism supplies that a description of its picture does not.

activities.dl: A team map of the device's parts and purposes with the assistant's labels annotated against it and a list of what could only be learned by handling the object.
activities.risk: The design needs inexpensive devices to disassemble and one camera-equipped, signed-in device per team; photographs show only the object, with no people or personal data.

activities.t: Predicting and Testing an AI-Drafted 5E Science Unit
activities.sum: Science teaching candidates write down what they expect a conversational assistant can and cannot do when asked to draft a unit on the 5E model, then test that expectation and reflect with Project Zero's I Used to Think... Now I Think... routine as published. The prediction is written before any tool is opened and names specifics: whether the draft will sequence the five phases correctly, get the science right, and fit a named performance expectation from the standards. Each candidate then prompts the assistant for a unit on a topic they know well, such as phase changes, and annotates the draft against the five phases, against the standard's wording, and against their own subject knowledge, noting activities placed in the wrong phase, content errors, and places where the draft is usable. With the annotated draft and the earlier prediction side by side, candidates complete the routine from the linked page, unchanged; the routine's text is not given to the tool. The reflection is about the tool's performance on a task from their own field.

activities.t: Sourcing Both Sides of a Headline Claim With AI Search
activities.sum: Journalism students weigh a contested headline claim, for example that later school start times raise student achievement, using the Tug for Truth routine as published on the Project Zero site, with a search-enabled assistant used to locate candidate evidence on each side. The routine is followed from the linked page and its text is not entered into the tool. Students pose their own questions to the assistant, asking separately for studies and reporting that support the claim and that cut against it, and collect the sources it returns. A source earns a place in the class display only after a student has opened it, confirmed that it exists and says what the assistant reported, and applied the program's source-validation checklist to it: who produced it, what kind of evidence it offers, how recent it is. Items the assistant cited that cannot be found, or that say something different, go on a separate list with a note on the discrepancy. The closing discussion considers where the confirmed evidence leaves the claim and what further reporting would be needed.

activities.t: Critiquing an AI-Written Student Explanation in Science Methods
activities.sum: Future science teachers critique a written explanation of a phenomenon that reads like student work but was produced by a conversational model, and plan the questions they would ask its author. The instructor generates the piece in advance, prompting for a middle school student's explanation of why water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass, and hands it out on paper with the prompt; the cohort uses no AI tool. Beforehand the cohort has read the Ambitious Science Teaching guide to face-to-face tools, as published by link, and has built for this phenomenon the kind of explanation checklist the guide describes. They read the AI-written explanation against their own checklist and mark which required ideas and relationships are present, absent, or named without reasoning. Because the piece presents a finished account with no trace of how its author got there, each participant drafts questions meant to draw out the reasoning a real student would need to supply, and the cohort compares drafts. The explanation's science is checked against the course text.

activities.gate: Participants mark which required ideas and relationships the explanation states, omits, or names without reasoning against the checklist the cohort built, and each drafts questions meant to draw out the reasoning a real student would need to supply.
activities.dl: A marked-up copy of the AI-written explanation against the cohort's checklist and a set of drafted questions aimed at eliciting the missing reasoning.

activities.t: Checking Generated Tree Images Against a Local Tree
activities.sum: Future elementary teachers planning a year-long tree observation unit for their own placement community test whether an image generator can supply seasonal images that match the trees their students would see. They first watch the Ambitious Science Teaching video post on a bilingual kindergarten tree and seasons unit, as published by link; nothing from it is entered into a tool. Each participant chooses a tree species that grows near their placement school and prompts the generator for that tree in each of the four seasons, in English and, where they can, in a second language spoken in the community. They tally what comes back: which species the images appear to show, whether leaf shape, bark, flowers and fruit fit the named tree, and what settings and people appear around it. The tallies are checked against the participants' own photographs of a local tree and a regional field guide. Discussion considers whose landscapes the default images resemble and whether any image is accurate enough to use beside children's own drawings and family accounts.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Each future teacher produces a tally of generated seasonal images for one local species, checked against their own photographs and a regional field guide, and a reasoned decision on whether any image would be used in the unit.
activities.dl: A tally sheet of generated seasonal images for one local tree species with accuracy notes and a decision, with reasons, on whether any image would be used in the unit.
activities.risk: Image generators often cap free use and require accounts, so shared instructor-run prompting is an alternative; the video post is viewed on its own site because all rights are reserved.

activities.t: Questioning Your Own Assignment Sheet with a Grounded Assistant
activities.sum: In a department assignment-review session, each instructor brings one of their own assignment sheets, here an introductory sociology essay prompt on how deviance is socially defined, and loads only that sheet into a document-grounded assistant. Colleagues then pose the questions a first-year student might ask: what the paper is for, what counts as applying labeling theory to a case, how the criterion weights translate into work. The assistant is restricted to the sheet, so each reply either quotes a passage or reports that the document does not say. Before reading any reply, the author writes down the answer they believe the sheet gives. The pairs of predicted and returned answers are sorted into demands on thinking and demands of procedure, and the silences are listed. The published TILT sociology example, a less-transparent and a more-transparent version of one assignment, is read alongside by link as a comparison specimen; it is not entered into the tool. Each author decides what, if anything, to revise.

activities.t: Comparing AI Search and the Catalog for Book Sources
activities.sum: Students starting a research project run the same search twice, once in an AI search tool and once in the library catalog, and compare what each returns as book sources. The search terms are the student's own. For every title the AI tool suggests, the student looks for a matching catalog record and notes whether the book exists as described, whether the library holds it, and whether the author, edition, and year agree. For titles found in either list, the student writes what in the catalog record, such as subject headings, contents notes, or publication date, indicates the book would be useful for the topic. Titles the AI tool lists that have no record in the catalog or a union catalog are flagged as not found. Posted results are then read by peers, who comment on one another's relevance judgments. The comparison shows what each tool surfaces and what each leaves the searcher to confirm; the catalog record is the reference throughout.

activities.dl: A two-column search log listing titles from the AI tool and from the catalog, each with its catalog-record status and a sentence on what in the record indicates usefulness.
activities.risk: Students enter only topic keywords, not drafts or personal information; an AI search tool that works without sign-in, or a shared instructor session, avoids requiring accounts.

activities.t: Correcting an AI-Generated Court Structure Chart
activities.sum: Small groups in an introductory criminal justice course receive a printed chart of the state and federal court systems that the instructor generated beforehand with a conversational or diagramming AI tool. The chart looks finished, and it may contain errors of the kind such tools often produce: a trial court given appellate jurisdiction, a missing intermediate level, an appeal path drawn to the wrong court. Before seeing it, each student writes from memory which court would hear a felony trial, a small claims dispute, a federal civil suit, and an appeal from each, and rates their confidence in each answer. Groups then mark every label, level, and arrow on the chart as correct, wrong, or unverifiable, and annotate the corrections. The marked chart is compared with the organizational charts published by the federal judiciary and the state's own court system. Students use no AI tool during the session. Discussion can turn on which errors were caught, which were missed, and how confidence related to accuracy.

activities.dl: A group-annotated copy of the AI-generated court chart with each label, level and appeal path marked and corrected, plus each student's confidence-rated recall sheet.
activities.risk: Students need no device, account or payment; the chart is distributed on paper with a text description of its levels and paths available for students who use screen readers.

activities.t: Rehearsing a Family Conference on Classroom Behavior Expectations
activities.sum: Teacher candidates in an early childhood methods course rehearse a family conference with a conversational AI playing a parent, after drafting classroom rules and a behavior support plan for a child in an instructor-written vignette. The vignette and the candidate's own plan are the only material given to the tool; the IRIS case study unit on early childhood behavior management is read as published on the IRIS site, and its strategy sheets serve as the reference candidates consult. In the role-play the simulated parent asks why a rule is worded as it is, questions whether it fits the family's routines at home, and may resist parts of the plan. The candidate explains, adjusts, or holds a position. Afterward, candidates annotate the transcript, tying each thing they said to a strategy in the published sheets or marking it as unsupported, and they revise the plan. A debrief with the instructor or a cooperating teacher takes up what a text exchange leaves out of a live conference with a family.

activities.t: Sorting AI-Suggested Supports into Accommodations and Modifications
activities.sum: Candidates in a special education or inclusive-practice course ask a conversational AI for 'accommodations' for a student described in an instructor-written profile, then sort what comes back. The published IRIS activity on accommodations versus modifications is completed first, as it stands on the IRIS site, and none of its scenarios are entered into the tool. The profile is fictional, for example a seventh grader with a specific learning disability in written expression in a general education science class. The tool often returns a mixed list under the single heading it was asked for: extended time and speech-to-text beside shortened assignments or a simplified text. Candidates label each suggestion as an accommodation or a modification, justify the call in a sentence, and mark each as accepted, amended, or declined for this student. They also record any suggestion that would need information the profile does not contain. The sorted list is checked against the definitions in the published overview and the course's reference on individualized education programs.

activities.t: Auditing a Delegated Evidence Search for a Named Practice
activities.sum: A teacher-education faculty member preparing an evidence review on a named instructional program delegates a bounded search to an agentic research tool and then audits each step of what it did. Before delegating, the faculty member writes down their initial thoughts: which studies they expect to find, for which grade levels and student populations, and what would count as a match for the setting they are writing about. The agent is given the program name and those inclusion criteria, searches across sites, and returns a report with citations and a log of its steps. The audit works through the log. Each citation is resolved in ERIC or at the publisher; each study's sample, grade band, and setting are read in the methods section and compared with what the report says; any What Works Clearinghouse intervention report is checked for its rating and the population it covers. Studies the agent omitted are added from a database search. The initial thoughts are then revisited against the audited set. The IRIS module on fidelity of implementation supplies the topic only.

activities.gate: The faculty member sets the inclusion criteria and expectations before delegating, decides from each methods section whether a cited study matches the setting, adds the studies the agent omitted, and revisits the initial expectations against the audited set.
activities.dl: An audited evidence table for the named program, listing each study with its verified sample, grade band and setting, alongside the faculty member's initial and revised expectations.
activities.risk: Agentic research features are often limited to paid or institutionally licensed tiers; only a program name and inclusion criteria are entered, and no unpublished data or student information.

activities.t: Spoken and Typed Explanations of Fraction Equivalence, Compared
activities.sum: Candidates in an elementary mathematics methods course explain why three-fourths and six-eighths name the same amount twice, once by speaking to a speech-to-text tool and once by typing, and compare what each medium kept. The task is specified by its objective only: an accurate explanation, pitched at fourth graders, that refers to a representation such as a number line or fraction strips. The speech tool returns a transcript, which may render spoken fractions, 'numerator', or 'equal parts' incorrectly and which carries the pauses and restarts of talk. Candidates correct the transcript against their own recording, then set the spoken and typed versions side by side and score both with the same criteria. They note which version states the multiplicative relationship more clearly, which leans on the representation, and what the transcript lost that the voice carried. A short written comparison addresses whether written prose is essential to this objective or one of several acceptable media, the question raised by the CAST consideration on multiple media for communication.

activities.t: Marking Meaning Shifts in AI Simplifications of Methods Prose
activities.sum: Graduate students in an education research methods course receive AI-written plain-language versions of a dense methods passage and mark where the simplification changed what a technical term means. The instructor prepares the materials ahead of time by giving a conversational AI tool a paragraph from an openly licensed article, one reporting score reliability, a confidence interval, and a statistically significant difference with a small effect size, and saving two or three of its rewrites. In class, students first write their own gloss of each term from the original paragraph, unaided. They then read the rewrites beside the original and annotate each place where clearer syntax came with a changed claim: 'significant' read as important, 'reliable' as accurate, an interval described as the range of most students' scores. For each mark, the student writes the corrected plain-language sentence. Annotations are checked against the original passage and the definitions in the course's measurement reference. Students use no AI tool; the rewrites are specimens.

activities.gate: Each student writes an unaided gloss of each term, marks every place a rewrite changed what a technical term means, and writes a corrected plain-language sentence for each mark.
activities.dl: An annotated set of AI rewrites with each meaning shift marked and a corrected plain-language sentence written for it, alongside the student's own unaided glosses.

activities.t: Reviewing a Lesson-Plan Comment Bank in a Hosted Assistant
activities.sum: A methods instructor reviews the bank of reusable comments they attach to lesson-plan submissions, using an institutionally hosted assistant to sort the comments and draft alternatives. Only the instructor's own comment bank and the assignment rubric are loaded; no student work or names enter the system. The assistant labels each comment as one that only judges ('objective unclear', 'strong hook') or one that names a next action, and for the first kind it drafts a version pointing to something the candidate could do, such as rewriting the objective with an observable verb and a condition. The instructor has already sorted a sample of the comments by hand, and compares that sort with the assistant's before reading the drafts. Each draft is then accepted, amended, or rejected, with a brief reason, and checked against the rubric row it refers to so that the rewritten comment still describes the criterion. The CAST consideration on action-oriented feedback is read as published as the lens for the sort. The result is a revised bank and a record of the instructor's decisions.
activities.f: Assessment and Feedback Design
activities.gate: The instructor decides, with a reason for each, which drafted comments to accept, amend, or reject, and whether each rewrite still describes the rubric criterion it refers to.
activities.dl: A revised comment bank for the lesson-plan assignment, with a log of which assistant drafts the instructor accepted, amended or rejected and why.
activities.risk: The work stays in an institutionally hosted environment and uses only instructor-authored comments and the rubric, so no student writing or identifying information is processed.

activities.t: Sparring with a Chatbot Before a Camera-Policy Case Discussion
activities.sum: Before a seminar discussion of the Justice in Schools case 'Remote Control', which students read as published, each student argues with a conversational AI about a general question the case raises: whether a school may require young children to keep cameras on during online class at home. The student writes a position in their own words and asks the tool to act as an opponent for several rounds; the case text is not pasted in. The tool tends to supply ready arguments about oversight, consistency, privacy, and equity. Students then read their transcript with a set of questions: whose voice is heard in these arguments, whose is missing, who decides, and at whose cost. They list the objections that changed their position, the ones they rejected and why, and the people in the case, such as particular families or the teachers on the team, whose situation the exchange never reached. The seminar itself runs without AI, and each student defends a decision for the fourth-grade team.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: The student writes a position in their own words, lists the objections that changed it and those rejected with reasons, names the people the exchange never reached, and defends a decision in a seminar run without AI.
activities.dl: A sparring transcript annotated for heard and missing voices, a list of objections accepted and rejected, and an oral defense of a decision in seminar.
activities.risk: Students enter only their own position statement and no case text; a student who does not use the tool can annotate a transcript the instructor supplies, and the seminar itself requires no technology.

activities.t: Checking an AI-Drafted Teacher Evaluation Against the Rubric
activities.sum: Students in an educational leadership course examine a teacher evaluation narrative drafted by a document-grounded assistant and decide whether they would sign it. Pairs give the assistant two documents: a publicly available teacher-evaluation rubric and a set of instructor-written observation notes on a fictional middle school science teacher whose lab routines run smoothly and whose questioning rarely goes beyond recall. It drafts a rating for each rubric domain with a supporting paragraph. Students trace every sentence of the draft to a line in the notes and a level descriptor in the rubric, marking evidence the draft weighed, evidence it passed over, and claims found in neither document. They assign their own ratings and write a short justification of each difference from the draft. The Justice in Schools case 'First Rate', read as published and not entered into the tool, then frames discussion of what a rating sets in motion and what remains the evaluator's responsibility when a draft arrives already written.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Pairs produce a trace of every sentence of the draft to the observation notes and rubric, their own rating for each domain, and a written justification of each difference from the draft.
activities.dl: A marked-up evaluation draft with each sentence traced to the notes and rubric, the pair's own domain ratings, and a written justification of each difference.
activities.risk: The observation notes describe a fictional teacher, so no personnel information about a real educator is entered; the rubric used is one that is publicly available.

activities.t: Locating and Verifying Statutory Guidance Behind a School Decision
activities.sum: Students studying the Justice in Schools case 'No Laughing Matter', read as published, use an AI search tool to locate the statutory guidance on the Prevent duty for schools in England and verify what the tool says the guidance requires. The query is the student's own; the case text is not entered. The tool returns a summary with links and may paraphrase loosely, cite superseded versions, or attribute requirements to the guidance that are not found in it. Students open the current official publication, find each passage the summary relies on, and record the paragraph number, the exact wording, and whether the summary's paraphrase holds. They note the date and version of the document they are reading. With the verified passages in hand, each student writes a brief analysis of whether the head teacher's stated justification in the case is supported by, in tension with, or outside the scope of the guidance. Seminar discussion of the case's wider questions about expression and inclusion proceeds from the verified text.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Students record the paragraph, exact wording, and version behind each claim in the summary, judge whether each paraphrase holds, and write their own analysis of whether the head teacher's justification is supported by, in tension with, or outside the guidance.
activities.dl: A verification table pairing each claim in the AI summary with the official paragraph and wording, and a brief written analysis of the head teacher's justification.
activities.risk: Students enter only their own query, not the case text; the official guidance is free to read online, and the case's subject matter may call for advance notice about its religiously sensitive content.

activities.t: Comparing a Model's Weld Defect Calls with Instructor Inspection
activities.sum: Learners in a first-year welding lab photograph their own practice welds and compare a multimodal model's reading of each photograph with the instructor's visual inspection. After completing a fillet or groove weld coupon, the learner first inspects it and records what they see: undercut, porosity, overlap, incomplete fusion, or an acceptable profile. The model is then given the photograph and asked what discontinuities are visible. It may name a defect that is not present, miss one that lighting or angle obscures, or describe the bead in general terms. The instructor inspects the physical coupon against the visual acceptance criteria the program uses and completes the assessment sheet. Learners tabulate the three readings for each coupon, their own, the model's, and the instructor's, and note where a photograph could not show what a gauge or a change of viewing angle revealed. The SkillsCommons record for WELD 154 supplies the occupational setting; no course documents from it are uploaded.

activities.gate: The learner records their own inspection of each coupon before the model sees it, tabulates it beside the model's and the instructor's readings, and notes what the photograph could not show that a gauge or another viewing angle revealed.
activities.dl: A table for each practice coupon comparing the learner's inspection, the model's defect call and the instructor's assessment, with notes on what the photograph could not show.
activities.risk: A camera phone and a multimodal tool are needed; a shared lab device and instructor-run session avoid requiring personal accounts, and photographs show only the coupon, not people or the shop.

activities.t: Correcting an Agent-Compiled Timeline After an Interprofessional Simulation
activities.sum: After a simulation day in which several health and public-safety programs work one instructor-written scenario in sequence, learners correct an incident timeline that an agentic AI system compiled from their notes. Each program submits its own documentation: a rescue run report, a nursing handoff note, a laboratory requisition, an officer's scene notes. Under instructor supervision, the agent collects the submissions, orders the events, reconciles times, and produces a single timeline with a log of what it took from which note. In the debrief, mixed-program groups read the timeline against the facilitator's event log and the session recording. They mark events placed out of order, handoffs the timeline merged or dropped, and entries where the agent resolved a conflict between two notes without saying so. Each program then identifies which of the errors began in its own documentation and which in the compilation. The simulation uses no real patient information. The idea of a single scenario passing through many occupational programs comes from the LATI Healthcare Mega Simulation record.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Mixed-program groups mark events out of order, handoffs merged or dropped, and conflicts resolved without notice, checked against the event log and recording, and each program identifies which errors began in its own documentation.
activities.dl: A corrected incident timeline annotated by mixed-program groups, with each error attributed to a program's documentation or to the compilation.
activities.risk: Learner-written notes are processed by the agent, so an institutionally approved tool and learner notice are relevant; the scenario is fictional and contains no real patient information, and recordings are handled under the programs' existing simulation consent practices.

activities.t: Autocomplete and AI Search Answers Compared for Representation
activities.sum: Pairs in a first-year library session put the same identity and occupation query stems to two systems, a conventional search engine's autocomplete and an AI search assistant, and log what each returns. The session keeps the sequence of the Project CORA lesson it adapts: the librarian models a search on screen, pairs work through a worksheet, and a think-pair-share closes the half hour. The worksheet here has two columns. In one, pairs copy the completions the search engine offers for each stem; in the other, they record the assistant's answer to the completed question and the sources it links. Pairs then label each entry as informing, steering, or narrowing: whether the system leaves several options in view, pushes toward one, or delivers a single synthesized account. Discussion turns on which groups are described differently in the two columns and on where each description appears to come from. A statement about a group in the assistant's answer is opened at its linked source and read there before the pair records it as supported.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Pairs produce a two-column log with each entry labeled informing, steering or narrowing, read each statement about a group at its linked source before recording it as supported, and give a spoken account of one difference in representation.
activities.dl: A completed two-column evidence log with each entry classified and a short spoken account of one difference in how a group is represented.
activities.risk: Query stems are written by the librarian and pairs share one device, so no student needs a personal account; some completions may be offensive, and the stems can be screened beforehand.

activities.t: Mapping Chatbot Data Flows Without Entering Personal Information
activities.sum: Participants in a library workshop on generative AI and privacy work from a printed packet and type nothing into any tool. The packet holds the public privacy notices and terms of use of two conversational AI services, reached by link, and three sample exchanges the librarian produced beforehand from invented prompts containing no personal details. Small groups read the terms closely and mark what the service says it retains, who else receives it, how long it is kept, and whether prompts are used for training. Each data flow they find is then placed on the Agent-Impact Matrix for Artificial Intelligence used in the published Hidden Layer workshop, so that the group names who acts and who is affected. The sample exchanges give the groups something concrete to trace: for a given prompt, which clauses apply to it. The session rests on a distinction between using a tool fluently and knowing how it is funded and governed. A placement on the matrix stands only when the group can point to the clause in the notice that supports it.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: Each group produces a matrix of the data flows it found in the terms, naming who acts and who is affected, with every placement tied to the clause of the privacy notice or terms that supports it.
activities.dl: A completed matrix of data flows for one service, each entry annotated with the clause of the privacy notice or terms it rests on.
activities.risk: No account, device, or personal information is required of participants; privacy notices are long legal texts, so excerpts with plain-language glosses and accessible digital copies support participants who use screen readers.

activities.t: Three-Way Reference Check on Grounded and Ungrounded AI Lists
activities.sum: Students request five references on an instructor-assigned topic from two tools, a source-grounded assistant that retrieves from indexed literature and a general chat model working without retrieval, and then try to find every item. The check is the one set out in the published 5-Minute Reference Check: each reference is looked up by resolving its DOI at doi.org or by searching the exact title in a scholarly search engine or library discovery, and is classified as found-and-matches, found-but-differs, or not-found. Items that are not found are retried before a conclusion is drawn, and entries that differ are corrected from the actual record. Tallies for the two lists go on a shared board. Because output from generative systems may include references that are well formed and point to no existing work, the lists are treated as claims to be tested, not as bibliographies. Students then revise one prompt, for instance by asking for DOIs, rerun it, and note whether the tally changes. Every classification is recorded with the lookup that produced it.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students look up every reference, classify each as found and matching, found but differing, or not found with the lookup that settled it, correct entries that differ, and note whether a revised prompt changed the tally.
activities.dl: A classification table for ten references with the lookup evidence for each, the two tallies, and a note on what the revised prompt changed.
activities.risk: The topic prompt is supplied by the instructor, so no student writing enters a tool; source-grounded assistants are often subscription products, and a shared class or library login avoids individual cost.

activities.t: Scholarly Party Guest Lists by Citation Chaining and AI Search
activities.sum: Groups plan a 'scholarly party' around one starting article and then compare their guest list with one an AI research assistant builds from the same article. As in the published Scholarly Party activity, each group evaluates its article, sets a party theme that serves as an early research question, uses citation tracking to decide which scholars to invite, and looks for gaps: disciplines or viewpoints missing from the list. Here the group also gives the assistant the article's citation and the theme and asks who belongs in the conversation. The two lists are set side by side. For each invitee the assistant proposes, the group looks the scholar and work up in a library database and records whether the work exists, whether it cites or is cited by the starting article, or whether the connection cannot be traced. Invitees found by only one method are discussed in the facilitator-led debrief, where the assistant's list is treated as one more contribution open to challenge, alongside each group's own reading of who is missing.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The group builds its own guest list by citation tracking, records for each invitee the assistant proposed whether the work exists and connects to the starting article, and names the disciplines or viewpoints missing.
activities.dl: An annotated guest list showing which invitees came from citation tracking, which from the assistant, the verification result for each, and the gaps the group identified.
activities.risk: Only the article's citation and the group's theme are entered, not the article text; AI research assistants vary in free-tier limits, so one shared account per group keeps cost and sign-up to a minimum.

activities.t: Staff Workshop on Chat-Proposed Author Name Merges
activities.sum: Metadata and repository staff meet for a working session on a recurring chore, reconciling variant author names, and compare two ways of proposing merges before deciding how either fits the unit's routine. The session uses the Library Carpentry OpenRefine lesson's sample of article metadata. Staff split the multi-valued author column, run Cluster and Edit with the key-collision fingerprint method, and note the clusters it forms. The list of distinct name forms from the same column then goes to a chat model with a request for proposed merges and a reason for each. Working in pairs, staff log every proposal from either method as accepted, amended, or rejected, with the grounds for the decision; names that may belong to different people are set aside for a human lookup. The session treats the two methods and the staff as a division of labor, in which the tools surface candidates and the decision and its record stay with the cataloger. Discussion closes on which categories of merge the unit would hand to either method.
activities.f: Faculty and Staff Development
activities.gate: Staff decide whether each proposed merge is accepted, amended, or rejected and record the grounds, set aside names that may belong to different people for a human lookup, and decide which categories of merge the unit would hand to either method.
activities.dl: A merge log listing each proposed cluster, its origin, the decision taken, and the grounds, plus a short list of cases reserved for human lookup.
activities.risk: The openly licensed sample file is used so that no local patron, author, or unpublished repository data enters an external tool; OpenRefine is free software that runs locally.

activities.t: Annotating Archival Photographs Before a Vision Model Describes Them
activities.sum: Students in a library, archives, or museum studies course each annotate the same small set of public-domain photographs from a digital collection, compare their labels with peers, and only then see how a vision-language model describes the same images. The order follows the bias episode of the Intro to AI for GLAM course, where learners label images independently, compare, and afterwards view a classifier's predictions; here a model's free-text descriptions take the classifier's place. Students submit each photograph with a neutral request for a description and place the output beside their own and their peers' annotations. They mark which cultural details the model names, which it omits, and which it renders in generic or English-default terms, such as a specific garment or ceremony reduced to a broad category. Two questions organize the written comparison: whose way of seeing the image is reflected in each description, and who decided. The holding institution's catalog record, withheld until this point, is then opened, and all three sets of labels are read against it.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students produce their own annotations of each photograph before seeing the model's, and a written comparison of whose way of seeing each description reflects, read against the holding institution's catalog record.
activities.dl: A comparison table for each photograph setting the student's, peers', and model's descriptions beside the catalog record, with a short written analysis of omissions and default terms.
activities.risk: Photographs are chosen from public-domain or openly licensed collections so that upload is permitted, and images of identifiable living people or culturally restricted material are left out; a shared account avoids individual sign-up.

activities.t: Drafting and Correcting SPARQL for a Wikidata Research Query
activities.sum: A researcher assembling a dataset from Wikidata, for example the publishers and places of publication of a set of nineteenth-century periodicals, has a coding assistant draft the SPARQL and then corrects it against the live knowledge graph. Before requesting anything, the researcher writes the question in plain language, sketches the columns expected, and lists a handful of items already known to belong in the result. The assistant's draft is run in the Wikidata Query Service. Property and item identifiers in the query are a frequent point of error, since a model may supply an identifier that exists but refers to something else, so each one is opened on its Wikidata page and its label read. The known items serve as a test: when one is absent from the results, the query or the underlying data is at fault, and a maintenance-style query for items missing the relevant statement shows which. The approach follows the Library Carpentry Wikidata lesson's move from a first single-item query to maintenance queries. Corrections are kept in a dated query log alongside each version.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher states the question, expected columns, and known items before asking, checks every property and item identifier against its page, and decides whether a missing known item reflects a faulty query or a gap in the data.
activities.dl: A tested SPARQL query, a dated log of each draft and correction, and a note on gaps in Wikidata's coverage that bear on the dataset.
activities.risk: Wikidata and its query service are free and need no account for querying; only the plain-language question goes to the assistant, and data retrieved from Wikidata carry their own reuse terms.

activities.t: Decoding AI Descriptions Written for Two National Audiences
activities.sum: Students ask a chat model to describe one current international issue for news audiences in two different countries and then analyze the two texts as media documents. The exercise follows a lesson from Project Look Sharp's Global Media Perspectives kit, taught as published and reached by link, in which students compare coverage of an issue across countries of production. None of the kit's documents or questions is entered into the model; the issue and the analysis questions are written by the instructor. Students record what each output foregrounds, whose position is given first, which terms are used for the parties, and what is left out. Where the class has the languages, the request is repeated in a second language, and the same prompt is run on a second system, so that differences attributable to language or to developer can be seen. The discussion asks whether the model's 'local' version reflects that country's own reporting or an outside, often English-language, picture of it. Factual statements in each output are checked against reporting by news organizations based in the country named.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students record what each output foregrounds, whose position comes first, which terms name the parties and what is left out, and mark each factual statement as confirmed or not by reporting from news organizations in the country named.
activities.dl: A side-by-side decoding of two AI-written descriptions, with framing differences annotated and each factual statement marked as confirmed or not confirmed by in-country reporting.
activities.risk: Prompts are instructor-written and no kit material is uploaded; the kit's lesson files require a free login on the publisher's site, and multilingual students may be asked to translate only if they volunteer.

activities.t: Interviewing an AI Stakeholder Before a Water Rights Role-Play
activities.sum: In a unit on water and agriculture, each student group interviews a chat model that has been directed to speak as one party to a water-allocation dispute, such as an irrigation district manager, a municipal utility planner, or a bottling company representative. The interviews prepare the class for the perspectives role-play in Project Look Sharp's kit Media Constructions of Sustainability: Food, Water, and Agriculture, which is then taught as published, by link. The persona briefs given to the model are written by the instructor from public records, and no kit reading or handout is entered into the tool. Groups ask what the party wants, what it fears, and what evidence it relies on, and from the transcript they draw a stakeholder map of priorities and points of conflict. A persona's answers are treated as claims about a position, not as the voice of the people represented. Before the role-play, each group checks three statements from its transcript against the party's own published documents, such as agency reports, utility plans, or company filings, and corrects its map.

activities.gate: Student groups produce their own interview questions, a stakeholder map of priorities and points of conflict drawn from the transcript, and a note checking three statements against the party's own published documents, with the map corrected.
activities.dl: An interview transcript, a stakeholder map of priorities and conflicts, and a short verification note on three statements checked against public documents.
activities.risk: Persona briefs are instructor-written and students type only interview questions; voice mode is optional and a text transcript is kept for accessibility, and personas representing communities are confined to institutional roles documented in public records.

activities.t: Auditing Age in AI Images of Creative Work
activities.sum: Students run a fixed set of prompts through an image generator, naming creative and helping occupations such as musician, music teacher, woodworker, and home health aide without stating an age, and count who appears. The audit accompanies Project Look Sharp's kit Creativity & Aging Through the Lens of Film, whose film-clip lessons are taught as published, by link, and from which nothing is entered into the generator. Each prompt is generated a set number of times, and pairs tally the apparent age group and gender of the figures using a codebook the class writes. A second round adds 'older' to each prompt, and students code how the generator then signals age: setting, posture, props, activity level, and whether the figure is shown making something or being helped. The analysis traces the patterns to what such systems learn from existing images and asks whether the outputs repeat or depart from the portrayals studied in the film lessons. Pairs exchange image sets and recode a sample to test the codebook. The age tallies are set against published labor-force figures for the occupations named.

activities.gate: Students produce a class-written codebook, tallies of apparent age and gender for both rounds, a recoding check by a second pair, and a written analysis set against labor-force figures for the occupations named.
activities.dl: A prompt log, tally tables for both rounds, a codebook with an inter-coder check, and a short written analysis of how age is depicted.
activities.risk: Image generators commonly cap free generations, so prompts are split across pairs or run on an institutional license; images are described in text in the log for students who use screen readers, and no film clip or kit handout is uploaded.

activities.t: Research Quest with an AI Informant of Mixed Reliability
activities.sum: Small groups play a cooperative research game in which a chatbot, set up by the instructor, speaks as an informant character whose leads cannot be taken on trust. The scenario, written by the instructor for the course, gives each party of three to five a question to answer and an argument to assemble, such as whether a town's vanished industry closed for the reason local memory gives. The informant offers leads in character: a title, an author, a claimed finding, a place to look. Some leads correspond to real sources in the library's holdings and some may not, because the model often produces plausible references that do not exist. A lead counts toward the party's progress only after a member has located the source in the catalog or a database and read enough to confirm the claim attached to it. Roles rotate each session, so that the player questioning the informant, the player searching and the player keeping the evidence record change. The party's closing argument cites only confirmed sources.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: The party produces an evidence record of each lead, where it was or was not located, and why it was trusted or set aside, and a jointly written argument citing only sources members confirmed.
activities.dl: A party evidence record listing each lead, whether and where it was located, and the group's reason for trusting or setting it aside, followed by a short jointly written argument.
activities.risk: One shared device per party is enough, so individual accounts are not required; the scenario text given to the chatbot is instructor-written and nothing from the published game is entered into a tool.

activities.t: Four Moves Applied to One AI Search Answer
activities.sum: First-year students take a single answer from an AI search tool and work through it with the four SIFT moves, keeping a record of every correction. Each student poses one factual question tied to the course, such as whether a city's lead-pipe replacement program reduced measured lead levels, and saves the answer with its citations. The Stop move is a written note of what the student already knows about the question and what the answer is for. For Investigate, each cited source is looked up to learn who is behind it. For Find, the student sets the answer aside and looks for reporting or expert consensus on the central claim. For Trace, one quotation or statistic in the answer is followed to its original context. The correction log has a line for each sentence of the answer: confirmed, corrected, or not supported by any source found, with the source that settled it. Students finish by rewriting the answer in their own words from the sources they verified.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: The student produces a sentence-by-sentence correction log naming the source that settled each line, and a rewritten answer in their own words drawn from the sources they verified.
activities.dl: A sentence-by-sentence correction log for one AI search answer, with the settling source for each line, and a rewritten answer based on verified sources.
activities.risk: Several AI search tools answer a limited number of questions without an account; students enter only a question, and those who prefer not to use a tool can work from an answer the instructor has saved.

activities.t: Checking an AI Profile of an Outside Organization
activities.sum: A committee that reviews outside organizations, such as groups offering free curriculum materials, guest speakers or sponsored research summaries, adds a short paired check to its intake routine. For each organization, one member asks an AI search tool who is behind it, who funds it and what it advocates, and saves the answer with its citations. A second member, without seeing that answer, carries out the quick independent lookup described in Mike Caulfield's post on investigating a source, which members read as published by link, and then glances at the references of the encyclopedia article that lookup leads to. The two accounts are compared on three points: funding, affiliations, and stated purpose. The committee notes where the AI answer repeats the organization's self-description, which often happens when the organization's own site is the main source the tool retrieved, and where it cites anything independent. Disagreements between the two accounts are resolved by going to the cited documents, and the outcome is filed with the committee's record for that organization.

activities.gate: The committee compares the two accounts on funding, affiliations and stated purpose, resolves each disagreement by going to the cited documents, and files the outcome with its record for that organization.
activities.dl: A one-page intake record per organization comparing the AI profile and the independent lookup on funding, affiliation and purpose, with the documents that resolved any disagreement.
activities.risk: The routine needs no paid tool and no student data; only the names of outside organizations are entered, and the linked post describing the lookup technique is read at its original address, not uploaded.

activities.t: What the Article Implies but Never States
activities.sum: Journalism students use a document-grounded assistant to surface what a news article implies without saying, then test those implications against wider coverage. The instructor chooses an openly licensed or public-domain article on a contested local event, one in which the individual statements are checkable. Before using the tool, each student writes two sentences on how the article left them feeling about the event and what they think it wants a reader to conclude. The article is then loaded into the assistant, which is asked to list conclusions a reader would likely draw that the text never states, and to quote the passages that invite each one. Students check every quoted passage against the article, since the assistant may paraphrase and present it as quotation. They then look for other reporting and expert accounts of the same event and ask of each implication: is it supported there, contradicted, or left open? A final seminar turns on whose voices and what context the article's arrangement left out.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: The student writes a first reaction before using the tool, then produces an implication table giving each unstated conclusion, the passages that invite it, and whether other coverage supports, contradicts or leaves it open.
activities.dl: An implication table listing each unstated conclusion, the passages that invite it, and its standing against other coverage, with a short account of absent voices and context.
activities.risk: The article entered into the tool is openly licensed or public-domain and instructor-selected; the linked essay is read at its original address and is not uploaded, and free document-grounded tools usually require an account.
