activities.t: Whom a Chatbot Names as an Authority
activities.sum: After completing a self-paced lesson on authority as constructed and contextual, students ask a chatbot who the authorities are on a topic from their course and examine the pattern in its answer. Groups take one topic, such as groundwater management or postpartum care, and pose the question several ways: for a general reader, for practitioners in a named region, for the community most affected, and, where a group member can, in a second language. Each response is saved. The names and bodies returned are tallied by type: university researchers, government agencies, professional associations, practitioners, community organizations. Groups look up a sample of the named people to confirm that they exist and hold the roles described. The discussion compares the tallies across the versions of the question, asking which kinds of authority the chatbot returns by default, which appear only when a context is specified, and who is named by a subject librarian or a course reading and absent from every response.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: The group produces a tally of the authorities named under each version of the question and an account of which kinds appeared by default, which only with a context, and who was absent from every response.
activities.dl: A tally sheet of the authorities named under each version of the question, with a group account of which kinds appeared by default and which were absent.
activities.risk: A free chatbot tier is sufficient and one device per group reduces account requirements; the lesson is assigned by link as published on the project's site, where some external components may no longer work.

activities.t: Evidence Types in an AI Assistant's Clinical Answer
activities.sum: Students in clinical programs put an instructor-written clinical question to an AI research assistant and judge whether the kinds of studies it returns suit the kind of question asked. Questions differ by type across the class: a therapy question such as whether chlorhexidine bathing reduces central-line infections in adult intensive care, a prognosis question, a question about patients' experience of a treatment. Before searching, each student states which research designs would best answer their question. The assistant's answer and its cited studies are saved. The student then opens each cited study and classifies it from its methods section: systematic review, randomized trial, cohort study, qualitative study, guideline, or something else. Three things are recorded for each: whether the study exists as cited, whether the assistant's description of its design is accurate, and whether that design fits the question type. Each returned study is accepted, replaced or rejected with a reason, and gaps are filled from a database search using the appropriate study-type filter.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each student states which research designs would best answer their question, then classifies every cited study from its methods section, records whether it exists as cited and fits the question, and fills gaps from a filtered database search.
activities.dl: An evidence table classifying each AI-returned study by design and by fit to the question type, with accept, replace or reject decisions and the database-found additions.
activities.risk: No patient information is entered, only an instructor-written question; AI research assistants often draw mainly on open-access papers, so library databases are needed to see what was missed.

activities.t: Campus-Licensed and Free AI Tools: What Each Can Reach
activities.sum: A library working group compares what a campus-licensed AI tool and a free consumer one can reach when asked the same course-related questions, and records who pays for each route to the information. Members draft ten questions drawn from actual course guides across disciplines. Each question is put to both tools, and the sources each answer cites are sorted into four groups: openly available, behind a paywall the library subscribes to, behind a paywall it does not, and not locatable. For each tool the group also notes the terms that apply: who holds the license, what the institution pays, and what the provider's data terms say about retention of what users enter. The same questions are then run in the library's discovery search to see what the collection provides that neither tool surfaced. The findings are written up under three headings, teaching implications, governance and day-to-day operations, as a short briefing for the committee that advises on campus AI tool provision.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: The working group sorts every cited source by access status, sets each tool's license, cost, and data terms beside it, notes what the collection provides that neither tool surfaced, and writes the briefing for the advisory committee.
activities.dl: A briefing with a source-access table for both tools, a summary of costs and data terms, and a list of subscribed content neither tool reached.
activities.risk: The work uses tools the institution already licenses plus a free tier, and enters only staff-written questions; license costs may be confidential and are reported at whatever level of detail the institution allows.

activities.t: Tracing a Coding Assistant's Drawing Rules to the Diagram
activities.sum: Studio students diagram the logic of a precedent drawn from self-assembly or nano-scale systems and, before opening any tool, write down the rules they expect a drawing generator to need. Each student then describes the diagram in plain language to a coding assistant, which returns a candidate Processing sketch. The sketch is run, and the student annotates its code line by line against the logic diagram, marking which generated rules correspond to a relation in the diagram, which were added by the assistant without any basis in the precedent, and which diagrammed relations are missing. Students record their own judgment of the sketch before asking the assistant to explain its choices, and note where the explanation and the code disagree. The assistant's sketch is then set aside and the student writes the generator, keeping only rules that can be traced to the diagram. At the pin-up, the diagram, the annotated candidate and the student-authored drawings hang side by side, so that every mark in the final drawing can be followed back to a stated rule.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Students produce a precedent logic diagram, their own expected rules, an annotated reading of the generated sketch, and a generative drawing machine of their own whose every rule traces back to the diagram.
activities.dl: A precedent logic diagram, an annotated AI-written Processing sketch, and a student-authored generative drawing machine with its output drawings.
activities.risk: Processing is free software, but a coding assistant may require an account or paid tier, and students new to programming may need paired work or a shared class instance to read generated code.

activities.t: Plaster Forecasts Checked Against the Sectioned Cast
activities.sum: Students design a spatial construct that works as formwork, cast plaster in the voids it defines, and cut sections through the result. Before pouring, each student describes the formwork in writing to a conversational assistant, giving dimensions, orientation, pour point and mix, and asks where the plaster will fill completely, where air may be trapped, and where the cast is likely to break on release. The forecast is printed and pinned beside the formwork. After the cast is sectioned, students mark each prediction on the cut face as confirmed, partly confirmed or contradicted, and add what the section shows that no forecast mentioned, such as settling lines, surface texture taken from the formwork, or voids the description never implied. A short written comparison separates errors that came from the student's own incomplete description from those that came from the assistant's general account of plaster. The physical section is treated as the evidence throughout, and the forecast as a claim to be tested against it.

activities.gate: Students build the formwork, cast and section the plaster, mark each prediction as confirmed, partly confirmed, or contradicted, note what the section shows that no forecast mentioned, and separate errors in their own description from the assistant's.

activities.t: AI-Written Wall Labels Checked Against Appropriation Art
activities.sum: Students receive three short wall labels that the instructor produced beforehand with a conversational AI tool, prompted only with each work's artist, title and date. The works are chosen from the exemplar set on a museum's published reference page for the term appropriation, which students open by link and read as published; no museum text or image is entered into the tool. Working in pairs and using no AI themselves, students test every sentence of each label. For each claim about what the artist borrowed, from where, and how it was altered, they look at the reproduction on the museum's object page, read the object record, and mark the claim as visible in the work, stated in the record, or not found in either. They also ask whether the label describes an intentional alteration, as the page's definition of the term requires, or only notes a resemblance. Each pair rewrites one label so that every sentence can be pointed to in the object or its record, and the class compares which kinds of claims most often lacked support.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Pairs mark every claim as visible in the work, stated in the record, or not found in either, judge whether each label describes an intentional alteration, and rewrite one label so every sentence can be pointed to in the object or its record.
activities.dl: Three annotated AI-written wall labels and one rewritten label in which each claim is tied to the object or its museum record.
activities.risk: Students need only a browser to reach the museum pages; image-dependent looking tasks call for verbal descriptions or tactile alternatives for blind and low-vision students, which the museum page is not confirmed to supply.

activities.t: Correcting a Machine Transcript of an Oral History Interview
activities.sum: Each student records an interview with an elder or other person they admire, following a national oral history program's published guidance and tools, which are used as provided by link. With the narrator's stated consent to this further step, the student runs the recording through a speech-to-text tool and receives a first-pass transcript. The student then listens to the full recording with the transcript in hand and corrects it. Every correction is entered in an error catalog under a category: names of people and places, dialect or regional vocabulary, overlapping speech, and non-verbal sound such as pauses, laughter or a change in voice that carried meaning the tool did not register. For three passages, the student writes a sentence on how the uncorrected transcript would have changed what the narrator appears to say. The corrected transcript goes back to the narrator for review before anything is deposited or shared, and the catalog is discussed in class as evidence of what a transcript, machine-made or human-made, leaves out of a spoken account.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Students produce the consented interview, a transcript corrected against their own recording, a categorized error catalog, and three notes on how the uncorrected transcript would have changed what the narrator appears to say.
activities.dl: A corrected interview transcript reviewed by the narrator, with a categorized catalog of transcription errors and three short interpretive notes.
activities.risk: A narrator's voice and personal account are sensitive data, so the design depends on explicit consent for transcription and on a tool that does not retain audio; captioned playback or an alternative role is needed for students who are deaf or hard of hearing.

activities.t: Illustrating Testimony: Generated Panels Checked Against the Interview
activities.sum: Journalism students interview a person about an event that person witnessed, with consent, and script a one-page comic from the interview in which every panel description is tied to a quoted or paraphrased line in their notes. The idea of treating a comic built from firsthand accounts as a primary source comes from a published news lesson on comics journalism, which can be read separately by link; none of its excerpts are used here. For two panels, an image generator produces an illustration from the student's panel description, with the interviewee's name and identifying details removed. The student also makes the same panels by hand, in whatever medium the course uses. Each generated panel is then audited against the interview notes. Students list every depicted detail, such as weather, damage, clothing, bystanders and facial expression, and mark whether the interviewee said it, implied it, or never mentioned it. They ask the same question of their own hand-made panel. A short editor's note states which version, if either, could be published as an account of what the interviewee reported, and why.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students produce the interview, a comic script tying each panel to their notes, hand-made panels, a detail audit, and an editor's note on which version could stand as an account of what the interviewee reported.
activities.dl: A scripted one-page interview comic, two panels in generated and hand-made versions, a detail audit, and an editor's note.
activities.risk: An interviewee's account is personal information, so the design depends on consent and on removing identifying details before any description is entered; free image tools may cap the number of generations.

activities.t: Sourcing National Debt Campaign Claims with a Grounded Assistant
activities.sum: Groups design a public awareness campaign about the US national debt, working from a published news lesson's campaign brief used as provided by link. Before any slogan or fact card is written, each group lists the questions its campaign needs answered: how large the debt is, what it is composed of, who holds it, and what it costs to service. The group looks up each answer directly in official federal publications and records the table and date. It then puts the same questions to a document-grounded assistant loaded only with those public-domain federal documents; the lesson's video and text are not placed in the tool. For every figure the assistant returns, the group opens the passage it cites and records whether the number, unit, date and definition match, for example whether a total refers to debt held by the public or to gross debt. Mismatches are logged and corrected. Campaign materials carry a source line for every figure, and during peer critique another group picks three claims at random and traces them to the table.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Each group looks up every answer in official federal publications before asking the assistant, checks each returned figure's number, unit, date, and definition against the cited passage, and gives every figure in its campaign a source line.
activities.dl: A campaign plan with slogans and fact cards in which each figure carries a source line, plus a log of assistant answers checked against official tables.
activities.risk: Document-grounded tools that accept uploaded collections may require accounts or a paid tier, so one instructor-built instance shared with groups keeps cost and sign-up off students.

activities.t: Arguing a Standards Decision Against a Rival Producer Persona
activities.sum: Students read a published journalism ethics case about a network standards editor's deadline decision on airing photographs, obtained from the publisher as provided, and each settles on a ruling before class. A conversational assistant is then set up with a short instructor-written persona: a producer at a competing network who argues that the pictures are already public, that audiences expect them, and that holding back concedes the story. The persona brief is the instructor's own; no case text is pasted into the tool, and students argue in their own words. Each student defends the ruling through several exchanges while the persona presses on competition and time. Afterward, students annotate the transcript. They mark which of their arguments rested on a written standards policy or a documented fact in the case, which rested on assertion, and where the persona made a claim about the events that the case does not contain. A no-AI seminar follows in which students compare annotated transcripts and state whether the pressure changed their ruling or only their reasons.

activities.gate: Students produce their own ruling before class, their arguments in its defense, and an annotated transcript marking which arguments rested on written policy or documented fact and where the persona made claims the case does not contain.

activities.t: Tracing AI Search Results on Community Newspaper Business Models
activities.sum: A faculty member preparing a study of how community newspapers have managed the move to digital revenue uses an AI research-search tool for the scoping stage of the literature review. The question comes from a published 2014 teaching case about a family-owned paper weighing whether to make several linked changes at once or in phases; the case is read as published and none of it is entered into the tool. The researcher writes guiding questions in their own words, such as what evidence exists on phased versus simultaneous transitions, and runs each through the search tool and, separately, through library databases. Every reference the tool returns goes into a log with four checks: the item exists in a publisher or library record, the authors and date match, the finding the tool attributes to it appears in the text, and the study concerns papers of comparable size. Items that cannot be traced are recorded as such and excluded. The researcher compares the two result sets, noting what each route found that the other missed, and writes the scoping memo only from verified items.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher writes the guiding questions, decides whether each returned reference exists, matches its authors and date, contains the attributed finding, and concerns comparable papers, and writes the scoping memo only from verified items.
activities.dl: A verified reference log and scoping memo for the researcher's own literature review, with untraceable items recorded and excluded.
activities.risk: Research-search tools vary in which paywalled journals they can read, so results may favor open-access and trade sources; the library database pass is the counterweight, and no student or participant data is involved.

activities.t: Does the Generated Melody Obey the Name and Meter?
activities.sum: Students in a music fundamentals or aural skills course each compose a short melody from a name, as in an openly licensed composition worksheet: the syllables fix the number of notes, each syllable receives a rhythmic value and a pitch, and every measure has to add up to the time signature. At college level the constraint set is extended with a stated key and a cadence on the final syllable. Each student then gives a music generation model the same constraints in words, using an invented name, and receives a short audio clip. The student transcribes the clip by ear into notation and checks it against the constraint list: whether the number of notes matches the syllable count, whether each measure contains the right number of beats, and whether the key and cadence were observed. Students perform both melodies and compare them. A brief written note identifies which constraints the model kept, which it ignored, and which of the student's own choices, such as placing the stressed syllable on a strong beat, came from knowing how the name is spoken.
activities.f: Computational Poetics and Procedural Generation
activities.gate: Each student composes a melody from a name under the stated constraints, transcribes the generated clip by ear, checks it against the constraint list, and notes which of their own choices came from knowing how the name is spoken.
activities.dl: A notated name melody, a transcription of the generated melody, and a constraint checklist comparing the two.
activities.risk: Music generation tools commonly limit free clips and require accounts, so a single class account may be used; transcription by ear calls for an alternative, such as working from a provided notation export, for students who are deaf or hard of hearing.

activities.t: Testing Chatbot-Suggested Interventions in a Forum Theatre Replay
activities.sum: A class devises and performs a short scene in which one character is treated unjustly, working in the Forum Theatre tradition that a published strategy page describes; the page may be read by link and is not reproduced. Between the first performance and the replay, small groups describe their own scene to a conversational assistant in a few sentences and ask what the mistreated character could try. Each group writes three of the suggestions on cards. During the replay, a spectator who stops the action draws a card and steps in to attempt that intervention against performers who stay in role and resist. An observer logs what happens: whether the suggested line could be said at all in the moment, how the antagonist responded, and what the spectator's body, voice and position in the space did that the card did not mention. Spectators then try interventions of their own. The debrief sorts the suggestions into those that held, those that collapsed against a resisting person, and those that assumed the antagonist would simply agree.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students enact each drawn suggestion against performers who resist in role, log what the spectator's body, voice, and position did that the card did not mention, try interventions of their own, and sort the suggestions by whether they held.
activities.dl: A performed forum scene with replayed interventions and an observer log sorting AI-suggested and spectator-devised interventions by outcome.
activities.risk: Scenes of mistreatment can touch students' own experience, so participation as spectator, observer or performer is a choice in this design; the chatbot step needs one device per group and a free tool.

activities.t: Auditing a Generated Neoclassical Image Before Drawing
activities.sum: Studio students choose a present-day moral principle or social issue and, before drawing, brief an image generator to render it in a Neoclassical style. Each student then audits the generated image against the design elements the class has identified by looking at Neoclassical paintings and sculpture: which features of the style the image reproduces, such as shallow stage-like space, sculptural figures and restrained gesture, and which it replaces with a generic antique look. The audit is written as a short list of observed features with the place in the image where each appears or is missing. Students go on to make a preliminary and then a final drawing or sculpture study of their own, deciding which conventions to keep and which the generated image handled poorly. Finished works are displayed in a crit in which classmates write their reading of each piece, with the visual clues that support it, before the maker states the intended message. The generated image and its audit hang beside the final work, so the group can see what came from the tool and what came from the maker.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Students audit the generated image feature by feature against design elements observed in period works, decide which conventions to keep, and make their own preliminary and final studies for a crit where classmates read each piece first.
activities.dl: A feature-by-feature audit of a generated image, a preliminary and a final drawing or sculpture study, and written peer interpretations of displayed work.
activities.risk: Image generators may require accounts or paid credits, and the anchor's license covers the lesson text only, so museum artwork images are viewed at the source and are not uploaded to any tool.

activities.t: Sorting AI Stories About a Painting by Evidence
activities.sum: Students receive three short AI-written stories about one painting, prepared in advance by the instructor, together with a high-resolution open-access image of the work. The instructor produces the stories by prompting a conversational model with only the painting's title and artist, choosing a public-domain narrative painting whose image the holding museum has released for open use. Before reading the stories, each student records what they can see in the picture: figures, gestures, setting, light, objects. Working in pairs, students mark every narrative detail in the three stories as visible in the work, plausibly inferred from something visible, or not supported by anything in the picture, and note the passage of the image that settles each call. Pairs compare their markings and discuss cases where they disagree about what counts as inference. Each student then writes a short narrative from the point of view of one figure in the painting, footnoting the visual evidence for each claim about what that figure sees or does. A museum's published school program on telling stories from paintings is offered by link as a companion for faculty planning a gallery visit.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Students record what they see before reading, mark each story detail as visible, inferred, or unsupported with the part of the image that settles it, and each writes a narrative footnoting the visual evidence for every claim.
activities.dl: A marked-up set of three AI-written stories and an original short narrative with visual evidence noted for each claim.
activities.risk: Students use no tool or account; the image needs to be an open-access reproduction, and image descriptions or tactile alternatives would be needed for students with low vision.

activities.t: Rehearsing a Restitution Case Against a Chatbot
activities.sum: In a unit on looting, restitution and repatriation, students prepare for a lawyers' role-play on the Parthenon sculptures by first arguing their assigned side against a conversational assistant. Each legal team instructs the assistant to take the opposing position, whether for retention in London or for return to Athens, and to rebut the team's points over several rounds. The team saves the transcript and sorts every argument the assistant made into those resting on a checkable fact, those resting on a legal or ethical principle, and those it cannot trace. Checkable facts, such as dates of removal, the terms of the permission claimed, or the content of museum and government statements, are looked up in the course readings and in the institutions' own published statements. Arguments that survive checking are carried into the live role-play, which runs without the assistant; arguments resting on untraceable claims are listed and dropped. After the role-play, the short comparison essay on a current heritage case asks students to name one argument from the rehearsal that changed their own position or sharpened it.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: Students sort every argument the assistant made by its basis, check its factual claims against course readings and institutional statements, argue the live role-play without it, and name one argument that changed or sharpened their own position.
activities.dl: An annotated rehearsal transcript sorting the assistant's arguments by basis, a live role-play performance, and a short comparison essay.
activities.risk: A free conversational tool is sufficient, though account creation may be required; teams can share one account, and the lesson's license (CC BY-NC) limits reuse of its text to non-commercial settings with attribution.

activities.t: Querying a Grounded Assistant on Art and Authority
activities.sum: For a midterm review in an art history survey, students question a document-grounded assistant about how five ancient works express political authority, then check every passage it cites. The assistant holds only material the instructor has loaded: openly licensed survey readings and public-domain translations such as the prologue and epilogue of Hammurabi's laws and the Res Gestae of Augustus. Before class, students rank civic issues that matter to them, and each takes one, such as access to justice, as the lens for the review. A student asks the assistant how a work such as the Stele of Hammurabi, Seated Khafre or the Augustus of Primaporta relates to that issue, opens each cited passage, and records whether the passage says what the answer attributes to it and whether the answer describes anything visible on the object. Because the collection contains texts and no images, claims about form, scale, material or pose are tested by looking at the object in the museum's online record. Students then write a comparison of two cultures' systems of power that keeps only verified statements and adds their own formal observations.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Each student records whether every cited passage says what the answer attributes to it and whether claims about the object match its museum record, then writes a comparison of two cultures keeping only verified statements and adding their own formal observations.
activities.dl: A citation check log for the assistant's answers and a written comparison of two works using only verified claims plus the student's own formal observations.
activities.risk: Document-grounded tools that accept an instructor-built collection may require accounts or a paid tier; the collection is limited to openly licensed and public-domain texts, and artwork images are viewed at museum sites and not uploaded.

activities.t: Occupation Prompt Audit of an Image Generator
activities.sum: Students generate images of people in ten occupations using one fixed prompt template, tally who is depicted, and then test which prompt revisions change the pattern. The class agrees on the template and the occupations, for example nurse, engineer, chief executive, cleaner and kindergarten teacher, and on a small coding sheet for apparent gender presentation, age, skin tone and setting, with an 'unclear' option. Each group produces the same number of images per occupation and enters its counts in a shared table. Coders compare a sample of each other's calls and discuss disagreements, since the categories are judgments about depictions and not facts about people. In a second round, groups revise the prompts in stated ways, such as adding a country, a decade or an explicit instruction about variety, and record which revisions shift the tallies and which leave them largely as they were. Results are set beside published labor statistics for the same occupations. Each group keeps a process log of prompts, counts and decisions, and closes by selecting one image it would be willing to use in a publication and explaining the choice.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Students code who each image depicts, reconcile disagreements between coders, record which prompt revisions shift the tallies, set the results beside labor statistics, and justify one image they would use in a publication.
activities.dl: A shared tally table, a process log of prompts and revisions, and a short justification for one selected image.
activities.risk: Generating several images per occupation can exhaust free credits, so a shared class account or instructor-run generation may be needed; coding apparent identity from images calls for care and an 'unclear' category.

activities.t: Committee Media Rights Register with Search Assistant
activities.sum: A program committee reviewing the media in its shared course materials uses a search-enabled assistant to locate openly licensed replacements, and confirms every reported license at the source page before anything is adopted. Members first inventory the images, audio and video clips in the shared slides and course shells and sort each item by the rights decision it calls for: copyrighted with permission on file, public domain, Creative Commons licensed, used under a fair use rationale, or generated or edited with AI. For items with no clear basis, a member describes the content needed and asks the assistant for openly licensed alternatives with the license it believes applies. The division of work is stated in the committee's procedure: the assistant searches and proposes; a named member opens each result, reads the license shown on the source page, and records whether it matches what the assistant reported. Mismatches and dead links are logged alongside confirmed items. The register that results gives, for each media item, its source, license, credit line and the date and name of the person who checked it.
activities.f: Designing Courses and Learning Materials with AI
activities.gate: The committee sorts each media item by the rights decision it calls for, and a named member reads the license on each source page, records whether it matches what was reported, and is entered in the register as the person who checked it.
activities.dl: A media rights register listing each item's source, confirmed license, credit line and checker, with a log of mismatches between reported and actual licenses.
activities.risk: Only descriptions of needed media are entered into the tool, not course files or student work; a free search-enabled assistant may suffice, and the register itself can be kept in a shared spreadsheet.

activities.t: Tracing an Assistant's Links to Original Reporting
activities.sum: Students ask a search-enabled assistant what happened in a current news event and then follow every link it cites to find out where the information was first reported. The instructor names two or three events from the past week. Each pair saves the assistant's answer and its list of sources, opens each link, and classifies what it finds: original reporting by a news organization with named reporters or documents, a wire story republished elsewhere, aggregation or commentary about someone else's reporting, a press release or official statement, or a page that does not contain the claim attributed to it. Where a link leads to commentary, the pair keeps going until it reaches the reporting the commentary depends on, and notes how many steps that took. Pairs then send the identical question to a second system and compare which original reporting each one surfaced and which it passed over. The class tallies the categories on a shared board. A news literacy organization's lesson on telling news from content about news is offered by link as a companion for faculty who want a full lesson on that distinction.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Student pairs produce a source-trace table classifying each cited link and recording the path back to original reporting, and a comparison of which reporting two systems surfaced or passed over.
activities.dl: A source-trace table for one assistant answer, classifying each cited link and recording the path back to original reporting.
activities.risk: A free search-enabled assistant is sufficient and pairs can share one account; paywalled news sites may block some traces unless the library's news databases are used.

activities.t: What a Research Agent Cannot Report
activities.sum: Reporting students delegate a bounded public-records question to an agentic research tool, audit each step it took, and then list what an investigative team would have had to do that the run could not. The question is set by the instructor from openly available local records, for example what a city's published inspection reports show about one category of business. Each group saves the agent's plan, the pages it visited and its final report, and checks every figure and attribution in the report against the page it came from. Steps are labeled as retrieval of an existing document, summary, calculation, or inference without a source. Alongside this, the class works through a published case activity on watchdog journalism, used as published by link, as its example of an investigation carried out on the ground. Groups then write a two-column account: what the agent established from documents already online, and what reporters do that leaves no document for a tool to find, such as locating people, gaining their trust, observing a site, and confirming identities. A closing memo proposes the reporting plan needed to turn the findings into a story.
activities.f: How Generative AI Works—and What It Can and Can't Do
activities.gate: Students check every figure and attribution against its source page, label each step the agent took, and write what reporters must do that leaves no document for a tool to find, closing with the reporting plan the story needs.
activities.dl: An annotated audit of the agent's run and a reporting-plan memo distinguishing document-based findings from reporting that requires presence and sources.
activities.risk: Agentic or deep-research modes are often limited to paid tiers, so an instructor-run session shared with the class may be needed; the question is confined to public records so no personal or confidential data enters the tool.

activities.t: Role-Playing a Reply to a Shared False Claim
activities.sum: Students practice responding to a friend or relative who has shared a false claim by rehearsing the conversation with a conversational assistant that plays that person. Each student writes a brief of their own: who the person is, how they know each other, what was shared, and how attached the person is to it. The claims are chosen by the class from already debunked examples listed by fact-checking organizations, so the factual question is settled before the conversation begins. The assistant is instructed to stay in character, to respond as that person plausibly would, and not to concede at once. After six to eight turns the student stops, saves the transcript, and marks the moments where the exchange opened up or closed down: a question that invited the other person to explain, a correction that landed as an accusation, a point of shared concern that was acknowledged or missed. Partners exchange transcripts and then replay one exchange face to face, each taking a turn as the person who shared the claim. A news literacy organization's slide activity and infographic on speaking up are offered by link as published companions.

activities.gate: Each student writes the brief for the person being played, marks where the rehearsed exchange opened up or closed down, and replays one exchange face to face with a partner.
activities.dl: An annotated rehearsal transcript and a face-to-face replay of one exchange with a partner.
activities.risk: A free conversational tool is sufficient; students write fictionalized briefs so that no real relative or friend is named or described in identifiable detail in the tool.

activities.t: Testing a Chatbot's Predictions About Chord Order
activities.sum: Beginning music students ask a conversational assistant to predict how reordering four common chords will change the feel of a loop, and then test each prediction by ear. The chords are the tonic, dominant, submediant and subdominant of a major key, the set behind a very widely used pop progression. Before consulting the assistant, each student writes their own guess about three reorderings: where the loop will feel most at rest, where it will pull forward, and whether it will sound brighter or darker. The assistant is then asked the same questions and its answers are saved. Students then listen to each ordering, either in a music software company's interactive browser lesson on this progression, used as published by link, or on a keyboard or guitar, and note what they hear, in their own words and with terms from class such as tension, release and cadence. The three accounts, the student's guess, the assistant's prediction and the listening notes, are set side by side. Discussion turns on where the verbal account matched the ear and where it was too general to test.
activities.f: Using AI to Read, Explain and Understand
activities.gate: Students guess first about three chord reorderings, listen to each ordering and describe it in class terms such as tension and release, and judge where the assistant's predictions matched what they heard or were too general to test.
activities.dl: A three-column comparison of the student's prediction, the assistant's prediction and listening notes for each chord ordering.
activities.risk: A free conversational tool and any instrument or free browser chord player are sufficient; students who are deaf or hard of hearing may need a visual or tactile representation of the progression.

activities.t: Trying an AI Staging Proposal on Its Feet
activities.sum: Acting and dramatic literature students receive a written staging proposal for one soliloquy from Hamlet, produced by a conversational model, and try it on their feet to find out which directions the language supports. The instructor generates the proposal in advance from the public-domain text of the speech, asking for blocking, pauses, gesture and the point of each move, and prints it without revision. Groups first read the speech aloud and mark its turns of thought, verse breaks and changes of address. They then stage the speech as the proposal directs and stop wherever a direction pulls against the text: a cross placed in the middle of a thought, a pause that breaks a verse line with no cue in the punctuation, a gesture toward someone the speech never addresses. For each direction, the group records kept, changed or cut, and quotes the line that decided it. Groups show their revised staging to one another and compare decisions. A theater company's teacher pack on the play, which approaches interpretive questions through physical rehearsal-room exercises, is offered by link as a companion for the session's wider practical work.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Groups mark the speech's turns of thought and verse breaks themselves, stage each direction, record it as kept, changed, or cut with the deciding line quoted, and perform their revised staging.
activities.dl: A performed staging of one soliloquy and an annotated proposal recording each direction as kept, changed or cut with the deciding line quoted.
activities.risk: Students use no tool or account; the session needs an open floor space, and staging tasks can be adapted for students with limited mobility by assigning directing and text-marking roles.

activities.t: Asking a Vision Model to Read Freeze Frames
activities.sum: Students studying Macbeth build freeze frames of chosen moments, photograph them, and ask a vision-capable model what emotion and relationship it reads in each still. Groups select a moment from the public-domain text and write down beforehand what they intend the image to show: who holds power, who is afraid, who is looking away. The photographs are the groups' own. The model is asked only to describe posture, gaze, distance and likely feeling, with no mention of the play. Its reading is set beside the group's stated intent and beside readings written by classmates who view the frame in the room. Where the model misses the intent, the group decides whether the physical choice was unclear, in which case they adjust level, spacing or focus and photograph again, or whether the model's reading reflects a narrow default about how emotion looks, in which case they keep the choice and say why. A short closing note quotes the lines each final frame carries. A theater company's program for deaf students, built on visually led work with the play, is offered by link as a companion.
activities.f: Visual, Multimodal and Performance Making
activities.gate: Each group writes what its freeze frame is meant to show, decides whether a missed reading means the staging was unclear or the model's default is narrow, restages or keeps the choice with a reason, and quotes the lines each frame carries.
activities.dl: A sequence of photographed freeze frames with intent statements, the model's and classmates' readings, and a note tying each final frame to quoted lines.
activities.risk: Photographs show students' faces and bodies, so consent, an opt-out role such as director or photographer, and an institutionally approved tool are relevant; visually led work may suit deaf and hard of hearing students, and local review may be required before images of students are uploaded.

activities.t: Tracing Chatbot Claims with a Citation-Showing Search Tool
activities.sum: Students work from a short chatbot answer on a topic from the course and test its factual claims one at a time with an AI search tool that shows its citations. The instructor generates the answer beforehand and hands it out with the prompt that produced it. Pairs split the answer into discrete claims, enter each into the search tool, and look for independent sources that bear on it, opening every cited page instead of relying on the tool's summary. A shared log records, for each claim, the sources found, whether they are independent of one another, and whether each citation the search tool offered supports what the tool said it did. The log therefore carries two layers of checking: the chatbot's claims against outside sources, and the search tool's citations against the pages they point to. The class closes by sorting the unsupported claims by type, such as a detail invented by the model, an outdated figure, or a one-sided framing. Day of AI's verification lesson is the idea-level starting point; none of its materials are used or entered into a tool.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: Student pairs produce a claim-by-claim log of the independent sources they located and opened, recording whether each citation the search tool offered supports what it said, and the class sorts unsupported claims by type.
activities.dl: A claim-by-claim verification log showing the sources located for each claim and whether each of the search tool's citations supports the statement attached to it.
activities.risk: Several AI search tools have free tiers, and the activity can run from one projected instructor account if students lack accounts; queries contain only claims from the instructor-supplied answer, so no personal or student-authored text is entered.

activities.t: Committee Fact-Finding for a Student-Drafted AI Policy
activities.sum: In a multi-week unit, student committees draft clauses of an AI-use policy for their own course or program, and the campus-licensed AI assistant serves as both a subject of the policy and a witness to be questioned. Each committee asks the institutional assistant about itself: what it retains from a conversation, who can see that record, whether inputs are used for training, which features are switched on locally. The answers are treated as testimony, not as fact. Committee members then read the institution's published AI guidance, its privacy policy, and the vendor terms the institution links to, and mark each of the tool's statements as confirmed, contradicted, or not addressed in writing. Clauses are drafted only from the confirmed column, and the committee's report lists the open questions it referred to the campus IT or privacy office. Committees present their clauses to the full class for amendment and a vote. The idea of students moving an AI policy through a mock legislature comes from Day of AI's Student Senate unit, which is not reproduced here; the only text the tool receives is students' questions.

activities.dl: A committee report containing drafted policy clauses, a table of the assistant's statements about itself marked confirmed, contradicted, or unaddressed, and a list of questions referred to campus offices.

activities.t: Checking a Scripted Setback Overlay Against Hand Map Analysis
activities.sum: Groups in an introductory earth science course carry out Karl Wirth's landfill-siting investigation by hand and then compare their result with a GIS overlay script written by a coding assistant. In the published problem, groups read maps of surface water, land use, bedrock and surficial geology, and depth to bedrock against state siting regulations, consult well logs for promising areas, and rank three candidate sites. Here, after the hand analysis is complete, each group describes the setback rules in plain language to a coding assistant and asks for a script that applies them to public county data layers and maps the excluded zones. The script's output is laid over the group's hand-drawn exclusions. Every difference is traced to its cause: a regulation the group misread, a buffer distance the script got wrong, a layer with a different projection or date, a rule the group never told the assistant about. The poster documents the division of work between people and tool, the discrepancies found, and which version the final ranking rests on and why. The script and the prompts that produced it are appended.

activities.gate: Groups rank the candidate sites from their own hand analysis, trace every difference from the scripted overlay to its cause, and state which version their final ranking rests on and why.
activities.dl: A poster ranking three candidate sites, with a discrepancy table reconciling the hand analysis and the scripted overlay and the script and prompts appended.
activities.risk: Free coding assistants and open-source GIS software suffice, though running a script may need lab machines or instructor support; the handouts are BY-NC-SA 3.0 and the Minnesota Geological Survey maps carry their own terms.

activities.t: Comparing Hand-Drawn Trees with Tree-Inference Software Output
activities.sum: First-year biology students draw phylogenetic trees by hand from three successive kinds of evidence and then compare their final tree with one produced by tree-inference software. The sequence follows Scott Cooper's interactive lecture segment: groups receive data on habitat and feeding behavior, then skeletal structures, then DNA sequences for a set of mammals, and redraw the tree as each data set arrives. In this version the hand-drawn DNA tree is set aside before any software is opened. The same sequences, or equivalents retrieved from a public sequence database, are then run through an alignment and tree-building tool, which in current packages may rely on statistical or machine-learned models of sequence change. The tool returns a finished tree with support values and no account of its reasoning. Groups mark each branch where the two trees differ and write the explanation the software does not give: which sites drive the difference, whether the alignment or the model accounts for it, and whether the support value warrants confidence. A selection of comparisons is projected and discussed.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Groups produce hand-drawn trees from three successive kinds of evidence before any software is opened, and write the explanation the software does not give for each branch where the two trees differ.
activities.dl: A half-sheet pairing the group's hand-drawn DNA tree with the software's tree, with a written explanation for each branch that differs.
activities.risk: Free web-based alignment and tree-building services need no account, and a single projected run can serve a large lecture; the item is BY-NC-SA 4.0 and its downloadable files may carry their own reuse notes.

activities.t: Quotation Audit with a Source-Bound Assistant for a History Essay
activities.sum: Students writing a short argument essay on whether Reconstruction was a revolution, and for whom, use a document-grounded assistant limited to the assigned primary sources as a finding aid, and audit everything it returns before any of it reaches a footnote. The assignment follows the closed-corpus design of Caley Horan's first essay for an MIT survey of United States history since 1865: one historiographical prompt, answered from a fixed set of course sources with at least three primary sources cited. The instructor loads a set of public-domain Reconstruction-era documents, such as congressional testimony, Freedmen's Bureau records, and the amendments, into the assistant. Students ask it where the sources speak to their developing claim, and it answers with quotations and locations. Each returned quotation is checked word for word against the document, read in its surrounding paragraph, and logged as accurate, altered, misattributed, or not found in the source. Only verified passages enter the essay, cited in Chicago style. The audit log is submitted with the draft, and the argument, selection, and interpretation remain the student's.

activities.dl: An argument essay of about 1,250 words with Chicago-style footnotes, submitted with a quotation audit log for every passage the assistant returned.
activities.risk: Only public-domain primary sources are loaded, since the readings attached to the original course need a separate rights check; an instructor-configured or institutional assistant spares students personal accounts, and the documents remain readable without the tool.

activities.t: Handing a Computational Protocol to an Agent to Find Gaps
activities.sum: A researcher who has written up the protocol for a computational step in their own study, such as a preprocessing pipeline or a statistical analysis, gives that protocol to an AI agent and watches where it cannot proceed. The design reworks the practical activity in Rebecca Saxe's Week 3 assignment for a graduate course on robust science, in which a methods section is checked against reporting guidelines and a protocol is written and its snags recorded. Here the agent receives only the written protocol and a synthetic or public sample data set, in a sandboxed environment, and is asked to carry out the steps exactly as written and to report every assumption it makes. Each stall, guess, or silent default is logged: an unstated software version, a parameter the author knew by habit, a file-naming convention never written down. The researcher sorts the log into gaps in the protocol and errors of the agent, revises the protocol, and repeats the run. The revised protocol is then checked against the reporting guideline for the field, and the run logs are kept with the project record.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher decides which stalls and guesses are gaps in their own protocol and which are errors of the agent, and revises the protocol until it meets the field's reporting guideline.
activities.dl: A revised computational protocol with a gap log from each agent run, sorted into omissions in the protocol and errors made by the agent.
activities.risk: Agentic tools that execute code are often paid and need a sandbox; only synthetic or public data are supplied, so unpublished results and participant data stay out of the tool.

activities.t: Rendering a Program Logic Model and Auditing the Picture
activities.sum: A program committee preparing for a review writes its program's logic model as a plain-text specification, has an AI diagramming tool render it, and audits the picture against the text. The work follows the build-and-test procedure in the Community Tool Box section on logic models by Bobby Milstein and Tom Chapel: the committee draws the logic out of existing program documents, listing purpose, context, inputs, activities, outputs, and effects, and writes each link as an if-then statement. The specification goes to a diagram-generating tool, which returns a drawn model. Members compare the two line by line and record every arrow, box, or outcome the tool added, merged, renamed, or dropped. Additions are not discarded on sight: each is accepted, amended, or rejected with a stated reason, since a plausible but unrequested arrow may expose a link the committee had assumed without writing down. The corrected model then goes through the section's forward and reverse logic checks, and each link is labeled by the kind of evaluation question, need, process, outcome, or cost, that would test it. The specification contains program-level information only.
activities.f: Faculty and Staff Development
activities.gate: The committee decides whether each arrow, box or outcome the tool added, merged, renamed or dropped is accepted, amended or rejected, and records the reason for each decision.
activities.dl: A corrected logic model diagram with its text specification and a change log recording each element the tool added, merged, renamed, or dropped and the committee's decision on it.
activities.risk: The specification holds program-level information only, with no student records or personnel details; image output from such tools is often not screen-reader accessible, so the text specification is kept as the accessible version of record.

activities.t: Field Notes Versus a Vision Model on Street Photographs
activities.sum: Public health students conduct a walking survey of a neighborhood and then compare their own field notes with a vision-capable model's coding of the photographs they took. The fieldwork follows the Community Tool Box section on windshield and walking surveys by Phil Rabinowitz: teams of two or three settle guiding questions, build a checklist matched to them, and record housing condition, sidewalks, public spaces, businesses, signage languages, street activity, and transit in notes and photographs. The walk itself is done without AI. Afterward, each team removes faces and license plates from a set of its photographs and asks a multimodal model to code them against the same checklist. The model's codes are set beside the team's notes for the same block. Teams list what the model reported that they missed, what it asserted that the image does not show, and what only presence on the street supplied: sound, smell, who greeted them, what the corner was like at five o'clock. The synthesis of assets, challenges, and differences between neighborhoods rests on the field notes, with the comparison reported as a methods appendix.

activities.risk: The walk requires travel and may raise mobility and safety considerations, so a windshield or transit-based route is an alternative; faces, plates, and house numbers are removed before upload, and photographing residents may call for local review.

activities.t: How a Chatbot Summarizes a Biased 1903 Article
activities.sum: Learners in a research methods course read passages from a 1903 magazine article on left-handedness, identify the assumptions it carries, and then examine what a chatbot does with those assumptions when asked to summarize the same passages. The reading follows Magdalena Grose-Hodge's FORRT lesson on implicit bias and normative science, which starts with a historical text where bias is easy to see before turning to current research writing. After marking the article's claims about gender, race, mental health, and criminality by hand, learners paste the public-domain passages into a conversational assistant and request a plain-language summary. They set the summary beside their own annotations and classify each sentence: the framing is repeated, softened, corrected, flagged, or replaced by a new norm of the model's own. The questions asked of the output are whose voice is carried forward, whose is missing, and what the tool treats as the neutral position. A second prompt asks for a neutral rewrite of one sentence, which is checked against the original for whether the historical claim is still reported accurately. Contemporary abstracts are then read on paper, without the tool.
activities.f: Auditing AI Outputs for Bias, Defaults and Influence
activities.gate: Learners mark the article's assumptions by hand first, classify each summary sentence as repeating, softening, correcting, flagging, or replacing the framing, and check whether a neutral rewrite still reports the historical claim accurately.
activities.dl: An annotated comparison in which each sentence of the AI summary is classified by what it does with the 1903 article's framing, with a short note on the accuracy of one neutral rewrite.
activities.risk: Only public-domain 1903 text is entered, so no copyrighted abstracts or student writing go into the tool; the source text contains offensive claims about several groups, and a single projected account allows participation without individual sign-up.

activities.t: Auditing an AI-Drafted Disclosure Against a Process Log
activities.sum: Students check whether an AI-drafted account of a fictional student's AI use is complete, using that student's process log as the record. The instructor writes the log: a dated sequence of the fictional student's prompts, pasted outputs, source lookups and draft revisions for a short essay in the course's subject. A document-grounded assistant, run by the instructor, receives only that log and is asked for a short disclosure statement on the fictional student's behalf. Working in pairs with printed copies, students trace each sentence of the drafted statement to log entries and list the uses the log shows that the statement omits, softens, or describes more generously than the entries warrant. Each pair then completes York University's AI-Based Tools: Declaration of Use form by hand for the fictional student, using the form as published and without entering it into any tool, and compares its completed form with the assistant's statement and with the instructor's actual course policy. Discussion turns on which omissions would matter under that policy and on what a log needs to contain for a disclosure to be checkable.

activities.t: Tracing an AI Answer's Claims Through Search-Backed Verification
activities.sum: Students take two factual claims from a saved AI answer on a course topic and follow them through a search-enabled assistant to the sources it cites, recording whether each cited page supports the claim. The instructor supplies the saved answer, generated beforehand without web access, so that every student starts from the same text. Each student asks the search-enabled assistant to verify the two chosen claims and then opens every link it returns. In a verification log the student records, for each link, whether the page exists, whether it says what the assistant reports, and whether it is a primary source, a secondary summary, or another machine-written text. The claims are then checked in a library database or the course text, which serves as the reference, and the student notes how relevant each source was to the question asked. With the log complete, students fill in York University's AI Use: Review and Reflection form as published, drawing the specific instances it asks for from their own log entries. The form itself is not entered into any tool.

activities.t: Testing AI Counterfactuals on the Fort Sumter Crisis
activities.sum: After completing Richard Latner's Crisis at Fort Sumter simulation as published, students ask a conversational assistant what would have followed had Lincoln taken a course he did not take, and then test each predicted consequence against the documentary record. The prompt is the student's own: a few sentences naming the alternative, for example evacuating the fort in March 1861, and asking for five consequences with reasons. Nothing from the simulation's pages, adviser texts or commentary is pasted into the tool. Students mark each consequence as supported, unsupported, or anachronistic, citing public-domain evidence: Lincoln's First Inaugural Address, cabinet members' written opinions on provisioning the fort, and correspondence printed in the Official Records. Where the assistant attributes a view to a named figure, students look for that view in the figure's own writing. In the class debrief, groups compare which kinds of claims the assistant handled with support, such as dates, offices and sequence, and which it asserted without evidence, such as motives and public reaction. Each student closes with a paragraph accepting, amending, or rejecting the counterfactual and giving grounds.
activities.f: Arguing With and Against AI
activities.gate: The student marks each predicted consequence supported, unsupported or anachronistic with a cited primary document, and writes a closing paragraph accepting, amending or rejecting the counterfactual with grounds.
activities.dl: An annotated table of the assistant's predicted consequences, each marked supported, unsupported or anachronistic with a primary-source citation, and a closing paragraph of judgment.
activities.risk: The simulation is listed as free of cost, and the primary documents are in the public domain online; rights on the simulation's own site were not established, so it is used by link only.

activities.t: Auditing an AI-Built Epidemic Curve
activities.sum: Students have a code-capable assistant build an epidemic curve and attack-rate table from an instructor-written outbreak dataset, then audit the result against the raw records. The activity follows a session with Outbreak at Watersedge, the public health discovery game, played as published to introduce the sequence of an outbreak investigation; none of the game's case files or other content enters the tool. The instructor's dataset is a fictional foodborne outbreak of about sixty records with onset dates, symptoms, exposures and a few deliberate irregularities: missing onset dates, mixed date formats, and two records that fall outside the stated case definition. The assistant is asked for code that cleans the file, applies the case definition, plots cases by onset date, and computes attack rates by exposure. Students run the code and then recount cases by hand from the line list. They compare the two tallies, find how the code handled each irregular record, and check the attack rates against a two-by-two table built by hand. In the debrief, each group reports which of the code's unannounced choices changed the shape of the curve.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Students recount cases by hand from the line list, build a two-by-two table to check the attack rates, and list how the code handled each irregular record and which choices changed the curve.
activities.dl: An audit memo comparing the generated curve and attack rates with hand counts, listing each data-handling choice the code made and its effect.
activities.risk: The dataset is fictional and instructor-written, so no health data or student work enters a tool; the code can be run in a free browser notebook, and the game is listed as free of cost.

activities.t: Clustering Faculty Concerns About AI After Stinky Fish
activities.sum: At the start of a faculty workshop on AI in teaching, participants complete the Stinky Fish exercise as published on its method page, each writing a concern about AI in their courses that they have been carrying and sharing it briefly with the group. Afterward, with participants' agreement, a facilitator types the written concerns without names into an institutionally hosted assistant, which is asked to group them into themes and name each theme. The method page itself is not entered into the tool. The proposed clusters are projected, and participants check them against the original cards on the wall: each person finds their own card, says whether the theme label fits what they meant, and moves it where it does not. The group records which concerns the assistant merged that their authors consider distinct, and which concerns, held by only one or two people, disappeared into a larger theme. A second pass sorts the corrected themes by whether they concern personal know-how with the tools, the meeting of personal and professional use, or use in teaching itself. The corrected map sets the agenda for the remaining sessions.
activities.f: Faculty and Staff Development
activities.gate: Each participant decides whether the theme given to their own concern fits what they meant, and the group records which distinct concerns were merged and which concerns held by one or two people disappeared into a larger theme.
activities.dl: A corrected theme map of the group's concerns, with a note of clusters the authors split or relabeled, used as the agenda for later sessions.
activities.risk: Concerns are transcribed without names and only with participants' agreement, in an institutionally hosted tool; anyone may keep a card out of the transcription.

activities.t: Second-Coding Panic Language in Historical Newspaper Pages
activities.sum: Students code the language and imagery of public-domain newspaper pages for moral panic features and then compare their coding with that of a multimodal AI model given the same page images. The class first works through the UK Data Service teaching resource on folk devils and moral panics as published, reading the archived materials from Stan Cohen's Mods and Rockers research on the Service's own site; none of those materials is uploaded to any tool. For the coding exercise the instructor selects scanned pages from a public-domain newspaper archive covering an earlier scare, such as 1890s reports on reckless bicycle riders. Each student notes an immediate reaction to a page, then codes it with an instructor-written codebook: who is named as the threat, exaggeration and prediction, calls for control, and how illustrations frame the group. The model receives the same images and codebook. Students tabulate agreement code by code, reread the page wherever they and the model differ, and decide which coding the page supports. A short memo separates what the student felt on first reading from what the text and images on the page show.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: Each student produces an immediate reaction and a coding of each page, decides which coding the page supports wherever student and model differ, and writes a memo separating what they felt on first reading from what the page shows.
activities.dl: A coding table with student and model codes side by side for each page, adjudication notes on every disagreement, and a short memo.
activities.risk: Only public-domain page scans and the instructor's codebook are uploaded; the archived UK Data Service materials carry their own access conditions and are read on that site only.

activities.t: Critiquing AI-Drafted Consent Wording Before Data Deposit
activities.sum: A researcher planning to archive interview data has a conversational assistant draft the data-sharing statements for a consent form and then critiques each draft the way the UK Data Service exercise Assessing consent form statements critiques its nine examples. The researcher begins without the tool, working through the exercise and its answers (Scott, UK Data Archive, 2026) to fix a personal standard for what ambiguous wording, unclear terms, and assurances that cannot realistically be kept look like. The assistant is then given a plain description of the planned study, written by the researcher, and asked for statements on anonymization, reuse, audio recordings, publication, destruction and archiving. For each one the researcher asks the exercise's questions: what this wording would mean for sharing the data, what is problematic or missing, and what wording would be clearer. Statements that promise more than the project can deliver, such as complete anonymity for audio, are rewritten to say plainly what steps will be taken. The revised form is checked clause by clause against the chosen repository's deposit and access conditions and the ethics board's required language.
activities.f: AI Ethics, Governance, Privacy and Public Discourse
activities.gate: The researcher fixes a standard for ambiguous wording and assurances that cannot be kept before using the tool, judges each drafted statement against it, rewrites promises the project cannot deliver, and checks every clause against repository and ethics-board conditions.
activities.dl: A revised consent form with a clause-by-clause note recording what the assistant drafted, what was changed, and the repository or ethics-board condition each clause meets.
activities.risk: Only a general description of the planned study goes into the tool; no participant data, names or unpublished instruments are entered, and the CC BY exercise is free to use with attribution.

activities.t: Voice Rehearsal for Raising a Data Integrity Concern
activities.sum: Graduate students rehearse aloud, with a voice-mode AI assistant playing a senior researcher, the conversation in which a trainee raises a concern about data in a document the senior researcher wrote. The assistant's brief is written by the instructor and uses an original scenario, for example a postdoctoral fellow who finds that a figure in a draft manuscript does not match the lab's shared spreadsheet; the brief has the character offer a plausible explanation and resist requests to see the underlying files. Students work in threes: one speaks with the assistant, one observes with a prepared sheet, one keeps time. The observer notes each point where the speaker accepts an explanation without asking for the data and each point where the speaker names a specific next step. Roles rotate. The group then performs the ORI casebook role play In a Stew over Cooked Data between human partners, using its role materials as published and entering none of them into the tool. The debrief compares the two conversations and checks the steps students proposed against the institution's research misconduct procedure.
activities.f: Simulations, Personas and AI Role-Play
activities.gate: Students in each group of three rotate as speaker, observer, and timekeeper, record where the speaker accepted an explanation or named a next step, and check the next steps they proposed against the institution's misconduct procedure.
activities.dl: A spoken rehearsal and a human role play, each documented on an observer sheet, with a short list of proposed next steps checked against the misconduct procedure.
activities.risk: Voice mode needs a device with a microphone and a reasonably quiet space, and may record speech; a typed version of the rehearsal is an equivalent route for students who prefer not to use voice.

activities.t: Checking an AI Review of a Specific Aims Draft
activities.sum: Graduate students write a one-page specific aims draft for a fictional project in their own field and submit it to a document-grounded assistant that holds the current NIH application instructions, then check every requirement the assistant cites against those instructions. Beforehand, the class reads a funded R21 application posted by the National Cancer Institute, Rebekka Lee's Effective Training Models for Implementing Health-Promoting Practices Afterschool, as a finished example; it is read on the posting page, unchanged, and no part of it is entered into the tool. The assistant is asked to comment on the draft's aims and to give, for each comment, the instruction it relies on and its reasoning. Students mark each comment as grounded in the instructions, as a reviewing convention the instructions do not state, or as unsupported. They then return to the sample and observe how a funded application handled the same point, such as the pairing of an aim with a hypothesis. Revision follows, with a short note on which comments were adopted, which were declined, and why.

activities.gate: Students write their own aims page, mark each comment as grounded in the instructions, a reviewing convention, or unsupported, and revise with a note on which comments they adopted, which they declined, and why.
activities.dl: A revised specific aims page for a fictional project, with an annotated list of the assistant's comments marked grounded, conventional or unsupported.
activities.risk: Drafts describe fictional projects, so no unpublished research ideas enter a tool; the NCI sample is restricted to unchanged, credited, nonprofit educational use and is read at its posting page.

activities.t: Auditing an Agentic Folder Reorganization With a Checklist
activities.sum: A researcher lets an agentic AI tool reorganize a working copy of a project folder and then audits what it did using the research data management checklist from The Turing Way. The copy is made first and the original set to read-only, following the checklist's item on leaving raw data untouched with a backup; sensitive or consent-restricted files are left out of the copy. The tool is asked to propose and apply a folder structure and naming convention, write a README, and keep a log of every action. The researcher then works down the checklist's individual list and its research-team list, credited there to Borghi and van Gulick (2022): could every group member find and use the materials, are naming conventions and folder structures in place, is documentation kept with the data, could an outside researcher use what is there. A file-by-file comparison of the copy with the original, using checksums, shows whether any data file was altered and which changes the tool made without logging them. Changes that pass the audit are applied to the real project by hand.
activities.f: Research Methods and Scholarly Information Workflows
activities.gate: The researcher decides which of the tool's changes pass the checklist and the checksum comparison, identifies any it made without logging, and applies only the approved changes to the real project by hand.
activities.dl: A scored checklist for the reorganized copy, a list of unlogged or data-altering changes, and a set of changes approved for the real project.
activities.risk: Agentic tools often require a paid plan and broad file permissions; the audit runs on a copy that excludes sensitive or consent-restricted data, and nothing is changed in the original.

activities.t: Reviewing AI-Written Code With a Review Checklist
activities.sum: Students act as code reviewers for a small analysis function and test suite written by a code assistant, using the file-level questions in The Turing Way's Checklist for code review process. Each student specifies a function from the course's current material, for instance one that computes a rolling mean over a time series with missing values, and has the assistant produce the function and its unit tests. The student opens a pull request containing the generated code and reviews it as the checklist's reviewer role describes: whether inputs are checked, loops terminate, interfaces and types are clear, and the unit tests test what they claim. Students write additional tests for edge cases the generated tests skip, such as empty input or a window longer than the series, and run both sets. Program-level items are applied as well, including whether the licenses of all imported libraries are documented and compatible. The review ends with a written decision to approve, request changes, or reject, with each finding tied to a checklist item and a test result. Reviews are then presented to a small group, which questions the reviewer's decision.
activities.f: Verifying AI Output: Facts, Sources and Fabrication
activities.gate: The student writes the specification, adds tests for edge cases the generated tests skip, and decides to approve, request changes or reject, tying each finding to a checklist item and a test result, then defends it before a small group.
activities.dl: A written code review on a pull request, with added tests, findings keyed to checklist items, and an approve, request-changes or reject decision.
activities.risk: A free code assistant and a free repository host are sufficient, though both typically need an account; students' specifications, not graded work, are what enter the assistant.

activities.attr: “Checklist for code review process” by The Turing Way Community, The Turing Way research-practice handbook, https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/reviewing/reviewing-checklist.
